While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 6, 2026
Putin tells US envoys situation in Ukraine is ‘difficult’
Russian President Vladimir Putin met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the Kremlin on Sept 5, telling them at the start of the talks that the situation in Ukraine is “difficult”.
Putin praised US President Donald Trump’s efforts to end the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine.
Trump suggested on Sept 4 that the US had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war. He did not elaborate.
Russian state media said the talks lasted about three hours, and published video of the American motorcade leaving the Kremlin. There was no immediate comment from either side.
US military strikes oil tankers as Iran vows tougher reprisals
The United States said it destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Sept 5 in response to attempted missile attacks on naval vessels, prompting Iran’s military to warn of tougher reprisals if the strikes continued.
The latest round of clashes, which began with US raids last week, comes with both sides deadlocked in the six-month war as Iran maintains its stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz and Washington presses its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
In addition to the renewed military action, Washington is seeking to choke Iran’s economy, announcing sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic republic in a bid to further isolate it and force it into submission.
Algerian boy trapped in well for days found dead
Rescuers in Algeria on Sept 5 recovered the body of a 10-year-old boy who was trapped inside a well for four days, civil protection authorities said.
Efforts to rescue the boy, whom authorities identified only by his first name, Ayoub, had drawn widespread attention across the country, and social media was awash with calls to save him.
On the evening of Sept 5, however, the civil protection announced that “the child was found and recovered dead”.
Fernandez impresses on debut for Manchester City
Manchester City’s post-Rodri era is still in its infancy, but Enzo Fernandez offered a tantalising glimpse of the future on Sept 5 when the Argentine marked his surprise debut by helping to fire City to a 1-0 Premier League win over Coventry City.
Fernandez, signed from Chelsea on transfer deadline day for a British record-equalling £125 million (S$214 million), was not expecting to start until Nico O’Reilly suffered a back problem during the warm-up.
Thrown into the lineup at the last minute, the Argentina midfielder responded with a composed and influential display that underlined why City moved quickly to secure his signature.
Oasis bring swagger to Venice Film Festival
Liam Gallagher pumped his fist in the air and his brother Noel flashed a victory sign as the Oasis rock stars arrived by water taxi at the Venice Film Festival on Sept 5 ahead of a documentary chronicling their blockbuster reunion tour.
Asked by a Reuters reporter how it felt to be in Venice, Liam replied: “Biblical man, biblical.”
Noel opted for a more Italian response: “Bellissimo.”

Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald V
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:11:21 UTC
07:11:21 KST

The Prince of Wales is to represent his father at the funeral of King Harald V of Norway next week, Buckingham Palace has announced.
William, the heir to the throne, will be joined by his aunt the Princess Royal, who is attending in a private and personal capacity as godmother of the new king, Haakon VIII.
Norway has seen an outpouring of grief for the much-loved late monarch, who died on 28 August at the age of 89.
Harald has been hailed as an inclusive “people’s king” who modernised the Norwegian monarchy during his 35-year reign.
His funeral will take place on 9 September at Oslo Cathedral, with mourners including his widow, Sonja, now the queen mother.
In keeping with precedent that the sovereign does not attend funerals of other heads of state, the duty falls to William, a future king, to represent his father and pay his respects at the service.
Charles paid a touching tribute to his “dear cousin” and “much-loved kinsman and friend” after the news of Harald’s death was announced.
In a message of condolence, he praised Harald’s “unwavering dedication” and his “kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades”.
The late Queen Elizabeth II and King Harald were second cousins. They shared the same great-grandparents, King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra.
In April last year, William represented his father at the funeral of Pope Francis in the Vatican.
William and the now Princess of Wales carried out an official tour to Norway in 2018, dining with King Harald and Queen Sonja at the Royal Palace, where Harald described them as “family” and praised their support of the then Queen.
The Norwegian sovereign processed into the banquet arm in arm with the pregnant Catherine, who was expecting Prince Louis and wearing a flowing Alexander McQueen gown, with the gesture mirrored by Sonja and William who walked behind them.
William and Kate also spent time visiting the ski slopes with the then Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit, now the King and Queen.

German rocket reaches space as Europe enters satellite launch race

German rocket reaches space as Europe enters satellite launch race
Isar Aerospace, which launched its rocket from a spaceport in Norway, plans to offer a commercial satellite launch service
German start-up Isar Aerospace on Saturday launched its first rocket into space from a site in Arctic Norway, bringing Europe closer to offering satellite flights from its own soil.
The uncrewed Spectrum rocket was the first commercial flight to reach orbit from continental Europe, where several nations have said they want a share of a growing market for space missions.
“We’re in orbit! And just made European history,” Isar said in a post on social media.
The event was a breakthrough for the European launch industry, giving the continent better access to space, Norway’s minister of industry and commerce, Cecilie Myrseth, said in a statement.
“The fact that we can now launch satellites from Andoeya strengthens Norwegian and European security in the turbulent times we live in,” Myrseth said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Isar’s launch site in March, underscoring Europe’s efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the United States is shifting under US President Donald Trump.
Blasting off from Norway’s Arctic Andoeya Spaceport, the uncrewed Spectrum, designed for small and medium-sized payloads, carried five small satellites as well as an in-flight technological experiment, according to Isar.

US Envoys Head To Kyiv After  Stop In Moscow, Late-Night Meeting With Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:03:14 UTC
07:03:14 KST

KYIV -- After a day of crucial meetings in Moscow, including with President Vladimir Putin, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are switching wartime venues, heading to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy with aims of ending the conflict now in its fifth year.
Russian state news agency RIA Novosti reported that talks between the envoys and Putin lasted about three hours, with the US representatives leaving the Kremlin at about 11 p.m. on September 5. Shortly after midnight, TASS reported the Americans had departed Moscow.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, who participated in the session, called the talks "substantive, very frank, and constructive." He added that the envoys stated the US position and promised to present Putin's views to Ukrainian leaders during their talks in Kyiv.
"They not only expressed their traditional interest in bringing the hostilities to a quick end, they put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement," he said.
Ushakov insisted Russia would achieve its goals and that the "root causes" of the conflict must be resolved, Kremlin code for putting an end to Ukraine's hopes of NATO membership and steps to effectively disarm the Ukrainian military, among other historical grievances -- items Kyiv has long rejected.
There was no official US comment immediately after the meeting.
As the session started near 8 p.m., RIA Novosti quoted Putin as saying the three men would have to address a "difficult situation" during their Kremlin discussions.
The meeting appeared to get a late start after Putin spent the day opening a new subway line in Moscow, inaugurating a Siberian oil terminal by video link, and meeting with members of the ruling United Russia party.
US President Donald Trump had said the envoys would be presenting a peace deal to the Russians and then would relay the offer to Ukraine the next day.
Trump said Washington had "an idea for peace" and that his envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war," now in its fifth year since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done, and there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on September 4.
'Diplomatic Activities
Zelenskyy said he had spoken to the envoys on September 5, revealing few details about the call but saying that "the plan of diplomatic activities for tomorrow in Kyiv with the participation of the American team has been approved."
"We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a meaningful conversation," Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
The US envoys' visit to Kyiv would mark their first visit to Ukraine since taking leading roles in the administration's efforts to end the war and come amid a renewed diplomatic push aimed at reaching a peace agreement.
Trump made ending the largest war in Europe since 1945 a priority when he took office in January 2025, but an agreement has been elusive, and diplomacy had been largely stalled since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February.
Reflecting the hard-line stance put forward by Ushakov, Putin has shown no sign of compromise in recent comments, among other things insisting that Russia must control all of eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, including the parts its forces have failed to capture in years of heavy fighting.
Before the envoys departed the US, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces would "ensure the normal functioning of Russia airspace so that the negotiators can arrive there safely" and demanded that Moscow reciprocate.
Following his September 5 call with the envoys, Zelenskyy said that "from now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow."
Putin subsequently ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv from September 6-8, according to spokesman Dmitry Peskov, who made no mention of other parts of Ukraine amid reports that Russia had continued its attacks elsewhere.
Airport Attacks
Zelenskyy said Russian forces had targeted Kyiv's Zhulyany and Boryspil airports overnight on September 4-5, accusing Moscow of seeking to create uncertainty over the US envoys' planned journey to Ukraine.
The Kyiv visit will come just days after a Russian drone strike hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service -- known as the SBU and a key agency that would be responsible for the US envoys' safety during a visit.
"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said on X , adding there would be "no threats to diplomacy" from the Ukrainian side.
Flying into Kyiv would be highly unusual. Ukrainian airspace has been closed to regular civilian flights since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and visiting foreign leaders and officials have generally reached the capital by train.

Massive review confirms the connection between emotional intelligence and human flourishing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

A review of psychological research indicates that emotional intelligence has a robust and reliable connection to human flourishing, predicting success across school, work, and personal health. The findings suggest that people with higher emotional intelligence tend to experience greater well-being, though the strength of this connection depends on how the traits are measured. The research was recently published in the journal PNAS.
For decades, psychologists have debated what makes some people thrive while others struggle. One popular idea is emotional intelligence, a concept that rapidly gained public attention in the 1990s. Broadly speaking, the term refers to how well a person navigates their own feelings and the feelings of others.
Since its introduction, the idea has spawned thousands of academic papers and grown into a multibillion-dollar training industry. Yet, because researchers define and measure this concept in various ways, its exact relationship with life success has remained difficult to synthesize.
Psychologists generally divide emotional intelligence into three categories. The first is an ability-based model. This model treats emotional skills like a cognitive test, assuming there are objectively right and wrong answers when identifying or managing emotions.
The ability model specifically looks at how well people recognize emotions, use them to guide decisions, and regulate them. The second category is a trait-based model, which relies on self-reported personality characteristics. Under this model, researchers ask participants to rate their own adaptability, assertiveness, and impulse control.
A third category, called a mixed model, combines both objective abilities and self-reported traits into a single assessment. Beyond the differing definitions of emotional intelligence, researchers also look at a wide variety of life outcomes. To find out how these different models connect to positive life experiences, researchers Tyler J. Robinson and Ethan Zell from the University of North Carolina at Greensboro analyzed decades of data.
The researchers wanted to see if emotional intelligence consistently relates to human flourishing. Flourishing is a broad psychological term encompassing mental health, physical health, psychological adjustment, and workplace success. To answer this question, Robinson and Zell conducted a second-order meta-analysis.
A standard meta-analysis is a statistical technique that pools the results of many individual studies to find an overall trend. A second-order meta-analysis goes a step further, combining the results of multiple previous meta-analyses. This approach acts as a quantitative summary of previous summaries, providing a broad view of an entire scientific field.
By pooling data from 62 previous meta-analyses, the researchers gathered information from more than 3,000 individual studies. This massive sample included over one million participants, allowing the researchers to look for overarching patterns across different ages and cultures. The data included populations from Western nations, non-Western nations, children, adolescents, and adults.
The researchers found a reliable, positive association between overall emotional intelligence and human flourishing. This positive link appeared across 77 unique life outcomes. The most prominent associations emerged in areas like workplace leadership, job performance, and psychological adjustment.
The data showed that emotional intelligence was linked to better outcomes regardless of the participants’ age group or geographic region. When looking at different categories of life outcomes, the researchers noticed slight variations in the strength of the connection. Emotional intelligence was most strongly related to success in the workplace.
The connection was slightly weaker, though still reliably present, for cognitive abilities and general academic performance. The researchers also found strong associations between emotional intelligence and specific outcomes like lower rates of job burnout, higher subjective well-being, and better romantic relationship satisfaction.
To put these findings into perspective, the researchers compared emotional intelligence to the Big Five personality traits. The Big Five is a well-established psychological framework that measures openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. The analysis revealed that emotional intelligence is just as strongly, if not more strongly, associated with human flourishing than any of the Big Five personality traits.
Out of all the specific outcomes analyzed, only one showed a negative relationship with emotional intelligence. That outcome was a form of self-centeredness known as nonpathological narcissism. The researchers noted that individuals with this specific type of narcissism tend to artificially inflate their own scores on self-report questionnaires.
Because they overrate their own emotional abilities, the data showed an inverse relationship between their actual traits and their reported emotional intelligence. More conventional, pathological narcissism was linked to lower emotional intelligence. Measurement styles heavily altered the broader results as well.
The association with human flourishing was most pronounced when researchers used the mixed or trait-based models, which rely on participants rating their own emotional skills. When studies used objective performance tests to measure emotional abilities, the association with life outcomes was weaker. This pattern became especially apparent when looking at how both emotional intelligence and life outcomes were measured.
The researchers found the strongest connections when both variables were assessed using self-report questionnaires. When one variable was measured subjectively and the other was measured objectively, the relationship between the two shrunk considerably. This dependence on measurement methods highlights an important limitation in the data.
When participants fill out multiple surveys about themselves, they may naturally rate themselves positively across the board. This shared method of data collection can artificially inflate the statistical connection between self-reported emotional intelligence and self-reported life satisfaction. The researchers noted that the particularly strong link to workplace outcomes might be partly driven by this shared measurement style, as many workplace studies rely on self-reported surveys.
Because the data in this review is entirely correlational, it cannot prove that high emotional intelligence causes a person to flourish. It is entirely possible that flourishing in life makes a person more emotionally intelligent over time. Alternatively, a third unmeasured factor, such as a stable upbringing or access to resources, could independently contribute to both higher emotional intelligence and greater life success.
The researchers also excluded studies that evaluated training programs. Because of this exclusion, they could not determine if actively training emotional intelligence causes a subsequent increase in human flourishing. Objective tests of emotional intelligence also face modern challenges.
The authors pointed out that recent studies show artificial intelligence language models perform just as well as, or better than, humans on objective emotional intelligence tests. This raises questions about what these tests are actually measuring. It remains debated whether text-based tests capture practical emotional skills or if they simply measure a person’s reading comprehension and ability to understand written scenarios.
To improve the quality of future research, the authors suggest refining how emotional intelligence is categorized. They recommend moving away from the mixed model, which blends traits and abilities in a way that creates conceptual confusion. Instead, they suggest that future studies explicitly separate objective emotional abilities from self-reported personality traits. Separating these variables would help scientists determine exactly how distinct emotional skills contribute to a fulfilling life.
The study, “Robust associations of emotional intelligence with human flourishing: A second-order meta-analysis,” was authored by Tyler J. Robinson and Ethan Zell.

With bare hands, lone warrior cleans up dumpyard of a river
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:45:40 UTC
06:45:40 KST

21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown
BHOPAL: His online followers know him as 'Bittu Tabahi'. In reality, Surendra Singh Choudhary is the exact opposite of what the moniker 'Tabahi', meaning destruction, implies.For the past seven months, this 21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown, Biaora in MP's Rajgarh district, picking up plastic bottles, tangled weeds and other solid waste from Ajnar river, which had virtually become a dumpyard.With no heavy machinery or protective gear at his disposal, he removed the garbage with his bare hands, often at great risk to his health.Bittu's dogged pursuit has helped restore a section of the river, earning him widespread praise across the country and an invite from CM Mohan Yadav Saturday. They had a warm exchange at the CM's residence in Bhopal, where Yadav assured Bittu of every possible support from govt.The chief minister also shared a video on X, calling Bittu a "son of Biaora" who not only restored Ajnala (the river stretch passing through Biaora) to its original form through sheer resolve and effort, but also sent out a larger message that one man's determination is all it takes to bring meaningful change.
There were also reports that the CEO of an organisation from the Netherlands had offered him a job, but Bittu said he had only heard this from media reports. "I am yet to receive any information about it first hand," he told TOI.Encouraged by his success, Bittu, whose parents work in the health department, has decided to expand his work. "My sole objective is to keep my hometown clean. I have decided to take my work to other public places," he said.Bittu started his mission on Republic Day this year. Upset that everyone complained about the mess, but none - including the municipal administration - addressed it, the college-goer decided to get his hands dirty. From removing garbage piles on streets to pulling out weeds from water bodies, his activism eventually drew national attention.
Unfortunately, his selfless service is being undone by the same people he is trying to help. In his interaction with the chief minister, Bittu shared the pain of watching people throw garbage into the river again, oblivious to the effort that went into cleaning it. "I don't know why people keep dumping waste into the river," he said, his voice betraying anger.The silver lining is that the local municipal corporation has now woken up to its civic mandate, and has deployed JCBs and Poclain machines to clear waste piles from the streets. However, the larger problem - habitual littering and a lack of collective ownership - remains unaddressed.

Putin praises Moscow’s role in supporting Russian troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05

06:45:19 KST

Putin praises Moscow’s role in supporting Russian troops
Russian President Vladimir Putin has praised Moscow’s contribution to the country’s military and technological development, declaring that Russia will overcome the challenges it faces because they are “temporary and transient.”
The president made the remarks during an address marking Moscow’s 879th birthday, traditionally celebrated in early September. Putin congratulated residents of the capital and Russians across the country, describing Moscow as a symbol of Russian statehood, unity and resilience.
“Together with all citizens of our country, we will overcome any difficulty and any challenge. They are temporary and transient, while Moscow and Russia are eternal,” Putin said.
He drew parallels between the challenges facing the country today and key episodes in its history, including the 1812 French invasion and the Battle of Moscow against Nazi Germany in 1941.
“Today, the capital, together with the entire country, has mobilized all its forces, like 85 years ago, for the sake of the common rightful cause. Tens of thousands of Muscovites are fighting against the neo-Nazis on the line of engagement, advancing and displaying valour, courage and heroism.”
Putin highlighted Moscow’s contribution to Russia’s military-industrial sector, saying more than 450 defense plants, high-tech enterprises and companies in the capital are producing goods for the needs of the armed forces.
Moscow hospitals are also playing a major role in treating and rehabilitating wounded servicemen, Putin said, while specialists from the capital are involved in reconstruction efforts in Donbass.

More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:44:19 UTC
06:44:19 KST

More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup.
Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican.
That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times.
The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash.
Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times.
But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times.
Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic.
A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

Thousands at Jaguar Land Rover to be offered redundancies after falling profits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:42:11 UTC
06:42:11 KST

Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies after Britain’s largest car manufacturer had its revenues slashed by falling sales, a cyber-attack and Donald Trump’s tariffs.
JLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.
As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.
Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.
About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.
The job cuts will be unwelcome news for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who has pledged to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain.
Under his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Labour said it would underwrite a £1.5bn loan guarantee to JLR after it halted production for several weeks last year in response to a cyber-attack.
The attack led to a 27% drop in overall production and cost the company about £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLR posting a profit before tax of just £14m – down from £2.5bn the year before.
Tariffs on vehicles imported into the US – which Trump raised to 25% before agreeing a deal for 10% for the UK – also caused turmoil for the carmaker, which is attempting to push more luxury cars to the US market. This contributed to the company’s retail and wholesale volumes – sales via dealerships – falling by about 70,000 and 90,000 respectively.
“These challenges arrived with the global automotive industry already under continued pressure from cost inflation, slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles, and the deterioration of market conditions in China,” Balaji said in the company’s annual report published in May.
The carmaker this week launched its first electric Range Rover in an effort to appeal to climate-conscious fans of the luxury SUV – at a starting price of £154,070.

Gen Z is turning filial piety into a career path
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:30:06 UTC
06:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Gen Z is turning filial piety into a career path
Tough job and housing markets have graduates questioning whether the old bargain of hard work bringing progress and stability still applies
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Dr Ken Ip is an assistant professor specialising in business innovation and entrepreneurship at Saint Francis University, Hong Kong. 
Hong Kong has always had a simple answer to what young people should do with their lives: study hard, get a job, work harder, buy a flat and eventually complain about the next generation. That formula is becoming harder to sell.
A whole lexicon has grown up around Generation Z’s uneasy relationship with work. In mainland China, there are “full-time children”, young adults who stay home and receive an allowance from their parents in return for doing household chores and running errands. Elsewhere, there is the “kangaroo tribe”, an updated version of adults remaining financially dependent on their parents. There are Neets, or young people not in education, employment or training.
While the labels differ, the underlying phenomenon is harder to ignore. More young adults are struggling to make the traditional transition to independence.
Hong Kong offers an especially revealing case. Consider university graduates with a respectable degree and little work experience. They apply for dozens of jobs, perhaps hundreds, only to find that “entry level” increasingly means “entry level for someone who already has experience”.
Employers want experienced workers, but young people need jobs to gain that experience. A position for fresh graduates can demand several years of achievements before an applicant has even had a chance to begin.
Against this backdrop, becoming a full-time child looks less absurd than it sounds. If a young adult can stay at home, avoid Hong Kong’s punishing housing costs, receive an allowance and help around the house, why rush into a poorly paid job with little security and even less prospect of progression?

CBI has filed an FIR against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra
NEW DELHI: CBI has filed an FIR against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and some other individuals for allegedly defrauding LICHFL (LIC Housing Finance Ltd) of Rs 1,322 crore between 2018 and 2026. LICHFL alleged that Chandra had submitted a 'net worth certificate' of Rs 59,113 crore in 2018 while availing credit facilities but in 2024 stated that his net worth was just Rs 31.7 crore. The FIR was registered on a complaint filed by LICHFL on Aug 31.According to the FIR, LICHFL had sanctioned two loan facilities totalling Rs 980 crore to four companies. A Rs 500-crore facility was sanctioned to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt Ltd and Pan India Infraprojects Pvt Ltd, while another Rs 480 crore was given to Digital Subscriber Management and Consultancy Services Pvt Ltd and Spirit Infrapower and Multiventures Pvt Ltd.Chandra denied possessing net worth stated in certificatesBoth facilities were backed by personal guarantees furnished by Essel Group chairman Subhash Chandra. The complaint alleged that the loans were sanctioned on the basis of net-worth certificates submitted on behalf of Chandra. One certificate, issued in March 2018, allegedly showed his net worth at $6,197.6 million, equivalent to around Rs 59,113 crore, as of March 31, 2017.
Another certificate put his net worth at Rs 40,562 crore.However, the complaint stated, during the subsequent insolvency proceedings, Subhash Chandra had denied possessing the net worth reflected in the certificates. He allegedly stated that his net worth in 2024 was Rs 31.79 crore and that even in 2017-18 it had not exceeded Rs 40,000 crore.
The outstanding amount against the Vasant Sagar facility was stated to be Rs 570.50 crore, while Rs 507.25 crore was outstanding against the Digital Subscriber facility.LICHFL alleged that Chandra, in collusion with the borrower companies and their directors, induced the housing finance company to release the funds by submitting false and inflated documents. It further alleged that the funds were subsequently misappropriated and assets were stripped to frustrate recovery efforts.

Crime gangs use bots to lure young men in sextortion scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:23:26 UTC
06:23:26 KST

Crime gangs use bots in sexual extortion of young Australian men
In short:
Young Australian men are being targeted by criminal organisations, usually operating from overseas, in sexual extortion attempts.
South Australia Police said three in four sextortion victims were men, with a similar national trend.
Cybercrime and youth mental health advocates say destigmatisation and conversations in school and at home can help young people navigate the risk of sextortion and image-based abuse.
Criminal gangs continue to have Australian men and boys in their sights as targets for sexual extortion, with more than $200,000 defrauded from victims in one state.
Sextortion usually involve scammers 'catfishing' victims into sending intimate pictures of themselves, which are then used to solicit money or more explicit material.
South Australia Police received reports from 220 male victims of image-based abuse and sextortion in the last financial year, up from 170 in the previous period.
Financial losses in these crimes reached $217,000 in 2025-26, according to police who said the spike was "significantly influenced" by a small number of incidents, including one victim who was extorted $53,000.
"These offenders deliberately exploit fear, embarrassment and urgency, and we want victims to know they should not give in to those demands," said SA Police Cybercrime Investigation Section Sergeant David Mitchell.
Male victims, largely aged under 25, accounted for 75 per cent of sextortion reports to SA Police, and nationally it was a similar story.
While women were twice as likely to experience image-based abuse, men were over-represented — almost 90 per cent — as sextortion victims, according to Australia's eSafety Commissioner.
The eSafety Commissioner said scammers deliberately lured young men by using AI to generate fake but attractive online characters.
Blackmailers also used intimate photos and identity information from previous victims to build credibility with new targets.
"Financial sexual extortion often targets young men, with criminals tricking victims into sharing intimate images of themselves before demanding money and threatening to expose the images to family, friends or the general public," an eSafety Commissioner spokesperson said.
The targeting of young men has been around for a number of years, said Nicola Palfrey, Head of Clinical Practice at the youth mental health organisation Headspace Australia.
"We think of a lot of image-based abuse being targeted at younger women or female-identifying people, but unfortunately there's also quite a lot of targeting of young men in this space," she said.
An Australian Institute of Criminology (AIC) report found more than one in 10 adolescents aged 16-18 had experienced sexual extortion in their lifetime, and only a small fraction reported it to authorities.
Crime gangs behind bots
The report also showed while people known to victims can be responsible for non-consensual sharing of intimate images, sextortion attempts were often sophisticated acts by online perpetrators who the victims have never met in person.
"They're crime gangs … the research and evidence is really clear on that," Ms Palfrey said.
These gangs, like the Nigeria-based network known as the Yahoo Boys, often used fake accounts on platforms like Tinder, Instagram and Grindr to target victims.
Generative AI, face-swapping and voice-cloning technologies were also used to create increasingly realistic lures, the eSafety Commissioner said.
Large language models have also enabled scammers to industrialise their business model, said Rahat Masood, a cybersecurity researcher at UNSW.
"Most of these accounts are created by the social bots," Dr Masood said.
"At the back end, it's the human, but all these accounts have been created by the bots using some scripts.
"It's really easy to generate it now."
Once they engage a victim, scammers will move communications to encrypted messaging apps like WhatsApp or Telegram to continue the deception, eSafety found.
According to the AIC, around two in five adolescent victims have had non-intimate images of themselves run through generative AI to create sexualised fakes.
Avoiding tragedy requires community awareness
Ms Palfrey said the consequences of sextortion can be tragic, the most extreme included suicide and self harm.
"We've had documented cases where families have been generous enough and concerned enough about this phenomenon to share their stories where young people have taken their lives as a result of exploitation, being feeling cornered, and things escalating very quickly," she said.
Ms Palfrey said the threat of criminal activity in online spaces presented an opportunity for families to open conversations similar to discussions of puberty, romantic relationships and transitioning to adulthood.
"Online and offline worlds are not separate for young people,"
"How you navigate relationships, consent, trust, transparency, all of those sorts of things need to integrate the online and offline worlds … and there's a space where we have some wisdom, or some experience, or some reassurance to give young people about how they navigate that."
The eSafety Commissioner's most recent campaigns have been tailored to assist young male victims, while Dr Masood said some interventions could start in the classroom.
"We need to do more curriculum-based awareness," he said.
"In our education from the primary school to the high school, we need to include that. Early intervention in the case is extremely important."
A spokesperson for the eSafety Commissioner said they were "deeply concerned" about the impacts of sexual extortion, which has rapidly become "'a critical online safety issue" over the last few years.
They recommend victims report any offending to police or the eSafety Commissioner, block the perpetrator and get support when they fall victim to sextortion.

Govt has issued office memoranda making Aadhaar linking mandatory several times
Over 3,100 DBT schemes and 360 public services use Aadhaar-based authentication. Yet the bureaucracy that demands Aadhaar from citizens, often the poorest, has resisted linking their own Central Govt Health Scheme cards to Aadhaar.CGHS beneficiaries include serving and retired central govt employees and family members, sitting and former MPs, sitting and retired judges of SC and HCs, accredited journalists in DelhiAadhaar linking "has helped state ensure targeted, transparent and leak-proof delivery while eliminating duplicate and ineligible beneficiaries," said PIB. However, bureaucrats aren't walking the talk.What’s must for poor is voluntary for babusThere is no annual verification to weed out dead pensioners or their dependents who might have become ineligible. Two other central govt health schemes, the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme and the railway health scheme, have made it mandatory to link Aadhaar.Govt has issued office memoranda making Aadhaar linking mandatory several times starting from June 2015, but has had to withdraw it in the face of stiff resistance from its employees.The last such withdrawal happened in July 2024 when the govt was forced to keep the directive to link CGHS beneficiary ID with Ayushman Bharat Health account ID (ABHA ID), created using Aadhaar, “in abeyance till further orders”.
The linkage has since been made voluntary for central govt employees, though it is mandatory for a poor woman to get Rs 300 as daily wage under the employment guarantee scheme.While Aadhaar has been mandated for “welfare schemes funded from the Consolidated Fund of India”, including many DBT sche-mes, babus have been arguing that CGHS is a contributory scheme and not a DBT scheme, despite 90% of spending on the scheme coming from the Consolidated Fund of India.
Their contributions amount to a tiny part of the annual expenditure on the scheme.CGHS incidentally has a higher per capita expenditure when compared to ECHS and the railway health scheme. It would be even higher if deceased beneficiaries and ineligible dependents were weeded out. Pensioner cards made at the start of computerisation of CGHS in 2005 remain active in the system without any checks increasing the chances of fraud and misuse of such cards.

America’s political maps are shifting. So is who can win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

American Evolution
America’s political maps are shifting. So is who can win
The weight of a new era is pressing in. The second Trump presidency is unfolding against the backdrop of escalating political tensions, geoeconomic disruption and shifting demographics. Can the US adapt quickly enough? ST’s US bureau chief Bhagyashree Garekar reports as America celebrates its 250th anniversary in 2026.
- America's racial history still affects politics today, seen in towns like Vidor and ongoing tensions over voting rights and racial representation.
- Recent Supreme Court rulings have accelerated redistricting efforts that reduce black-majority districts, threatening black political representation in Congress.
- Despite challenges, black political ambition grows, with record numbers running for governor and efforts to build cross-racial coalitions to influence future electoral maps.
AI generated
VIDOR, Texas – A 10-minute detour to get to a cheaper hotel on a drive from Houston to Philadelphia led me to a “sundown town”.
That may evoke sunsets and beaches in a resort town. But that illusion was quickly dispelled. This label had overtones of menace, I soon discovered.
Waiting at the front desk to get the room keys, I asked what I thought was a casual question – what’s this place like?
The young receptionist, with hair swept up in a blonde ponytail, went quiet. “Well, it doesn’t have the best history for black and brown people,” she said after a beat.
“They say it was a sundown town. But I’ve been here for two years, and it’s all fine now,” she added quickly. “It has a reputation – I don’t know that it’s deserved.”
That was my abrupt introduction to Vidor, tagged for decades as the “most hate-filled town in Texas”. Curious to learn more, I googled local news. Only a few crime reports turned up, none too recent. And nothing leapt out during a late evening drive around the town, just modest low-rise houses, small shops and fast food restaurants.
A “sundown” sign that bluntly warned “whites only within city limits after dark” was reportedly removed from Vidor only some time in the 1970s or the 1980s. In scattered mentions on social media, some black motorists say they grew up being told to avoid Vidor and that, even now, they would not consider stopping there for a bite to eat or to refuel.
A database maintained by an educational site hosted by Tougaloo College, a historically black institution in Mississippi, says sundown towns numbered in the thousands and were found across the US from the late 19th century to the mid-20th century.
It’s not just the blacks who were kept out. Jews, Hispanics, Native Americans, Mormons and Asian Americans were also unwelcome in that era. The “Delta Chinese”, recruited to work on cotton plantations in Mississippi, suffered decades of segregation.
Vidor residents and officials claim things are vastly different now. They say it’s unfair to tarnish the town in 2026. The last bit of substantial nastiness was in the early 1990s over a federal judge’s order to desegregate the city’s public housing. In response, four black families moved in but eventually left after facing sustained hostilities from the white supremacist organisation, the Ku Klux Klan.
In 2020, at the height of the Black Lives Matter movement, a rally in the town drew a supportive crowd, mostly white. Some counter-protesters also showed up, with loaded guns and confederate flags, a controversial symbol of southern pride and also slavery. They shouted that it was the black rights movement that was racist because all lives mattered. A vivid account of that rally won The Economist a Pulitzer Prize in 2021.
The town, which wears a dour look, as though trying without success to surmount its past, remains nearly all-white today. Blacks count for a mere 0.3 per cent of residents. Its population peaked at 11,800 in 1980 and has been shrinking since.
Vidor may be the outlier, but in travels through several southern states – Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee – I saw evidence of America’s racial past still tailgating its present.
In a country where 14 per cent of the population is black, the second-biggest racial or ethnic minority after the Hispanics, the upcoming midterm elections have become more than the usual face-off between the Republicans and the Democrats.
Bigger and more basic questions appear to be on the ballot in the 250th year of American independence: who can vote, whose votes can make a difference, who actually belongs.
There is no official nationwide count yet of the black candidates running for Congress in 2026. And a few states are still to hold their primary nominating contests. But in 2025, 67 black lawmakers took the oath at Capitol Hill. Mostly Democrats, they were the largest black delegation in American history.
That progress – a fourfold increase from the figure in 1975 – mostly came from states redrawing congressional maps over the decades to create black-majority districts that could elect black candidates.
Those hard-won gains could be reversed in a matter of months, in a coordinated and wide-ranging exercise that has the power of the US Supreme Court behind it.
Analysts expect the Nov 3 midterm elections to produce the largest-ever decline in black representation in Congress after a number of states recently redrew their maps to eliminate black-majority districts.
The road from Selma
For miles on end, there were only a few cars on a scenic drive in late March from Selma to Montgomery, two of the most storied cities in the black civil rights movement.
Both lie on the muddy-brown Alabama River, connected by a bridge named after a 19th century Ku Klux Klan leader. One of the cities challenged where black Americans could sit and the other whether they could vote and wield political power.
Alabama’s capital, Montgomery, known for its white neoclassical buildings with columns, symmetrical facades and broad steps, looked ceremonial but forlorn. Its downtown yields layers of history but has suffered destructive tornadoes over the years, and some streets were closed for repairs. Gang fights and gun violence have been on the rise.
A plaque marks the spot where Rosa Parks boarded a public bus and refused to yield her seat for a white passenger, her rebellion sparking a mass protest that forced the authorities to end segregation on the city’s buses in 1956. It also brought to the national stage a dapper 26-year-old pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church.
A schoolchild skipping on the pavement could not direct me to the church where Martin Luther King Jr preached, although she knew “he did something good for us”.
The dainty red brick church was a short walk away, well preserved but silent on a cloudy, weekday morning. In 2025, thousands arrived here to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the “Bloody Sunday” march King led from Selma to Montgomery to demand voting rights for blacks.
Black residents made up half of Selma’s population then, but only 2 per cent were registered to vote. Although they had the constitutional guarantees, they were denied registration through poll taxes, literacy tests and threats of violence.
The 600 marchers protesting against the injustice were stopped and attacked as they crossed a small, grey bridge bearing the name of Edmund Pettus, a lawyer, brigadier-general, US senator and the Grand Dragon of the Alabama Ku Klux Klan. Shocking images of the event, on the front pages of newspapers and relayed on TV, built national support for the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Cut to today and President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which he insists is necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting fraudulently in elections, touches a raw nerve here.
The Act, which has stalled in Congress, includes measures that will require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote and a photo ID when they turn up at the ballot booth.
The White House has called these “commonsense election integrity measures that are strongly supported by the vast majority of Americans.” But in Selma, Montgomery and the wider civil rights community, distrust is rife.
“Of course, no one wants non-Americans to vote illegally. But is that really a big problem? The administration has provided no proof,” said Al Adams, a retired city worker in Montgomery.
“What we do know is that what Trump wants will create a burden that will fall unevenly on our community,” he said.
“Not everyone has their original birth certificates, name discrepancies on documents are very common, people cannot or will not make a trip in person to an election office to register (to vote). It is especially hard on the elderly, the disabled and folks in rural areas.
“Given our history, you will have to forgive us for concluding that the new rules will reduce black power. And, perhaps, that is the intention,” he said.
Cracking and packing the black vote
Anger runs even deeper against Trump’s push for redistricting in Republican-ruled states to limit losses in the looming midterm election, which almost always punishes the party of the White House incumbent.
The redrawing of state maps to maximise electoral advantage is hardly a new tactic. Nor is it illegal; the exercise does not deny anyone a vote. But it does impact who gets elected by laying down how voters are grouped into districts.
It affects black voters unusually directly, especially in the South, where they are geographically concentrated. As a group, they tend to support Democratic candidates at higher rates than the white majority.
Republicans argue that while they’re engaging in partisan gerrymandering to win elections, there is no racial intent. Voting rights advocates, however, say they are dismantling black-majority districts that have voted for black Democrats in the past.
But where race and party correlate, the distinction is hard to make.
Two map-drawing tactics are used to weaken a group’s electoral influence. One technique is “cracking”, or splitting a cluster of black communities across several majority-white districts, thus reducing the collective power of black voters.
The other is “packing” black voters into fewer districts, thus producing one safe black seat while reducing their influence in adjacent seats.
A Supreme Court decision in April 2026, which held that maps which consciously used race to create black-majority districts violated equal protections accorded to non-minority groups, was a catalyst. It sped up the process initiated by Texas and other red states in 2025 to improve the odds of retaining the US House of Representatives, where the Republican Party holds a narrow 219-212 majority, with four remaining seats vacant due to death or resignations.
By late August, at least 10 states, nine of them Republican, had carried out redistricting in ways that dilute the black voting power.
- In Louisiana, which is roughly one-third black, there were two majority-black districts in the 2024 elections. One of them was eliminated by carving out the black neighbourhoods in the cities of Baton Rouge and Shreveport and merging them with more white and Republican districts.
- In Alabama, two black-majority cities, Montgomery and Mobile, which were reliably Democratic, are now part of districts that are majority-white and pro-Republican.
- In Tennessee, Republican lawmakers dismantled the state’s only majority-black district, the 9th District, which was 62 per cent black and concentrated around Memphis. It was split into three rural, mostly white districts that are Republican footholds.
- In North Carolina, the district with the state’s highest black population (42 per cent) was merged into nearby solidly Republican areas in a way that left it less black (34 per cent).
- In Florida’s new map, four Democratic incumbents now reside in heavily Republican-leaning districts.
- Texas’ redistricting resulted in reduced black representation in the Houston and Dallas area districts.
But, in a curious juxtaposition, black political ambition is also scaling new heights just as electoral maps that produced black representation are being redrawn.
At the state level, the story is more encouraging.
Only three black Americans have ever been elected as governors. But in 2026, for the first time, a record eight black candidates – four from each party – are seeking the highest office in states that include battlegrounds such as Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin. Three are from southern states: Georgia, Florida and South Carolina.
This political season could produce Florida’s first black governor in Byron Donalds and Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms could be the nation’s first black woman governor. Both fancy their chances.
These contests matter more than the symbolic breakthroughs they represent; these are arenas where the black aspirants must escape the racialised political lanes to win in predominantly white electorates.
And in most states, redistricting begins and ends at the governor’s desk. A black candidate must first build the cross-racial coalitions to win and, if elected, has a chance to decide if future maps make such coalitions easier or harder to form.
With race still shaping access to power, America has not become colour-blind, but the lines drawn on maps need not become destiny.
It just means that the battle will go on.

Nigeria’s Plateau State shuts schools for diphtheria outbreak

Kabir Adeniyi
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
The Plateau State government in north-central Nigeria has ordered the indefinite closure of public and private primary and secondary schools beginning Sept. 7, following cases of diphtheria in four local government areas, an official said Saturday.
The directive affects schools that have already resumed academic activities and the measure will remain in force until further notice, according to a statement by Joyce Ramnap, the state commissioner for information and communication.
The government said cases had been reported in Jos North, Jos South, Bassa and Wase local government areas, prompting the closure as a preventive measure to limit the spread of the disease.
School proprietors, administrators and teachers were directed to comply with the order. Parents and guardians were urged to ensure pupils and students remain at home during the closure.
The development comes amid a worsening diphtheria situation in Plateau. The State Commissioner for Health Nicholas Baamlong said earlier this week that 23 people had died, and 143 suspected cases had been recorded, with nine patients receiving treatment at the Jos University Teaching Hospital and Plateau Specialist Hospital.
Baamlong identified shortages of diphtheria antitoxin and late presentation of patients at health facilities as major challenges in the response.
He also said the state faced difficulties confirming suspected cases because of a shortage of specialized containers needed to collect and transport samples for laboratory testing.
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has been notified of the outbreak, with the state government expecting federal support, including supplies of antitoxin and specialized sample-collection materials.
The NCDC said eight states -- Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Borno, Bauchi, Plateau, Sokoto and Zamfara -- accounted for 98% of confirmed cases as of the latest available data. It said 68% of confirmed cases involved those who were unvaccinated.
Diphtheria is a vaccine-preventable bacterial infection that can spread through respiratory droplets and cause serious complications affecting the throat, heart, nerves, and kidneys.

WASHINGTON - The United States said it destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Sept 5 in response to attempted missile attacks on naval vessels, prompting Iran’s military to warn of tougher reprisals if the strikes continued.
The latest round of clashes, which began with US raids last week, comes with both sides deadlocked in the six-month war as Iran maintains its stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz and Washington presses its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
In addition to the renewed military action, Washington is seeking to choke Iran’s economy, announcing sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic republic in a bid to further isolate it and force it into submission.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it targeted tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), accusing the most powerful arm of the Iranian military of unsuccessfully firing at American warships.
“Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask,” it said in a statement.
“American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo... in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship.”
Video posted by CENTCOM showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” it said.
After the strikes, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours.”
But Iran appeared undeterred, with the IRGC announcing later on Sept 5 that their naval forces had subsequently “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas.”
It warned other ships not to attempt to transit by unapproved routes.
CENTCOM did not immediately respond to AFP‘s questions about the IRGC claims. There were no immediate reports from the UKMTO shipping agency of civilian tankers being targeted in the strait.
The Iranian foreign ministry earlier hit out at Washington over the strikes on the oil tankers, calling them “illegal and aggressive actions.”
A correspondent for Iranian state TV in Jask in the southern province of Hormozgan said one of the tankers was empty, and the second was carrying oil. The crews were transported to shore on lifeboats, they said.
Another state TV correspondent on Kharg Island said the attack there caused no casualties.
Iran’s Khatam-al Anbiya central military command warned that if the US continued its attacks, then Iranian retaliation against US warships would be “more severe than before, and there is a possibility of their expansion.”
‘Small potatoes’
The Trump administration has been seeking to play down the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance went so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war,” claiming that “right now, there is no active shooting” despite the ongoing exchanges of fire.
US President Donald Trump backed his comments on Sept 4, calling the Iran war “small potatoes” for the US and insisting: “It’s not a big thing.”
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned this week that the Islamic republic had adopted a “new strategy” against Washington in the war that “will shatter your foundations.”
The US has been trying to step up pressure on Tehran over its blockade of the Hormuz Strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
A fragile ceasefire collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the strategic waterway.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as a “new US territory.”
Vance has also insisted that the US would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial shipping in the Hormuz.
But with fuel prices threatening to cost Trump’s Republicans their control of Congress at the ballot box, his administration has begun pushing the message that oil flows through the waterway are now returning to prewar levels.
“Their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone,” Vance said of Iran on Sept 3.
Before the latest hostilities erupted, the United States had appeared to be pivoting to economic warfare rather than military operations.
On Sept 4, the Treasury announced sanctions on a Turkish bank over its alleged ties to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, and last week Washington took a step towards cutting off a major Egyptian bank’s UAE operations from the US financial system.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has laid out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the American pressure campaign. AFP

US sanctions Turkish bank network Israel wanted closed over alleged IRGC oil financing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
20:49:28 UTC
05:49:28 KST

On September 4, 2026, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control designated Istanbul-based Golden Global Investment Bank, alongside its portfolio management and asset leasing subsidiaries, under Executive Order 13902. 
Operating within Operation Economic Outcast—launched in late August by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—the action closed a financial channel used to move restricted energy capital and generate liquidity for Iranian state military operations. The move demonstrated how specialized regional banks can process capital for state-sponsored actors while maintaining formal commercial access.
The designation reflects sustained counter-terrorism finance cooperation between Western and regional partners. For years, Israeli security agencies prioritized and flagged Turkish banking channels used by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force inside joint U.S.-Israeli intelligence frameworks. Washington acted on shared technical data mapping how Iranian state actors exploit vulnerabilities in Ankara's financial oversight. By severing Golden Global Investment Bank from foreign currency clearing systems, U.S. enforcement validated findings linking elements of Istanbul's commercial banking sector to Iranian military financing, disrupting a pipeline that Western and Israeli officials had repeatedly flagged.
Treasury findings detail the underlying evasion mechanism. Golden Global Investment Bank cleared proceeds from illicit Iranian crude oil sales to commercial buyers in China. Revenue entered Turkish bank accounts through shell companies designed to mask beneficial ownership. Once inside Turkey, rahbar money exchangers converted digital ledger balances into physical gold and foreign currency, obscuring the paper trail and providing the IRGC Quds Force with tens of millions of dollars for military operations.
Central to this arrangement was the network managed by Sıtkı Ayan, a Turkish businessman designated by OFAC in 2022 for managing IRGC Quds Force front companies. Ayan used Golden Global Investment Bank to obtain correspondent banking services closed to sanctioned entities. By providing clearing facilities to the Ayan network, the bank enabled Iranian state entities to monetize crude oil exports under the guise of routine trade while shielding primary transactions from Western regulators.
Golden Global Investment Bank illustrates how financial risk concentrates in niche institutions. Established in 2019 as an interest-free Islamic participation bank with roughly $34 million in capital, the entity occupied a minor footprint in Turkey’s commercial banking sector. Its small balance sheet allowed it to operate below the radar of foreign compliance monitors. Rather than building a standard commercial lending portfolio, the bank operated as a clearing vehicle designed to integrate sanctioned state actors into global commerce.
This pattern mirrors established Turkish economic practice under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. A decade ago, state-owned Halkbank facilitated a multi-billion-dollar oil-for-gold scheme to move Iranian energy revenues. Golden Global Investment Bank represents a modernized variant, using Islamic banking structures toward identical liquidity goals. This conduit functioned within a broader regulatory environment in Ankara that permits hostile regional entities, including Hamas political leadership, to operate legally and manage local asset portfolios. While Treasury's action focuses strictly on IRGC Quds Force facilitation, the bank operated inside a domestic framework that tolerated sanctioned financial activity.
To prevent capital migration, Treasury simultaneously designated the bank’s operating subsidiaries, Golden Global Portföy Yönetimi and Golden Global Varlık Kiralama. When primary lenders face enforcement, illicit networks routinely shift assets and client accounts to affiliated asset management or leasing firms. Sanctioning the parent entity and its subsidiaries in a single action blocked these evasion routes, excising the entire corporate structure from the international financial system.
The enforcement action establishes a clear precedent for secondary sanctions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent issued an explicit warning: any foreign financial institution clearing transactions for sanctioned Iranian entities faces immediate exclusion from the U.S. dollar system. By enforcing this standard against entities in a NATO member state, Washington eliminated the assumption that political alignment provides immunity from compliance enforcement.
The economic consequences for Turkey are direct. Dependent on foreign capital inflows to manage persistent inflation and foreign exchange requirements, the Turkish economy requires integration with global financial markets. International commercial banks and investors demand regulatory certainty before maintaining correspondent relationships or underwriting sovereign debt. President Erdogan’s effort to combine NATO status with a permissive stance toward Iranian military finance has reached a hard wall, elevating sovereign risk across Turkey’s banking sector.
By removing Golden Global Investment Bank from international commerce, Washington proved that diplomatic status cannot shield illicit clearing channels from enforcement. Turkey now faces a binary choice: enforce rigorous banking compliance and secure its standing in the Western financial system, or continue hosting Iranian military networks and accept compounding economic isolation. Erdogan’s dual-track game is over.
Amine Ayoub, a fellow at the Middle East Forum, is a policy analyst and writer based in Morocco. Follow him on X: @amineayoubx

A fire at a wedding party in Democratic Republic of Congo’s capital Kinshasa left at least 22 people dead, the regional mayor said on Saturday. Several others were injured.
The fire started on Friday night and continued into early Saturday in a building in Lingwala in northern Kinshasa. The building’s narrow hallways were constricted by people trying to escape the fire.
Several people - some alive and some dead - were laid by the roadside as attendees tried to help those who were still alive.
The mayor of Lingwala, Norbert Mushinga, told the Congolese Press Agency that the provisional death toll was 22. He said the toll could rise further.
The exact cause of the fire was unconfirmed. “It is a tragedy,” Jacquemin Shabani, Congo’s deputy prime minister and interior minister, said. The minister visited the site on Saturday morning.
Deadly fires are common in densely populated areas of Kinshasa where urban development is often implemented without provisions such as fire services.

The U.S. military struck three Iranian oil tankers on Sept. 5, as the Trump administration and Iran battle for control over the Strait of Hormuz.
A mix of Air Force and Navy aircraft carried out the attacks, including both fighters and drones, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine. The attack followed an unsuccessful Iranian ballistic missile attack on a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer. Neither U.S. ship was hit.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander, referring to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. “If you shoot at our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost—take out three of yours.”
Cooper’s statement continued: “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
The three Iranian tankers included M/T Downy, hit near Kharg Island, and the M/T Stark 1, which was struck near Jask, a coastal city in Iran. The M/T Downy and M/T Stark 1 were “permanently disabled,” according to CENTCOM. The third Iranian oil carrier was hit in the Gulf of Oman. Struck in multiple locations, that tanker was rendered inoperable and “completely destroyed,” according to CENTCOM. The Iranian crew was warned that it should abandon ship before the strike, the command said. CENTCOM later released a video of the attacks on the ships.
The U.S. attacks on the Iranian oil tankers are part of a new Trump administration policy to deter Iranian attacks on U.S. military forces and commercial vessels. Previously, the U.S. had focused its attacks on Iranian military targets, such as radars and surface-to-air missiles.
Iran’s foreign ministry called the attacks on oil tankers a “war crime” intended to further America’s “economic war” on the Iranian homeland. Cooper said the attacks on Iran’s oil carriers are justified because they generate revenue for the IRGC.
The IRGC said in its own statement that it would follow suit and that it targeted “three oil tankers traveling through an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three vessels affiliated with the United States in other areas.”
The U.S. is seeking to use economic sanctions and a blockade to pressure Iran to give up its attempt to control international shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and to agree to limits on its nuclear program.
