Dog Pennu finds a home after 1,497 days in Tartu shelter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

Dog Pennu finds a home after 1,497 days in Tartu shelter
This spring, the dog Pennu, who had lived for more than four years at the Tartu shelter for homeless animals, found his real home.
"Just like with people, some simply don't get lucky in life — the right one just doesn't come," shelter director Annika Mölder said, explaining why Pennu spent so many years waiting for a home.
In the end, he was taken home by shelter volunteer Elisabeth Kaldvee. Kaldvee has been a volunteer at the shelter for seven years, but with Pennu it was not love at first sight at all. At first, her heart was won by the dog boy living next to Pennu.
"Pennu kept jumping like a bat onto the fence and waited for scratches under the arm. Then I just tossed treats to him, but didn't pay much attention. He wasn't my main dog to work with. I went walking with him for the first time about three years ago," Kaldvee recalled.
Dog arrived after bite incident
Pennu arrived at the shelter from a home where he had bitten another dog and a child. "Right now it seems impossible," said Mölder. "The situation was probably such that the child was with the dog, and the dogs got into a conflict with each other, and maybe the child ended up in between. The owner then decided that he did not want to keep such an aggressive dog — too big a responsibility, which is also true."
Kaldvee recalled that when Pennu arrived at the shelter, it was clear that not much work had been done with him, because he had no habit of walking on a leash, he didn't know tricks, and contact with people was minimal. He was also very reactive toward other dogs. "A lot of work and training has been done."
Kaldvee has loved dogs her whole life. As a child, she constantly asked her parents to get her a dog, but it never happened. Now she sees that her parents acted correctly, because at that time it wasn't the right moment and she didn't know enough about dogs.
Volunteer becomes owner
"But the interest has always been there. A classmate invited me to the shelter when I was 18. We went together. For her it was the last time, I kept going. Especially when you choose one dog there to focus on, it's a bit like cheating, because you start feeling like you have your own dog," Kaldvee smiled.
Becoming attached to an animal waiting for a home at the shelter can also bring great heartbreak.
"I always like to say that my first heartbreak was at the shelter, when the first dog I seriously fell in love with was adopted. His name is Bruno. I mourned him for three months and took a break from the shelter. It's a bittersweet moment, because you're happy, but on the other hand he was a dog I invested so much in. It's hard to accept that he's no longer at the shelter," Kaldvee admitted.
Years of attachment grow
Why no one wanted Pennu, Kaldvee has thought about for years. At one point she even began to hope a little that no one would take Pennu, so she could adopt him herself at the right moment.
"He is such a cool‑natured dog. He is super friendly," the owner praised. "He is the first shelter dog I have seriously trained. It was a bit sad to think that all the work I had done would go to waste and I'd have to start from scratch with another dog. And also, when you work with a dog for three years straight, you grow together. He became my dog some time ago already. The shelter workers had long been asking when I would take Pennu home."
Pennu has accepted his new home very well.
Kaldvee encourages others to adopt older dogs too, because then you don't have to worry about puppy‑like mischief. "Once they get used to the home environment, they practically sleep the whole day."
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Argo Ideon

Flooding in Nepal and Tibet has claimed more than 1,375 lives
Kyiv • UNN
In Nepal, 1,344 people have died and nearly 4,900 are missing. In Tibet, 31 deaths and 531 missing people have been reported.
Since the catastrophic flood that struck Nepal's border with China ten days ago, at least 1,375 people have died and more than 5,000 remain missing, UNN reports, citing CNN.
Nepal
At least 1,344 people have died in Nepal, police said this morning.
Among the remains found and identified, 269 were women, 489 were men, and 85 were children, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said today in an updated report.
Another 4,898 people are still considered missing in Nepal, police said.
Among those missing are 589 foreign nationals, the NDRRMA said in its updated report.
According to the NDRRMA, a total of 13,098 people, including 303 foreigners, were rescued from the flood.
As of Wednesday, approximately 75 Americans were still considered missing, a U.S. State Department spokesperson said.
China
According to China's state-run Xinhua news agency, at least 31 people have died in the Tibet Autonomous Region.
Another 531 people in the region are considered missing, Xinhua reported yesterday.
During a press conference last Sunday, authorities said that at least 261 foreigners from 23 countries were among those missing.

Mladic's return to Serbia draws condemnation across Balkans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:13:00 UTC
22:13:00 KST

The return of the remains of convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic to Serbia has drawn condemnation across the Balkans, with officials accusing authorities of glorifying a man convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity.
Mladic, 84, died after suffering from health problems while serving a life sentence in a prison in The Hague, Netherlands. His remains were brought to Belgrade, where plans for a ceremonial reception and state funeral have sparked anger in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Slovenia and Croatia.
Mladic was convicted for his role in the 1992-95 Bosnian war, including the 1995 Srebrenica genocide in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
Denis Becirovic, chairman of Bosnia and Herzegovina's tripartite presidency and its Bosniak member, said holding a state ceremony for Mladic amounted to glorifying one of the most brutal criminals in modern history.
"The glorification of Ratko Mladic, a war criminal convicted by a final court ruling, is a direct blow to the values of the United Nations," Becirovic said in a statement posted on the presidency's website.
He urged the European Union, the Council of Europe, the United Nations and other international organizations to condemn governments and institutions that honor convicted war criminals and to take concrete action against them.
Becirovic also warned that honoring Mladic could have unpredictable consequences for the future of the region.
"This attitude toward a war criminal responsible for the genocide against Bosniaks is one of the cruelest provocations and insults to the victims of the genocide," he said.
Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer criticized the decision to honor Mladic during a meeting in Ljubljana with Croatian Foreign Minister Gordan Grlic Radman.
Kajzer said Mladic was being "glorified" in Serbia and argued that such treatment would do nothing to improve relations in the region.
"Glorifying or promoting these individuals in any way will certainly not contribute to Serbia's progress or to greater mutual understanding among neighbors and in the region," Kajzer said.
Radman said a state ceremony for Mladic would undermine efforts to strengthen stability and security in the Western Balkans while deepening existing divisions.
He also noted that Mladic had committed war crimes in Croatia and expressed regret that he had not been convicted for those crimes.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said decisions about Mladic's burial and funeral had been made by his family.
Vucic also said he would not attend the funeral because he had a previously scheduled visit to Uzbekistan.
A memorial ceremony for Mladic is scheduled for Sunday in Belgrade. His remains are expected to be placed on public display at a church Monday before being taken in a procession to Topcider Cemetery, where he will be buried.
Mladic was born in 1942 near Kalinovik in eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. He received his military training in Belgrade and served in the Yugoslav People's Army.
In May 1992, he became chief of staff of the newly formed Army of Republika Srpska, a position he held until 1996.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia indicted Mladic on July 24, 1995, while the Bosnian war was still underway.
After the war, he fled to Serbia and remained at large for about 16 years. Serbian authorities repeatedly said they were unable to locate him, but allegations emerged that people within state institutions had helped protect him.
Television footage later showed Mladic appearing in public during his years on the run, including social gatherings where he was seen talking with people, enjoying himself and posing for photographs.
He was arrested May 26, 2011, in the village of Lazarevo near the northern Serbian city of Zrenjanin and transferred to The Hague five days later.
His trial began May 16, 2012. Mladic denied the charges against him.
He was ultimately convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, including his role in the Srebrenica massacre, in which 8,372 Bosniak civilians were killed in July 1995.

MOGADISHU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Somalia has formally become the 50th country to ratify the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) agreement, depositing its instrument of ratification with the African Union.
The Minister of Commerce and Industry Gamal Mohamed Hassan submitted the instrument on Friday following its approval by Parliament and presidential assent from President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud.

"This milestone reaffirms Somalia's commitment to Africa's economic integration and strengthens our collective efforts to build one African market," it said.
Somalia's attention now shifts to the practical steps required for Somali businesses and products to actively participate in the continental market. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: Father's wartime diary demonstrates best, worst of human nature: Lisbon Maru survivor's son
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:11:45 CST
22:11:45 KST

by Yu Aicen, Zhang Feng
LONDON, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- "From the island a never-to-be-forgotten sight met our eyes, for as far as the eye could see, the ocean was dotted with men and wreckage..."
These are the words of Andrew Salmon, a British Royal Artillery sergeant who was rescued by Chinese fishermen in the Lisbon Maru incident. There is an unusual calmness in his account as he recalls an ordeal that brought him face to face with death.
It was Andrew's wish to have his account published. He wanted to tell the story of his harrowing experience and how he survived with the help of Chinese fishermen. But that wish was never fulfilled before his death in 2000. More than two decades later, his son, Kenneth Salmon, took up the task and finally saw the manuscript published this year under the title "Surviving the Lisbon Maru."
"I had always felt a little bit guilty about not taking my father's manuscript and doing something with it," Kenneth said in a recent interview with Xinhua, describing how he felt before taking on the project. "I knew that it was his, if you like, his dying wish that the book would be published."
Andrew's manuscript largely corroborates what is already known about the calamitous incident. In October 1942, the Japanese-requisitioned Lisbon Maru, carrying more than 1,800 British prisoners of war (POWs), was torpedoed by a U.S. submarine near Dongji, Zhoushan, in eastern China. As the ship sank, local Chinese fishermen came to the rescue. Historical records show that 198 Chinese fishermen helped 384 POWs reach safety.
After escaping the sinking ship, Andrew spent about two hours in the water before joining another survivor, "Ginger" Howell, on a piece of floating wreckage. They were eventually rescued after Ginger, who spoke Shanghainese, hailed a fisherman in a sampan.
"The fisherman picked us up and took us to the opposite side of the island where there was a tiny beach on which he dropped us, fortunately, as the side nearest the Lisbon Maru was steep and rocky," Andrew wrote.
He went on to describe the survivors' first night after the incident on an uninhabited island, where they "huddled together for warmth." They were later taken by a fisherman to "a larger island," where they were given food and clothing, which they "welcomed gratefully," before being recaptured by Japanese soldiers.
"He was lucky that he got out..." Kenneth said. "And he was lucky that he was taken ashore, and the Chinese fishing community gave him food, drink, and shelter, and, of course, warmth, which was very important."
But many others were not so fortunate. A total of 843 POWs died in the incident. Some went down with the ship, while others drowned or were killed by Japanese soldiers during the desperate escape.
The decision to finally complete his father's unfinished book took shape in 2024, when Kenneth was inspired by the release of the documentary film "The Sinking of the Lisbon Maru" and encouraged by people around him.
"When my father retired, it was his desire to do something tangible to memorialize people who were involved in the Lisbon Maru, not only the prisoners of war, but also the Chinese fishermen who rescued them."
He, in his term, "eventually gave in to that pressure," and started to work on the unfinished manuscripts. They include not only Andrew's writing, but also first-hand accounts from the fellow survivors that he was in touch with.
Kenneth completed the book using his father's unfinished manuscript, which in turn drew on Andrew's wartime diary. He believes his father carried the diary with him when he escaped from the Lisbon Maru, allowing its pages to survive against all odds, just as their author did.
Kenneth also wrote parts of the book himself, filling in gaps and adding his own account of two visits to Dongji, in 2024 and 2025, to pay tribute to the waters that witnessed his father's most traumatic experience.
"I had prepared a wreath of poppies with my father's photo in the center, which I threw into the sea," read in one of the several chapters by Kenneth, describing his journey to Dongji in 2024. "That particular wreath had adorned my father's coffin in 2000 and it seemed an appropriate offering."
"These first-hand accounts by survivors provide a deeply personal perspective on the tragedy," Kenneth said. "They show that wars are fought by ordinary people and this story demonstrates both the very best, and the very worst, of human nature in the reality of war." ■

Feature: Syrian displaced girl stitches yarn into hope in E. Lebanon
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:11:34 CST
22:11:34 KST

BEIRUT, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- For 13-year-old Syrian girl Bissan Hikma al-Halabi, crochet began as a way to pass the time in displacement in Lebanon.
But it became so much more: an outlet for her creativity, a source of satisfaction and a path toward a small business that provides a source of income for her family.
In a side room of her family's home in Joub Jannine, a town in eastern Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, balls of brightly colored yarn, scissors, needles and stuffing materials surround the wooden table where she works on her latest creations.
With a crochet hook in one hand and yarn running through the other, al-Halabi carefully turns loops of thread into dolls, bags and other pieces.
"After I finish my schoolwork, I pick up the hook and yarn and start crocheting. Crochet is not just a hobby for me, it has become part of my life," said al-Halabi.
Al-Halabi was born and raised in Lebanon. Her family had fled the al-Amara neighborhood of the Syrian capital Damascus and lived in Lebanon since 2012.
Three years ago, she began learning crochet from her mother, who is skilled in the craft. "The difficult economic situation faced by my family was my main motivation for learning it, as I wanted to help my mother," she recalled.
Al-Halabi began with simple pieces, learning the basic stitches before moving on to more complicated designs. Some pieces take several hours to complete, while larger or more intricate designs can require several days of work.
"I started with simple things and gradually moved on to more varied designs, making bags, accessories, toys and dolls, children's clothes, bedroom items and decorations," she said.
She also takes care to give each piece its own character, from choosing the colors and determining the shape and size to adding the final details.
"If I don't like one of the stitches, I undo it and make it again," she said, describing the patience and concentration required to complete her work.
So far, al-Halabi has made around 100 crochet pieces, spanning 17 different types. Her products are priced between 10 and 25 U.S. dollars, depending on their size and level of detail.
This summer, she took part in five fairs in towns across the Bekaa Valley, alongside other artisans. At the fairs, hundreds of visitors were drawn to the tent displaying her handmade pieces, helping her earn more than 1,500 U.S. dollars in net profits.
"My participation was well received by visitors, particularly mothers who showed interest in handicrafts," she said. "The dolls and toys I made also attracted children."
What started as a pastime has also opened up new possibilities for her future.
She said that she wants to expand her production, market her creations, participate in more exhibitions, to eventually turn her craft into a small business that could provide more income for her family.
Her participation in exhibitions has also brought her work wider attention and encouragement.
Shawki Dallal, head of the Rashaya Fine Arts Workshop, said the organization was pleased to support and showcase al-Halabi's work, describing crochet as a craft that combines creativity, precision and patience.
Dallal said the girl is among the Syrian children living in Lebanon who deserve opportunities to develop their abilities.
"It is a humanitarian message that gives hope to a child who creates beauty with her own hands," he said. ■

Chinese festival featuring traditional culture, cuisine kicks off in German city of Duisburg
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:11:09 CST
22:11:09 KST

DUISBURG, Germany, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Duisburg China Festival kicked off here on Friday afternoon, with participation from some Chinese and German cities, aimed at strengthening ties between the two countries.
The three-day festival features a wide range of cultural booths and interactive zones showcasing traditional Chinese cuisine, culture and contemporary art.
On Friday evening, top-tier performing arts troupes from Wuhan, capital city of central China's Hubei Province, jointly staged the festival's opening gala. Nearly 40 artists presented more than a dozen distinctive programs spanning Peking opera, Hanju opera, Chuju opera, acrobatics, and ethnic song and dance.
The Duisburg China Festival is a vivid expression of exchange between China and Germany, allowing Germans to experience and understand China up close, said Chang Haitao, acting consul general of the Chinese Consulate General in Dusseldorf.
In 1982, Duisburg and Wuhan became sister cities, the first of its kind between Germany and China. The two cities have maintained close people-to-people and economic exchanges, forging a bond between them ever since.
Impressed by the performance of the Chinese artists, Duisburg Mayor Soeren Link said that the opening gala was unforgettable for its standard, quality, richness, and the many different facets it presented.
Duisburg attaches great importance to its sister-city relationship with Wuhan and hopes to continue strengthening German-Chinese friendship as well as exchange and dialogue between the two sides, said Link.
Markus Teuber, commissioner for China affairs at the Mayor's Office of Duisburg, said the rich array of theatrical, song and dance performances brought by Wuhan offered German audiences an excellent window into Chinese culture, and expressed hope that the two cities will continue to deepen cultural exchange in the future.
For Yang Jing, deputy director of the Wuhan Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism, the presence of Wuhan city at the festival "marks an important step in Wuhan culture's global outreach."
The Duisburg China Festival is an annual signature cultural event for the city, injecting fresh grassroots momentum into the development of German-Chinese friendship. ■

Tanzania contains Mount Kilimanjaro fire by over 90 pct

DAR ES SALAAM, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania has contained a fire outbreak on Mount Kilimanjaro by more than 90 percent, with firefighting teams working to extinguish the remaining flames, Minister for Natural Resources and Tourism Ashatu Kijaji said on Saturday.
Kijaji made the remarks in Moshi in the northern Kilimanjaro Region after inspecting the affected area and briefing journalists on the firefighting progress. The blaze was first reported on Thursday at around 3:30 p.m. local time in Kilimanjaro National Park.
According to the minister, the government immediately deployed conservation officers and personnel from the Tanzania National Parks (TANAPA) and the Tanzania Forest Services Agency (TFS), working together with the Tanzania Fire and Rescue Force, to combat the outbreak.
The remaining pockets of fire are mainly concentrated around tree stumps and valleys, where teams are first focusing on preventing further spread before dealing with smoldering stumps, she noted.
Kijaji added that the cause of the fire has not yet been established, noting that authorities would conduct a detailed assessment of the impacts on wildlife and other resources once the blaze is completely put out.
Helicopters have also been deployed during the past two days to support ground teams. Meanwhile, the minister assured the public that tourists, tour guides, conservation officers, and firefighters are safe, with no human casualties reported so far. ■

Ambassadors from the G7 nations held talks this week with an International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission led by Gavin Gray to assess Ukraine’s economic outlook, macro-financial stability, and structural reform progress.

The IMF mission, which began its work in Ukraine on Aug. 31, is currently conducting meetings with government officials and other stakeholders to evaluate the domestic economy and verify compliance with existing cooperation agreements.
In June, Ukraine and the IMF reached a staff-level agreement regarding the first review of the four-year, $8.1 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program. This agreement is intended to facilitate a subsequent funding tranche of approximately $690 million.
Ongoing IMF loan program and economic outlook
The current discussions follow a July assessment of the $8.1 billion EFF program, during which the IMF reported total disbursements to Ukraine had reached approximately $2.2 billion.
At that time, the IMF determined that Ukraine had maintained broad macroeconomic and financial stability despite the ongoing Russian invasion.
However, the organization noted that the country’s economic outlook had weakened, attributing the decline to intensified Russian strikes on critical infrastructure and the external economic spillovers of the war in the Middle East.

While the IMF characterized Ukraine’s overall performance under the program as “broadly satisfactory,” it observed that the implementation of several structural benchmarks had been delayed or missed.
In response, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva stated that maintaining macroeconomic stability remains Ukraine’s immediate priority, calling for the government to maintain prudent fiscal and monetary policies alongside measures to safeguard the financial sector.

Fitch upgrades Portugal's rating to A+ and says outlook is "stable"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:07:50 UTC
22:07:50 KST

On Friday, the financial agency raised Portugal's debt rating from "A" to "A+", with a "stable" outlook, the agency said in a published note.
Ratings agency Fitch has upgraded Portugal's sovereign debt rating from "A" to "A+", with a "stable outlook", the company said in a notice published on its website (source in Portuguese), keeping pace with the recent wave of confidence shown by other ratings agencies and investors in the country, according to Portugal's Agency for Investment and Foreign Trade (AICEP). According to the Portuguese government, "all financial ratings agencies" assign Portugal an "A" rating.
In August, Standard & Poor's (S&P) (source in Portuguese) confirmed its unsolicited sovereign credit ratings for Portugal of "A+/A-1" for long- and short-term foreign and local currency debt, and maintained the positive outlook. Morningstar DBRS also confirmed, in July 2025 (source in Portuguese), the Republic of Portugal's rating at "A" (high), with a "stable outlook".
Fitch Ratings' announcement on Friday is based on the strengthening of Portugal's public finances, in particular the projected reduction in debt and more robust economic growth than in other countries, underpinned by a "strong political commitment to fiscal prudence".
"The upgrade reflects the strengthening of Portugal's public finances, including a projected path of declining public debt and budget balances that are considerably stronger than those of comparable countries, supported by a strong political commitment to fiscal prudence," Fitch says.
According to the agency, Portugal's ratings are supported by governance indicators above the median for countries rated "A", as well as institutional strengths linked to membership of the European Union and the euro area. These factors are, however, offset by still-high levels of accumulated public and external debt.
Fitch adds that the "prudence" of policies, repeatedly better-than-expected budget performance and persistent current-account surpluses have strengthened the resilience of the Portuguese economy and its ability to "absorb shocks".
The agency expects public debt to fall from 89.7% of GDP in 2025 to 87.0% in 2026 and 82.9% in 2028, supported by the maintenance of primary surpluses and moderate nominal growth. Even so, the ratio is expected to remain above the forecast median of 59.5% of GDP for countries rated "A".
On Thursday, the Minister of State and Finance, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, said that the fall in the debt-to-GDP ratio "is the result of the work of families and businesses in recent years (source in Portuguese)", stressing that this process "cannot be interrupted and that it is necessary to maintain the pace of public debt reduction". Joaquim Sarmento added that it is necessary "to sharply reduce bureaucracy, which stifles companies and citizens and limits and delays private investment, especially foreign direct investment", which will have "a strong impact on our country's potential GDP", he said.
On X, the finance minister hailed the "excellent news for Portugal, which regains an A+ rating for the first time since March 2011".
This morning, the President of the Republic also welcomed the agency's rating decision. "This is excellent news for the country and an important external recognition of Portugal's performance, the result of a medium- and long-term evolution, sustained by the efforts of the Portuguese people and by a responsible orientation maintained under different governments," António José Seguro writes on the Presidency website (source in Portuguese). "A better rating will improve financing conditions for the state, businesses and families, support investment and job creation and allow more public resources to be directed towards people's needs," the president hopes.
"When the year 2026 comes to be read in retrospect, this will surely be one of its most relevant economic news stories," Seguro adds.
Increase in defence spending puts public finances under pressure
Fitch estimates that the budget surplus will fall from 0.7% of GDP in 2025 to 0.1% in 2026, affected by emergency support and reconstruction spending related to storms, by the tax-cut and housing measures set out in the 2026 State Budget, by peak investment linked to the loan component of the Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) and by higher spending on wages and pensions.
These effects are expected to be partially offset by higher social contributions, linked to continued employment growth, and by a significant dividend distribution from Caixa Geral de Depósitos, according to the agency.
For 2027 and 2028, Fitch forecasts an average deficit of around 0.4% of GDP. The agency anticipates that demographic ageing and lower migration "will increase spending and put pressure on social contributions", although it notes that the Social Security Financial Stabilisation Fund, with assets equivalent to 13.9% of GDP at the end of 2025, "provides a substantial safety margin".
The cost of housing is also a concern, although the rapid rise in house prices has not yet translated into "significant short-term macro-financial risks"; it may "increase vulnerabilities in the property market and is aggravating pressures on affordability", the agency stresses.
In the first quarter of 2026, residential property prices were about 99% above the level recorded in the fourth quarter of 2019, compared with 31% in the euro area.
Low housing supply and strong demand, linked to high immigration, suggest that pressures in the property market are mainly "structural, limiting the likelihood of a sharp correction in the short term", says Fitch, which suggests that "a solid banking sector should help contain the financial risks related to the property market" and the resulting build-up of household debt.
Another factor to bear in mind is NATO's target of reaching 5% of GDP in defence spending by 2035, which Fitch expects will "add pressure to public finances in the medium term". Even so, the international ratings agency considers that the track record of budgetary policy, relatively stable over successive changes of government, mitigates the risks associated with greater political uncertainty.

Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:07:36 UTC

Iran President Pezeshkian calls for unity as US ramps up economic pressure
Amid rising public discontent, Iranian authorities say adversaries are focused on encouraging domestic unrest.
Tehran, Iran – President Masoud Pezeshkian has insisted that officials and Iranians will stand united in the face of United States economic pressure, saying national cohesion was enough to “neutralise” any attempts to create discord within the country.
The US announced an “Economic D-Day” against Tehran last month, the toughest sanctions regime in Washington’s history aimed at severing all economic lifelines that “sustain the Iranian regime and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)”.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pentagon polygraphs dozens of US military staff over media leaks
- list 2 of 4Oil and politics: What Trump’s ‘historic’ deal means for Venezuela
- list 3 of 4Qatar removed from Fitch’s negative watch list as risks to LNG sites ease
- list 4 of 4Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
Pezeshkian said the economic measures will not force his government to make any abrupt policy shifts, which might lead to further unrest in the country.
“Through war, blockade and sanctions, the enemies seek to create division, fissures and unrest inside the country,” the president reportedly told officials on Friday.
Pezeshkian was likely referring to events in 2019 and 2020, which began with protests against high fuel prices and unravelled into a wider antigovernment uprising.
“People are now on the edge; if I impose another pressure, they may fall off,” Pezeshkian reminded the country during a televised appearance earlier this week.
He did confirm that his administration will still double the price of one of three tiers of petrol quotas offered to private vehicles over the coming weeks and reduce monthly petrol quotas.
Iran still faces critical energy supply shortages due to rampant fuel smuggling, severe damage or neglect of oil and gas infrastructure, and expensive yet low-quality, fuel-hungry vehicles.
But any wider petrol price hike would impact logistics costs and feed rampant inflation, which is affecting all Iranian households, the president has indicated.
Iran’s national currency hit a new all-time low of more than 2.25 million rials per US dollar when Tehran’s market opened for the start of the working week on Saturday.
Meanwhile, the ongoing military confrontation between Iran and the US, which has been a major catalyst for Tehran’s present economic decline, shows no sign of abating.
The US military bombed an oil tanker near Iran’s Kharg Island on Saturday, several days after another round of attacks on southern Iran and shipping in Hormuz.
Washington has prevented Iranian tankers from leaving the country’s southern shores as part of its naval blockade to choke off crude exports.
Iran’s government has said it will return to commitments under a memorandum of understanding signed between Washington and Tehran in June but that fell apart shortly after, if the US does the same.
‘National security’
The compounding pressures and rising public discontent have prompted news warnings from Iranian authorities about potential public unrest in recent weeks.
At the end of August, the intelligence directorate of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that the US, Israel and their Western allies have shifted towards “pressure from within” to compel protests from Iranians.
Last week, judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei warned that his judges will prosecute those found to be damaging national security “more decisively than all previous eras”, as Iranian enemies seek to stoke unrest, he said.
“The fourth battlefield is the street – the social field,” Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said, naming the other three elements as military operations, diplomatic talks, and economic services to the people.
Police chief Ahmad-Reza Radan also identified livelihoods, unemployment, the economy and petrol as possible “pretexts” for localised or nationwide protests. He ordered continuous monitoring and the readiness of forces under his control to prepare for unrest.
The latest message attributed to Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei in late August also indicated a focus on national unity.
“I declare decisively that anything harmful to social cohesion is prohibited,” the statement read, which has been adorned on posters and banners by his supporters across the country.
Civil authorities have also intensified punishments against people and businesses found to be acting against national security.
On Thursday, Iran’s Supreme Court confirmed that prominent businessman Sadegh Saedinia was sentenced to at least 12.5 years in prison and will have his millions of dollars in assets confiscated by the state for what they said was support for nationwide protests in January.
His brand – which included cafes, food companies and hospitality complexes across the country – had posted two Instagram stories to announce a strike in support of the protesters. Saedinia later released a “confession” to say he regretted the action.
Iranian authorities classify the January nationwide protests as a “coup” orchestrated by the US, Israel and their allies, and carried out by armed agents inside the country.
Some of the dozens who have been executed by judicial authorities since the start of the war with the US on February 28 were said to be involved in these protests.

Prosecutor General's Office confirms that searches were conducted at premises used by its head
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:04:00 EEST
22:04:00 KST

Prosecutor General's Office confirms that "premises used by prosecutor general" were searched
The Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Office has confirmed that detectives from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) carried out searches at official premises used by Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, his first deputy Maria Vdovychenko and other staff from the Prosecutor General's Office at around midnight.
Source: Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Office
Details: The Office of the Prosecutor General (OPG) said that the searches gave detectives access to case files concerning possible unlawful actions by individuals close to the leadership of the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO).
According to the OPG, the case has been investigated under the OPG's procedural supervision, and SAPO's leadership has been aware of the investigation and its progress.
NABU has also gained access to materials from another case, including information gathered in the course of covert investigative operations into possible unlawful activities by NABU and SAPO staff.
The OPG said it is seeking to determine whether the detectives had been granted access appropriate to the case for which the searches were conducted, whether the materials had been examined, copied, or seized, and whether the actions had been authorised by a court.
Quote: "At around midnight, NABU detectives did in fact conduct investigative actions at the offices used by the Prosecutor General, the First Deputy Prosecutor General and other staff and departments of the Office of the Prosecutor General.
The scale of these investigative actions, the grounds for them and the list of materials accessed require a separate legal assessment."
More details: Regarding Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, the OPG noted that the search warrant refers to conversations between an OPG employee and others about "dark tiles" and the installation of an alarm system and internal sensors in premises used by the prosecutor general. The OPG says the investigators believe the conversations were connected with funds that may have been obtained illegally.
However, the OPG maintains that the materials cited in the warrant contain no direct evidence that Kravchenko instructed anyone to facilitate the operations of scam call centres, obstruct their exposure or investigation, warn them about investigative actions, receive funds or unlawful benefits from the operations, or pay for renovations and other services using illicit funds.
The OPG says any link between these everyday conversations and possible criminal activity in the case file is "largely based on speculation".
The OPG also highlighted a conversation about possible amendments to Order No. 309 on the work of prosecutors in criminal proceedings. According to the investigators, an OPG employee referred to an agreement with the "boss", which they understood to mean the prosecutor general. This conversation was one of the grounds for conducting the investigative actions.
The OPG emphasises that Kravchenko did not sign the amendments, which were neither adopted nor brought into force.
Regarding First Deputy Prosecutor General Mariia Vdovychenko, the OPG said the conversations cited in the search warrant were about investigative actions to target scam call centres and efforts to combat their activities, but, the OPG said, investigators had used these conversations as evidence that she may have facilitated the call centres' activities.
Background: On the evening of 4 September, OPG spokesperson Mariana Haiovska emphasised in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda that no investigative actions had been carried out either at the prosecutor general's home or in his office.
Sources in political circles told Ukrainska Pravda that Kravchenko's whereabouts have been unknown since NABU and SAPO launched Operation Carthage. However, the OPG insisted that Kravchenko had been at his workplace on Saturday.

Russia announces three-day halt in strikes as Trump envoys visit for Ukraine talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:03:00 UTC
22:03:00 KST

US envoys meet with Putin, leave Russia for Kyiv
Published September 5, 2026last updated September 6, 2026
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday evening.
"The situation is of course not simple," Putin told the US officials in footage aired on Russian state media.
Putin and US envoys held "useful" talks on a range of ideas to end the war in Ukraine, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters.
According to Russian media outlets, US envoys left Moscow after the meeting.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump said Kushner and Witkoff were traveling to Russia with a new proposal, but he did not provide any details on the potential peace plan, including whether it involved Ukraine giving territory to Russia as he has previously suggested. Instead, he said, "We have an idea for peace."
Russia, Ukraine pause strikes for three days
The Kremlin said Russian forces would pause strikes against Kyiv for three days in conjunction with the peace negotiations.
Putin "ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told state media.
The order came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had already committed to pausing airstrikes for the talks.
"As with previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are concerned about their safety, not about Russia," Zelenskyy said.
US envoys to make first visit to Kyiv
Zelenskyy announced on Friday that Kushner and Witkoff would visit Ukraine on Sunday following talks in Moscow.
Recent media reports have questioned whether the pair would indeed travel to Ukraine. Despite trips to Moscow to meet with Russian officials, the US envoys have not visited Kyiv since Trump's reelection last year.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he had been in contact with Kushner and Witkoff.
"I have just spoken with the US president’s envoys," Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
"From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process."
Trump had promised to end the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, on his first day back in office, but has more recently said that the feat was more complicated than expected. In the past, he has blamed Ukraine for the Russian invasion and a "personality problem" between the countries' leaders for the continued fighting.

====================================================================================================

Watching violent online pornography is linked to poorer sexual health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:00:47 UTC
22:00:47 KST

Young adults who watch violent online pornography tend to report worse sexual well-being, lower empathy, and more acceptance of violence against women than those who watch nonviolent content. These patterns, which look different for men and women, suggest that the specific types of sexual media people consume might shape their interpersonal relationships and physical experiences. The research was published in the journal Behavioral Sciences.
The World Health Organization defines sexual health as a broad state of physical, emotional, and social well-being. This definition goes beyond the mere absence of disease to include psychosocial skills that help people form healthy relationships. Two of these foundational skills are empathy, which involves understanding and sharing the feelings of another person, and sexual assertiveness.
Sexual assertiveness refers to a person’s ability to communicate their desires, initiate wanted encounters, and refuse unwanted sexual activity. Higher levels of this skill protect against sexual coercion and encourage safer sexual practices. Empathy also plays a role in sexual health by fostering mutual satisfaction and reducing the likelihood of aggressive behaviors.
While people consume large amounts of online pornography, research on how different types of explicit media relate to sexual well-being remains mixed. Prior studies often grouped all pornography together, masking how specific content might correlate with different outcomes. Psychological models of media consumption suggest that the consequences of watching pornography depend heavily on the specific context and material viewed.
In recent years, highly accessible online platforms have exposed young viewers to increasingly extreme content during their formative years. To address the knowledge gap regarding specific content, public health researcher Belén Sanz-Barbero from Spain’s National School of Public Health and her colleagues investigated how different forms of violent pornography associate with various dimensions of sexual health.
The researchers organized a large online survey of 3,607 young adults living in Spain between the ages of 18 and 35. For their primary analysis, they isolated a subgroup of 1,985 individuals who reported being sexually active and having watched pornography in the past year. This final group included 1,249 men and 736 women.
The participants answered detailed questionnaires regarding their pornography viewing habits and sexual experiences. To avoid social desirability bias, the tendency for survey respondents to answer questions in a way that will be viewed favorably by others, the researchers avoided using extreme words like rape. Instead, they provided subtle descriptions of sexual encounters and asked participants to rate how often they watched those specific scenarios.
The researchers then categorized the participants based on the most extreme type of pornography they regularly consumed. The three categories were pornography with no explicit violence, pornography featuring degrading or humiliating acts without physical violence, and pornography featuring physical violence. Degrading content included scenes featuring insults, threats, or domination practices that did not inflict physical pain.
Physically violent content included depictions of nonconsensual acts, the use of force, or painful submission practices. The survey instrument also measured the participants’ empathy, sexual assertiveness, and acceptance of violence against women. Additional sections of the questionnaire asked respondents about their sexual satisfaction, their ability to reach orgasm, and whether they had been recently diagnosed with any sexually transmitted infections.
The researchers found that consuming violent pornography was widespread among the study participants. More than 63 percent of the men and nearly 51 percent of the women reported watching pornography that contained physical violence. Men who watched these physically violent videos scored lower on psychological tests measuring empathy and sexual assertiveness compared to men who watched nonviolent pornography.
Both men and women who watched physically violent pornography demonstrated a higher acceptance of violence against women. Men who watched degrading or humiliating content also showed this increased acceptance. The researchers noticed distinct differences between men and women regarding physical sexual function and interpersonal satisfaction.
Men who watched physically violent content were more likely to report enjoying and having fun during sexual activities than those watching nonviolent videos. At the same time, these men were more likely to report feeling discomfort during real world sexual encounters. They also experienced greater difficulty getting or maintaining an erection and were much more likely to use sexual enhancement drugs.
Past studies have shown that the prevalence of erectile dysfunction in men under 40 has increased in recent decades. The researchers proposed that unrealistic sexual fantasies created by violent pornography might cause feelings of distress or moral incongruence when they are not fulfilled in real life. This distress could ultimately interfere with physical sexual function and satisfaction.
For women, watching physically violent pornography was associated with a higher likelihood of struggling to reach orgasm when with a partner. However, these women did not report this same difficulty when experiencing sexual activity alone. The researchers proposed that unrealistic expectations created by violent media might make it harder for viewers to communicate their boundaries or achieve satisfaction with real partners.
The survey also tracked recent diagnoses of sexually transmitted infections like gonorrhea, human papillomavirus, and chlamydia. Individuals of both sexes who watched violent pornography reported higher rates of these recent infections. However, the differences were not statistically significant after the researchers adjusted the data for other demographic variables.
Because this research relied on a survey administered at a single point in time, it cannot prove that watching violent pornography causes these negative sexual health outcomes. The relationship might work in the opposite direction. For example, individuals who already struggle with low empathy or sexual dysfunction might seek out more extreme or violent material to achieve sexual arousal.
The psychological theory of empathy suggests that media consumers often identify with one specific actor in a scene, leading to an empathetic disconnection from the other people involved. It is possible that men with naturally lower empathy are drawn to media that allows them to disconnect from the experiences of women. Women might possess a greater emotional resilience to the effects of violent pornography due to different patterns of empathetic identification.
The survey also depended on participants accurately and honestly reporting their viewing habits. Even with built-in statistical adjustments for social desirability, people might naturally underreport socially unacceptable behaviors and overreport positive traits. The researchers also noted that their sample focused heavily on sexually active individuals, which might limit how well the findings apply to broader populations.
Future longitudinal studies tracking viewers over several years will help determine whether exposure to violent pornography directly alters psychosocial development. Until then, public health interventions targeting young adults could focus on building communication skills and critical thinking regarding the sexual scripts modeled in digital media. Recognizing violent pornography as an emerging factor in sexual health could help educators promote safer and more respectful relationships.
The findings offer a new perspective on how digital media habits align with physical and emotional well-being. The study, “Violent Content in Online Pornography Is Associated with Sexual Health of Women and Men,” was authored by Belén Sanz-Barbero, Vanesa Pérez-Martínez, Ana Rico, Laura Otero-García, Marta Fernández-López, Ariadna Cerdán-Torregrosa, and Carmen Vives-Cases.

====================================================================================================

After overtourism besieged Big Sur, the worst finally happened: ‘People kept saying someone is going to die’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:00:36 UTC
22:00:36 KST

California’s rugged Big Sur coastline is often called a slice of heaven, 120 miles (195km) of unspoiled rocky promontories, sandy beaches and redwood forests at the foot of the Santa Lucia mountains. This year, it has endured a long summer of hell.
Wildfires, road closures and repeated disruptions to the local hotel, restaurant and campsite businesses all have posed significant challenges in an era of climate change and unpredictable weather patterns. One large fire broke out in the highlands east of Big Sur in early August and is still less than 25% contained. A second fire erupted 30 miles to the south two weeks later and is so inaccessible to firefighters that it has grown bigger than the first and is barely contained at all.
Residents of the area have long known that the threat of natural catastrophe is part of what it means to live in a remote and beautiful place. But for many, the events of this summer have renewed questions about the sustainability of mass tourism in the area, particularly in the age of Instagram.
The tourist industry accounts for about 90% of the local economy, so visitors are certainly welcome. But nobody feels comfortable with chaos on the roads, tourists who leave their messes behind or a pair of recent traffic deaths that have plunged the community into mourning. Like other global hotspots, from Italy to the Galápagos, Big Sur is asking: how many is too many?
Henry Miller once described this coast as a place imbued with “the peace of God, and the serene security created by a handful of good neighbors living at one with the creature world”. But many coastal residents worry that sort of peace is rapidly eluding their grasp.
A reopening marred by selfie-snappers
The disruptions began at the beginning of the year with the long-awaited reopening of Highway 1, a two-lane road that provides the only vehicle access to Big Sur from the Monterey peninsula in the north to Cambria in the south. For three years, the route had been cut in two by extensive repair work in the wake of heavy landslides, another abiding natural threat. The region lost about 20% of its tourists over that time, at a cost of millions of dollars a month. Hearst Castle, on the southern end of the peninsula, lost as many as 40%.
The reopening immediately caused visitor numbers to shoot back up, but residents and local officials noticed that along with the nature lovers and the hikers came many more tourists interested almost exclusively in snapping selfies at a handful of well-advertised locations before moving swiftly on.
Such visitors weren’t shy about stopping in the middle of the road to take pictures at the spectacular, arched Bixby Bridge, even if it meant snarling traffic for miles in each direction. Local media was filled with stories of visitors trampling on plants, camping illegally and tossing their trash in all directions. In July, a selfie-ruining banner appeared on the Bixby Bridge that read: “Overtourism is killing Big Sur.” But it made little difference.
“Visitor behavior has changed so much,” said Kate Daniels, who represents Big Sur on the Monterey county council and successfully pressed for a parking moratorium at the Bixby Bridge that went into effect last month. “This is one of the most beautiful places you’ve ever seen, yet people have decided their goal is to take a picture of themselves on a bridge … It’s really difficult and dangerous, and that road cannot handle it.”
‘It was a nightmare’
For many residents, the low point came in mid-August, when Monterey county hosted its annual Car Week extravaganza, featuring thousands of vintage and exotic cars and a line-up of events in and around the city of Monterey and the golf courses of Pebble Beach.
Some of the event’s 100,000 visitors repurposed the Big Sur coastline as a playground for their souped-up coupes and convertibles. They had done much the same the previous year, but now the Timber fire was raging, every change in the wind was apt to carry the smell of burning forest and the community had no patience for it.
Even as fire trucks were trying to set up defensive lines in an effort to save buildings and people, car aficionados were filmed making high-speed dashes down the straightest stretches of Highway 1, doing doughnuts at traffic intersections and gathering dozens of vehicles for group photographs. Photos and videos posted online showed fire trucks struggling at times to move on a highway clogged with brightly painted sports cars.
“It was a nightmare,” Daniels said. “Car Week has been going on for decades and it never used to be like this, but now it’s this hyper-masculine racing culture thing. People kept saying that someone is going to die.”
By the end, people did die.
On the final weekend, a 20-year-old out-of-towner at the wheel of a Dodge Challenger coupe plowed into Brian Roberts, a popular figure in Big Sur who went by the nickname Brewski and, according to his friends, had spent many of the previous days railing against the behavior of the Car Week attendees. Accounts differ about how the accident happened – some of Roberts’s friends say he was crossing Highway 1 to admire the sunset, while others say he was in the road yelling at cars after he found them blocking the turn-off to Palo Colorado Road, where he lived.
Days later, an 80ft skid mark was still plainly visible, along with circular burn marks where vehicles appear to have been doing doughnuts. One of Roberts’s friends, Brendon Shave, arrived on the scene shortly after the accident and found bloodstains smeared across the median line and on the tarmac.
The following day, another 20-year-old visitor from outside San Francisco smashed a silver BMW convertible into a tree a few miles north of Big Sur, killing one of his passengers and injuring himself and two other friends. Police said the driver recorded a blood alcohol level of 0.13, well above the legal limit, and they were investigating the death as gross vehicular manslaughter.
Traffic deaths are a fact of life in Big Sur, with news reports suggesting that one occurs every few months, either because drivers go too fast along the windy, narrow road or because they become distracted by the natural beauty and plunge off the side.
Still, Roberts’s death has moved people to particular outrage.
“The community felt disrespected because the land was on fire,” said Lindsey Kirk, a friend of Roberts’s from the San Francisco Bay Area who spends as much time as she can spare in Big Sur. “It’s crazy that the fire services couldn’t get through because of all the cars they brought in.”
Shave, who runs a hair salon in Carmel, a 20-minute drive from where Roberts died, blamed authorities in Monterey county who, he said, used the beauty of Big Sur as a draw for big events – marathons and golf tournaments as well as the annual car show – but did little to look out for its residents. “People live here,” he said, “to get away from all the stuff that Monterey county keeps sending our way.”
See Monterey, which promotes tourism in the region, has repeatedly urged visitors to Big Sur to stick to the speed limit and park legally and put out one statement headlined: “Big Sur Deserves Big Respect.”
But the organization also encouraged Car Week attendees to explore far and wide, including the Big Sur coast. Eleven days after Roberts’s death, See Monterey put out a statement proclaiming “a banner year”, with hotel revenue up, visitor spending exceeding $100m and more than $4m raised for charity.
Left unmentioned were the many area businesses that closed for the week or threw up metal fences and hired security guards so their parking lots would not turn into impromptu, days long motor sports rallies.
The visitors noticed. The driver of a McLaren supercar denied entry to an In-N-Out Burger attracted national attention when his brother protested on his behalf: “That’s profiling! That’s racism towards cars.”
‘We lost a good human being’
Days after the last Lamborghinis and Porsches left town, a flare-up in the Timber fire sent cascades of sparks and ash down from Mount Manuel and prompted what many Big Sur residents felt should have happened much sooner: a comprehensive closure of Highway 1 encompassing most of the hotels and restaurants and some of the most heavily visited spots, including Pfeiffer Beach and McWay Falls.
Authorities gave residents 24 hours either to stock up on essentials or leave town. Roberts’s mourners cheered – “Tourism is a problem, not a boon,” said Ivy La Velle, who described herself as his best friend – but others acknowledged it was never easy to make such a call.
When the community shuts down, many of the hourly workers at the restaurants and hotels lose their source of income. If the fires force them to evacuate – dozens of them are housed by the resorts and campsites that employ them – their problems are compounded by unexpected housing and other expenses.
Ryne Leuzinger, board chair of the Community Association of Big Sur, said his organization had been cutting $300 checks to help the neediest community members get by, and another group, the Big Sur Big Share, had spent the last several weeks making sure that people temporarily without an income had enough to eat.
Big Sur prides itself on its communal spirit, which was on vivid display the night before the closure, when 200 mourners crowded on to the back patio of the River Inn resort to pay homage to Roberts’s life, surrounded by flowers and crystals. Roberts worked as a maintenance worker and gardener at the Alila Ventana resort but also helped with firefighting efforts in the final weeks of his life and enjoyed a wide circle of friends.
“Brian was a big member of the community,” Shave said. “We lost a good human being.”
Speakers recalled how he would park a motorbike in the same spot at the River Inn, one of his favorite haunts, and spend his nights smoking and drinking rum and Cokes. “He had terrible taste in cocktails,” La Velle said afterwards, laughing. “It wasn’t even good rum.” Roberts’s parents, who had driven out from the midwest, did not pay for anything because his friends raised money to pay for their lodging, meals, funeral expenses and a $1,200 bill incurred when police towed his parked truck after the fatal accident.
The next day, even as a bedraggled parade of dirt- and ash-covered cars and trucks made their way north before the closure deadline, mourners gathered at the makeshift memorial on the side of Highway 1 near the spot where Roberts was hit.
Kirk, the friend from the San Francisco area, laid some lapis stones and a bouquet at a shrine that also featured a pack of American Spirit cigarettes, Roberts’s favorite brand, and an empty bottle of Sailor Jerry rum. “He was always around for anyone who needed anything,” she said. “He was a wonderful guy.”
Sarah Sweeney, who in less uncertain times sells sushi from a truck, said Roberts embodied a certain Big Sur ethos now under threat, because he was passionate about a community that rejects the ordinary rhythms of modern life and, perhaps, wants to run away from them. “I call this place Neverland,” she said, “and we’re all Peter Pan. Or the lost boys. There are a lot of lost boys around here.”

Nearly half of new fighter jet jobs based in North West
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:00:22 BST
22:00:22 KST

Nearly half of the jobs supported by the UK’s Future Combat Air System programme are based in the North West of England, with the programme currently supporting more than 4,500 jobs across the country, Defence Minister Luke Pollard has said.
The figures were disclosed in a series of written parliamentary answers to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson covering the regional distribution of FCAS employment, mid-career reskilling and the retention of graduates and apprentices recruited by Team Tempest.
Pollard said: “The Future Combat Air System (FCAS) programme supports jobs across the UK, including all nine regions of England plus Scotland, making defence an engine for growth. Around 43% of jobs are based in the North West of England, 19% in the South West of England, 16% in the Midlands, and Scotland accounts for about 8% of the workforce. The remaining 22% of jobs are split between other regions, including London and the East of England.”
The Defence Investment Plan states that 90 per cent of jobs supported by FCAS programmes are outside London and the South East of England. Anderson asked the MOD to provide the regional split behind that figure.
In a separate answer on mid-career reskilling, Pollard said: “The advanced knowledge, skills, and competencies required by the Future Combat Air System (FCAS) programme, with the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) at its core, is getting more people in highly skilled jobs. FCAS supports over 4,500 jobs across the UK, with thousands more expected to be supported.”
Anderson had asked how many people had been reskilled mid-career as part of FCAS and GCAP. The MOD did not provide a figure, with Pollard saying: “Each Team Tempest industry partner offers a range of career pathways however neither the process nor underlying detailed information are managed centrally.”
A further question asked how many of the 3,000 graduates and apprentices recruited by Team Tempest since 2022 remain employed on the project.
Pollard replied: “The Future Combat Air System (FCAS) programme is creating opportunities for young people across the UK. Around 3,000 graduates and apprentices have been recruited by the Team Tempest industry partners since 2022, providing the opportunity to work on a range of combat air programmes, including sixth-generation combat aircraft development through FCAS.”
He again said detailed employment information was not managed centrally, adding: “Each Team Tempest industry partner offers a range of career pathways however neither the process nor underlying detailed information are managed centrally.”
FCAS is the wider UK programme covering future combat air capability, with the Global Combat Air Programme at its core. GCAP brings together the UK, Italy and Japan to develop a next-generation combat aircraft and associated systems for service in the 2030s.

China launches plan for 3D satellite network to monitor sun and cosmic explosions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:00:06 UTC
22:00:06 KST

China launches plan for 3D satellite network to monitor sun and cosmic explosions
The project will involve partners from at least five other countries as they track the development of space weather
China has started an international project to build a three-dimensional satellite network between Earth and the moon that will track solar activity and study some of the universe’s most powerful explosions.
The project plans to send 30 backpack-sized CubeSats into highly elliptical orbits around Earth in the next four years or so, according to the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory, which will lead the project.
The laboratory said on Friday the constellation would “fill a global gap in systematic observations of cislunar space”. Participants include Egypt, Indonesia, Senegal, Serbia and Thailand.
A separate group of CubeSats will be sent into orbit around the moon to search for lunar resources, but further details have not been disclosed.
“Cislunar space extends from low-Earth orbit to about 2 million km [1.2 million miles] from Earth. It is a new frontier for human activity and a key region for future crewed missions to the moon and the construction of lunar bases,” the laboratory said.
Scientists have long relied on individual spacecraft to study this enormous region, leaving many areas unexplored.
With dozens of satellites observing from different locations at once, scientists can track energetic particles and magnetic disturbances from the sun as they sweep through the region, revealing how space weather develops.

====================================================================================================

Future Airmen to Get Less Sleep, More Stress in Basic Training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-LACKLAND, Texas—The Air Force has started challenging new trainees with less sleep and will soon ramp up the stress level in Basic Military Training to better prepare the future Airmen for the increased strain of combat operations such as Epic Fury.
The service’s 7.5 weeks of BMT already forced Airmen to endure the high stress of constant corrections, long hours of training, and sleep periods interrupted by guard duty.
But in late August, BMT officials here began an effort that will force trainees to handle additional sleep deprivation by increasing the frequency of nocturnal training. In the coming weeks, officials hope to add “stress inoculation” to the effort that’s designed to increase training stress but also teach trainees techniques to function more effectively under it, Col. Kellie Courtland, commander of the 37th Training Wing that oversees BMT, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach directed BMT officials to make the new training changes after combat operations—such as the recent air campaign against Iran—showed that some young Airmen struggled under the strain of the increased operational pace, Courtland added.
The Air Force is “realizing that there are people that are not responding to being able to perform well when they’re sleep deprived, or there’s a lot of stress, … or hard events happen; they’re having a hard time recovering from that,” Courtland said. “The idea is to practice that a little bit more and get used to that level of stress and sleep deprivation because it’s going to happen at different points throughout your career but definitely when you’re out in those wartime environments.”
This is the latest change in a larger effort to overhaul BMT to instill a mindset of “airmindedness” in all Airmen to ensure they know how to work in small teams to defend, operate, generate, and sustain airpower.
Less Sleep
The first week of BMT will remain unchanged since new trainees are already “sleep deprived” from the complete culture shock of the new environment, Courtland said. Beginning in week two, military training instructors, or MTIs, will increase the amount of nighttime entry-control procedures, or guard duty, that each 60-member flight must share. In the past, shifts were two hours long. Now they are one hour each, which requires more trainees to be up on any given night.
Before “you would only have four to eight people basically getting woken up during the night that would do their entry control procedures,” Courtland said. “Now you’ve got 21 trainees that have to get up, spend an hour doing entry control procedures.”
On top of guard shifts, more nighttime training activities are added in the fourth and fifth week in the lead up to PACER FORGE, the final field training exercise that stresses trainees’ agile combat employment skills.
In the fourth week, “we will do different exercises, like maybe an accountability exercise,” said 37th Training Wing Command Chief Master Sgt. Caleb Vaden, describing how all trainees fall out of the dorm, so leaders can ensure everyone is present.
“That usually takes about an hour, and they’ll fall back into their sleeping area,” Vaden said. “Everything we do here is tied to a training objective.”
During the fifth week, trainees will see more nocturnal training events as they begin to prepare for PACER FORGE, where trainees traditionally get little sleep during the 57-hour training event, Vaden said.
“We are working on an exercise where they would fall out, work on that F-16, fall under attack, have to go to a bunker, and then they’re going to go forward to their forward site,” Vaden said. “So essentially, they’re getting additional sleep deprivation before they even get to the PACER FORGE site. We’re getting them up early, keeping them up, not letting them sleep very much. … it just keeps amping up as you get closer and closer to PACER FORGE.
More Stress
The plan to prepare trainees to endure more stress effectively is still under review, Courtland said, but the idea is to not only introduce more stress into training activities but also teach trainees techniques for recognizing and coping with extreme pressure.
“It’s more understanding how you work through stress when you are stressed out,” Courtland said. “The idea is they get stressed out more here. It’s intense. They get that stress, but then we are walking them through it— ‘hey, you probably felt really stressed in that moment, here’s something you could have done, or here’s something that may have helped.’”
For example, trainees may be taught to use box breathing, a technique that uses equal counts of inhaling, holding, exhaling, and pausing to calm the nervous system, said Courtland, who would not discuss the list of techniques that is currently under review. If all goes well, the new stress portion of training could be approved by the end of September, she added.
“At the same time that we’re teaching them how to deal with stress, we are going to be turning up the stress and turning up the intensity,” she said.
MTIs will use regular after-action reviews of training events to ensure trainees understand how the increased stress affected their performance, Vaden said.
“I will more than likely see degradation in teamwork. I’ll see degradation in leadership. I’ll see degradation in situational awareness; I’ll see degradation in a lot of things,” Vaden said. “We’re just going to use those performance measures when we’re assessing.”
Courtland added that the success of the effort will involve seeing if trainees use the new stress techniques under increased pressure. “The goal is to teach them the tools, stress the hell out of them, and see if they know how to use the tools correctly.”
In other changes to BMT, training officials have partially completed a portion of the new air base training range that includes a non-flying F-16 Fighting Falcon. Trainees have begun learning and practicing how to re-arm the fighter with mock AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles and other training munitions that mock Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System rockets. The new air base training range will soon include two retired C-130 Hercules aircraft which arrived here in August.

Putin orders 72-hour halt to strikes on Kyiv as US envoys arrive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered a 72-hour halt to strikes on Kyiv, the Kremlin said Saturday, as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow seeking to revive stalled efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,” presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russia’s Tass news agency.
Peskov said the decision was linked to preparations for Witkoff and Kushner’s planned visit to Kyiv on Sunday, which Ukrainian officials have confirmed.
He also said the U.S. envoys would meet with Putin during their trip but dismissed the prospect of new proposals to end the war, saying there was “no talk of new ideas” for resolving the conflict.
The visit comes as Russia and Ukraine intensify aerial attacks, more than four years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Kyiv would suspend airstrikes during the envoys’ visit and called on Russia to do the same, raising hopes for at least a temporary reduction in hostilities as diplomatic efforts resume.
Washington’s push to end the fighting, now in its fifth year, has lost momentum as U.S. attention has been focused for the past six months on its war with Iran. The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, was in January, when they met Putin at the Kremlin. They have never previously visited Kyiv.
The envoys were met at the airport in Moscow by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Tass reported. Dmitriev shared photos of himself meeting the U.S. delegation as they disembarked, alongside the caption, “Welcome to Moscow, Peacemakers.”
With peace efforts stalled, Russia has intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with relentless bombardments recently stretching into daylight hours as Ukraine faces shortages of air defense systems.
On Friday, a Russian drone hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv, the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, known as the SBU, which is one of the agencies involved in carrying out deep-strike operations inside Russia.
Ukraine’s long-range strikes have hit Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce hubs, seeking to undermine the Kremlin’s war effort and economy while making ordinary citizens feel the consequences of the war.
The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, while the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.
In a social media post Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out overnight strikes on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports and linked the attack to the planned U.S. visit.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” he said.
“We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.”
Russian attacks killed five people and wounded five more at an industrial facility in Ukraine’s southern Dnipropetrovsk region, local military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha said. He described those killed as employees at the site.
“A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives,” he said.
A 62-year-old man was wounded and several homes and an apartment building were damaged in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said.
In a statement Saturday, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants in the region, describing them as “major suppliers of metal products for Ukraine’s military production.”
A further two people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on Ukraine’s Kyiv region, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. In the Boryspil district, a fire sparked by a strike partially destroyed a nine-story residential building.
Russian forces also repeatedly struck a shopping center in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging retail premises and sparking fires, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. A 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl were hurt.
Emergency crews responding to the incident were repeatedly forced to withdraw to safety because of the threat of further strikes, returning whenever conditions allowed, the emergency service said.
Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones overnight, Ukraine’s air force said. The drones included Shahed-type aircraft, around half of them jet-powered, as well as Geran and decoy drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 128 drones, according to the air force.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian attacks wounded three people, including a 14-year-old girl, in Russia’s border region of Belgorod, local officials said.
In a statement, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said its forces had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.
