Census 2027: The 14 questions and why opposition fears an NPR 'backdoor'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:06:05 UTC
19:06:05 KST

Opposition is raising questions over the methodology of population enumeration, alleging that it too has a “deeper nefarious purpose”
NEW DELHI: Although six years late, enumerators have started knocking on doors for the decennial headcount in Ladakh and snowbound regions such as Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand starting September 1.But doubts and fears have preceded the Census, turning what was meant to be a routine exercise to track population growth and aid policy planning into a fresh political flashpoint.
Until now, the caste census had been the main point of contention between the opposition and the government. The opposition had questioned the intent and methodology of an exercise being conducted in the country after almost 100 years.The contention has now moved beyond the caste census, and the opposition is also raising questions over the methodology of population enumeration, alleging that it too has a “deeper nefarious purpose”.
What is the controversy?
On August 14, the Centre notified the list of questions that officials will ask during population enumeration. The questionnaire, however, contains 14 new or modified questions compared with the 2011 Census.These include spouse's name, nationality as declared, father's particulars, mother's particulars, SC/ST/caste, literacy and digital literacy, highest educational level attained and stream/discipline, place of Covid-19 vaccination, total number of bank accounts, mobile number, Aadhaar number, voter ID number, passport number for Indian passport holders, and availability of a driving licence.
Interestingly, several of these questions, including details of a person's father and mother and their places of birth, were also part of the National Population Register (NPR) schedule notified in 2020.Moreover, the Union Budget presented on February 1 this year allocated Rs 6,000 crore for the NPR and Census 2027, even though the government has not yet notified any schedule for the NPR.The Budget document said the allocation included provisions for the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India and various schemes of the Registrar General of India, with Rs 6,000 crore earmarked for NPR and Census 2027.
What are the opposition's charges
Following the notification of the questionnaire, the opposition has accused the Centre of turning the Census exercise into a “backdoor for the NPR, and eventually, NRC”.Congress Rajya Sabha member Jairam Ramesh said the methodology of asking questions in Census 2027 is flawed and alleged that questions on religion, date of birth, place of birth and parents' details had never been asked in previous enumerations.“Census is confidential. Clearly, Census 27 has a deeper nefarious purpose,” he said in a post on X.Similarly, former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee alleged that the Centre was planning to conduct the Census in the form of NPR.“They have started the census. Census in the form of NPR. You have to provide your bank account number, mobile number and Aadhaar number. You must disclose the full details of all family members,” Mamata said.“No political party has been informed. At least the Trinamool Congress was not informed. Nobody knows whose name will be deleted. Is it going to be another SIR? Who knows,” she added.Even during the run-up to the Bengal assembly elections, she alleged that the Centre was planning to 'take away' people's citizenship in the name of NRC.Former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan also raised questions over the inclusion of the new questions, arguing that the Census should not be used to divide people.“The reported inclusion of questions about parents’ place of birth and religion in the upcoming Census is deeply troubling. The Census must not become a backdoor for the NPR and, eventually, the NRC. Citizenship cannot be tied to religion, and no census should be used to divide our people. The Union Government must immediately drop such divisive questions. Secular forces must stand united against this dangerous move,” Vijayan said.
Difference between Census and NPR
Census and NPR differ in their legal basis, objectives and the nature of information they are designed to collect.The Census is a statistical exercise meant to produce data on population, literacy, occupation, migration, housing and, in 2027, caste. It is used for making policies, allocating resources and delimitation.On the other hand, the National Population Register is a continuously updated register of “usual residents” created under the Citizenship Act, 1955.It is designed to maintain an identifiable database of people who have lived in a locality for at least six months or intend to stay there for the next six months, irrespective of their citizenship.
The NPR collects detailed identity information, including names, parents' particulars, place of birth, nationality as declared, address and identity documents such as Aadhaar, voter ID and passport, as well as mobile numbers. The data collected through NPR is linked to the proposed National Register of Citizens.Under Rule 3 of the Citizenship Rules, the Centre may order preparation of the National Population Register, from which the Local Register of citizens is prepared after verification.Rule 4 provides that individuals whose citizenship is doubtful can be flagged in the Population Register for further enquiry.The NPR data was first collected in 2010 alongside the 2011 Census house-listing exercise and updated through a door-to-door survey in 2015.However, both the Census and NPR are conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, under the Union Ministry of Home Affairs.
What the law says
Can Census data be shared?
The inclusion of the new questions has raised a larger question: Can information collected during the Census be accessed or used by government agencies for purposes beyond the exercise itself?The law says no. Section 15 of the Census Act, 1948 provides a strong legal shield around personal information collected during the Census.“No person shall have a right to inspect any book, register or record made by a census-officer in the discharge of his duty,” the Act says.“No entry in any such book, register, record or schedule shall be admissible as evidence in any civil proceeding whatsoever or in any criminal proceeding other than a prosecution under this Act or any other law for any act or omission which constitutes an offence under this Act,” it further says.This means that the information collected through the census cannot be used by other government agencies to determine the citizenship of a person.Speaking to The Times of India, advocate Ajinkya Udane said it would therefore be incorrect to accuse the government of divulging information collected through the Census.“Through the census, private information of people is being asked. However, the Census Act bars the government from divulging this information to its agencies,” Udane said.“So, to accuse the government of doing something which the law bars it from doing is not correct,” he added.Cyber and privacy law expert advocate Prashant Mali, however, stressed that Census data must remain a statistical instrument and “not become a backdoor for state surveillance”.“Section 15 of the Census Act creates a strong statutory confidentiality barrier. Individual census records are not open to inspection and are not admissible as evidence. Therefore, census information cannot legitimately be converted into an evidentiary database for citizenship determination merely because another government authority wants to use it,” Mali said.
Census data must remain a statistical instrument and “not become a backdoor for state surveillance”.
He said that even if a census record, or personal information traceable back to it, is accessed or used in a manner prohibited by Section 15, describing it as “independent intelligence” would not cure the underlying violation.“Substance must prevail over form. If the underlying census record or identifiable information has been accessed or used contrary to Section 15, I feel calling it independent intelligence does not cure the problem,” he said.“I feel the State cannot do indirectly through a citizenship inquiry what Section 15 of the Census Act prohibits it from doing directly through the Census record. A lawful purpose for processing does not automatically create a lawful source of data,” he told The Times of India.During the conversation, Mali said that the interaction between the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) and the Census Act will also be interesting to watch during the exercise.“DPDPA (Digital Personal Data Protection Act) Sections 3–17 are scheduled to come into force 18 months after 13 November 2025, i.e. 13 May 2027, while Census 2027 field operations occur around that period,” Mali said.
“This makes the interaction between the Census Act and DPDPA particularly interesting for the 2027 exercise,” he added.The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) is primary law which will dictate how the personal data is collected, processed and stored.It sets out obligations for entities handling personal data - such as obtaining consent, limiting use to the stated purpose, and ensuring data security - and grants individuals rights over their own data, including access and correction.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Russia’s elite drone unit says it used 1 million FPV drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:04:55 UTC
19:04:55 KST

- Russia's Rubicon drone unit claims it used over 1 million FPV drones and struck 280,000 targets in Ukraine from January 2025 to August 2026, an unverified, self-reported figure.
- Independent analysts say Rubicon grew from 1,450 to about 5,000 personnel by 2026, but that Ukraine has since regained an edge in mid-range drone warfare.
Russia’s Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies claims its operators used more than 1 million First-Person-View (FPV) drones and struck over 280,000 targets in Ukraine between January 2025 and August 2026, according to a statement the unit posted to its official Telegram channel. The figures come only from Russia’s elite drone unit itself and have not been independently verified.
Rubicon said the 20-month total makes it “the undisputed leader” in FPV drone use among all Russian units fighting in Ukraine. The unit also said it has published more than 45,000 videos of strikes on its Telegram channel, with new footage posted daily showing operations, tactics and the unit’s history.
As with the strike and drone-use figures, these numbers are self-reported by the unit and cannot be independently confirmed.
Rubicon was established on August 2, 2024, by order of Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov, according to reporting by the newsletter Two Marines, run by analyst Rob Lee and Ukrainian marine drone operator Dmytro Putiata. The center was created partly in response to Ukraine’s own specialized drone units and its “Drone Line” initiative, and was designed to centralize Russian research, procurement and combat deployment of drones, ground robots and unmanned boats under one command, rather than leaving that work scattered across volunteer-funded projects.
An investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty identified the unit’s commander as Colonel Sergei Budnikov, a 37-year-old former artillery and marine officer, with facilities including a training site at Patriot Park near Moscow.
Independent reporting has documented Rubicon’s rapid growth. The unit expanded from roughly 1,450 personnel in 2025 to about 5,000 by 2026, organized into battalion-sized detachments that each field dozens of quadcopter and fixed-wing strike teams, according to the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s analysis of the Two Marines data. That same analysis cautioned that Rubicon’s fast expansion has strained its recruitment pipeline and diluted the specialized training that made its early detachments effective.
Rubicon first drew significant attention for its role helping Russian forces cut off Ukrainian supply lines during the fighting in Russia’s Kursk Oblast in late 2024 and early 2025, after Ukraine’s surprise incursion there in August 2024. Ukrainian commanders quoted in independent reporting described the unit’s fiber-optic guided drones, which resist electronic jamming, as a serious problem, and Rubicon has continued operating on active fronts including the Kupiansk axis, where a Ukrainian brigade officer told Ukrainian outlet Suspilne in October that the unit’s use of remote mining and FPV drones was disrupting Ukrainian logistics.
Independent assessments diverge from Rubicon’s own self-promotion, however. While the unit’s tactics contributed to Russian gains around Pokrovsk, Myrnohrad and Kostyantynivka in 2025, the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s analysis found that Rubicon did not fundamentally change the broader stalemate in drone warfare along the front, and that by 2026 Ukraine had regained an edge in mid-range drone operations. Neither Rubicon’s claimed strike totals nor its claim of “undisputed” leadership among Russian drone units have been corroborated by Ukrainian officials or independent battlefield analysts.

Health warnings could reduce youth’s hours spent on social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:02:10 UTC
19:02:10 KST

Pop-up messages that warn of the harms of social media could help reduce youth’s social media use, a new study found.
Alcohol and tobacco products have health warnings about the negative impacts. Researchers say that social media could benefit from similar warnings too, such as “Using social media causes sleep problems. This is bad for your health,” and “Social media is associated with significant mental health harms for children and young adults.”
Exactly such pop-up messages showed up in a study published on JAMA Health Forum. The messages informed about the harmful impact of social media — such as depression, anxiety, worsened body image and sleep disruption. Researchers hope this could be yet another tool in the toolbox aimed at managing youth’s social media time more healthily.
“With substances like tobacco and alcohol, we find, on average, that well-designed warning labels change behavior,” lead study author Anna Grummon, assistant professor of paediatrics, said. As social media is a completely different product compared to cigarettes or alcohol, “where you just put the warning on the product and it lives there,” these warnings have to be “basically pop-ups,” Grummon said.
Researchers saw that over 1,000 youth aged 13 to 29-years increased their understanding of social media risks to their mental well-being after being exposed to 14 warnings on six health topics while scrolling. The warnings covered social media addiction, negative body image, sleep disruption, depression, anxiety, overall mental health harms and the fact that social media has not been proven safe for young people.
Participants consistently reported that the warning messages would reduce their social media use, authors said.
Youth rated each message in response to two questions: “How much does this message discourage you from wanting to use social media?” and “How much does this message increase your awareness of the harms of using social media?”
The messages that worked the best were those that warned about mental health harms, such as depression and anxiety, except the addiction warning.
While the data does not show why those messages performed best, “if I were to speculate, I would say that these are harms that resonate with people,” Grummon said. “People may think, ‘That’s right, I can see that happening to my friends or to me,’ and these are outcomes people care about.”

US ambassador visits Palestinian town amid rise in West Bank settler violence
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee met on Saturday with Palestinians, including the families of US citizens killed by Israeli settlers, in a Palestinian town in the occupied West Bank that has been the target of repeated settler attacks.
Settler violence in the West Bank has risen sharply since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition government, the most right-wing in Israel's history, took office in late 2022.
During the visit, Huckabee said that there was no plan underway to force Palestinians out of Gaza, after Israeli ministers laid out ideas on how to expel the war-battered territory's two million people.
"I can tell you categorically there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will," Ambassador Mike Huckabee told reporters as he visited Palestinian-Americans in the West Bank.
Several settlements have been established around Turmus Ayya, the Palestinian town near Ramallah that Huckabee was visiting on Saturday. Its residents say that harassment by militant Israeli settlers is common and that they are unable to stop them from entering the town and damaging their homes.
"We have many issues that we will address," Nawwaf Zaghoul, the town's mayor, told reporters ahead of the meeting, describing what he said were constant attacks by settlers.

The ambassador also said that the Israeli government has a responsibility to ensure the safety of Palestinians in the West Bank after a sharp rise in settler attacks.
"One of the messages that we have been sending and we will continue to send is that people in these communities have a right to live with a level of security and safety, and that the government has a responsibility to make sure that that happens," he told reporters.

"We are hoping that (the ambassador) will do something for us regarding these lawless settlers," Turmus Ayya resident Sameer Hazama said ahead of the meeting with the ambassador.
Huckabee visited Taybeh, one of the only Christian villages remaining in the West Bank, in June 2025 after a church there was vandalised. Huckabee said at the time that the desecration of a place of worship was an act of terror and a crime.
Netanyahu's government has also overseen an expansion of settlements across the West Bank, further entrenching Israeli control over territory that Palestinians seek for a future state.
Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, with the United Nations and most countries deeming the territory to be occupied. Israel's government says that the land is disputed, not occupied.
Huckabee refers to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, a term used by the Israeli government but not adopted by the US government. He has visited Shiloh, a settlement near Turmus Ayya, at least twice since 2025.

US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Moscow for talks on peace in Ukraine
MOSCOW - US special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Sept 5 for talks on ending the war in Ukraine, with the warring sides offering to curtail attacks during the discussions.
Russian spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS news agency that President Vladimir Putin would meet Witkoff and Kushner in the Kremlin later on Sept 5. The US envoys are then expected to visit Kyiv the following day.
US President Donald Trump suggested on Sept 4 that the United States had a fresh concrete proposal aimed at ending the war, which is now in its fifth year. He did not, however, elaborate on what that proposal would be.
Witkoff and Kushner landed at Moscow’s governmental airport where they were met by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev. A motorcade then took the three men into the city, a Reuters witness said.
Dmitriev, who told Reuters in June that he had remained in contact with the US negotiators during a pause in their visits to Russia, took part in all their previous meetings with Putin alongside the Russian President’s foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov.
He also played a role in negotiating US sanction waivers for Russian oil in 2026.
Peskov said in a statement posted on the Kremlin’s channel in Max messenger that Putin had ordered the military not to strike Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight on Sept 5, in connection with Witkoff and Kushner’s visit to the Ukrainian capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Sept 5 he had spoken to the two US envoys who are set to visit Ukraine on Sept 6.
He added that Ukraine was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow from now through Sept 7 and expected Russia to reciprocate by halting strikes on Kyiv.
A vast gulf in positions
The Russian Defence Ministry reported 53 Ukrainian drones in Russian airspace on Sept 5, significantly fewer than the average seen in recent months.
Moscow is celebrating City Day on Sept 5, with hundreds of thousands of people taking part in open-air festivities across the city.
A vast gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the 4½-year-old war, the deadliest in Europe since World War II.
A source close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of a possible trip by Trump’s envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.
“There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region,” the source told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident – based on reports from his commanders – that this would happen by the end of 2026.
Kremlin’s position ‘unshakeable’
Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow’s slow rate of progress. Ukraine refuses to surrender land that it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.
The Kremlin said on Sept 4 the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago – that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO – was “unshakeable”.
Since the last peace talks in February, each side has intensified long-range air attacks deep inside the other’s territory, while the war at sea has also escalated.
On the ground, the front lines have remained largely static, with Russia making only gradual gains in its attempt to take the whole of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to a summer of fuel shortages and rising prices for Russian motorists, while some 30 attacks on giant warehouses belonging mostly to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, have affected the consumer economy. REUTERS

NBU expanded businesses’ and communities’ access to credit amid intensified attacks by the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
The NBU adopted a second package of measures to support producers and communities. The list of eligible collateral and the rules for using portfolio guarantees have been expanded.
In response to the intensification of attacks on the production and warehouse facilities of business entities, as well as critical and social infrastructure facilities, the National Bank of Ukraine adopted a package of measures to support manufacturers, as well as local communities in financing their development, particularly in terms of restoring and supporting critical infrastructure. The NBU press service reported this on September 5, UNN reports.
Details
"The National Bank’s Board adopted the second package of announced measures to support manufacturers, as well as local communities in financing their development, particularly in terms of restoring and supporting critical infrastructure," the statement said.
In particular, the NBU reported that:
-  the list of eligible collateral for loans was expanded to include property rights to monetary funds (proceeds) for shipped goods (products) / completed work / provided services, and requirements for its eligibility were established, along with a liquidity ratio for such collateral of 0.3; the liquidity ratio for collateral in the form of unconditional and irrevocable guarantees from city and regional councils was also increased to 0.8; 
-  uniform approaches were introduced for taking portfolio guarantees into account when mitigating credit risk. 
As emphasized by the National Bank, these steps will help expand access to credit resources for retailers and manufacturers that do not have sufficient fixed assets to pledge as collateral, as well as for municipal and other enterprises whose capacity to implement important infrastructure projects with the guarantee support of local government bodies will increase significantly.
We remind you
As of August 11, 2026, the National Bank of Ukraine launched the easing of currency restrictions for businesses, the financial sector, and the population.

Over half the risk for postpartum psychosis is tied to genetics, large study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:35 UTC
19:00:35 KST

New research published in Molecular Psychiatry indicates that postpartum psychosis is heavily influenced by both common and rare genetic factors, with about half of the risk tied to genetics. The study also identified a specific gene involved in cholesterol production that provides evidence for shared biological pathways between postpartum psychosis, schizophrenia, and certain autoimmune conditions.
Postpartum psychosis is a rare but severe mental health emergency that occurs in roughly 1 to 2 out of every 1,000 mothers shortly after childbirth. It involves an abrupt onset of symptoms like mania, severe depression, confusion, and psychosis, which is when a person loses touch with reality through hallucinations or delusions. The condition poses heavy risks to both the mother and the infant, often requiring immediate medical hospitalization.
Earlier research established that this vulnerability has deep biological roots. A 2001 study showed that the tendency to experience a severe psychotic episode triggered specifically by childbirth runs strongly in families. Moving beyond familial history, a 2013 study discovered that women experiencing their first episode of postpartum psychosis show disruptions in their immune systems.
Alongside these immune factors, metabolic changes have also been implicated, as a 2017 meta-analysis suggested that people going through their first psychotic episode tend to have altered cholesterol levels. These findings paved the way for large-scale genetic sequencing to pinpoint the exact genes and shared biological pathways involved. To build on these insights, researchers led by Seulgi Jung and study co-author Behrang Mahjani, an assistant professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai who directs the Mahjani Lab, aimed to detail the specific genetic architecture of postpartum psychosis.
“Postpartum psychosis is a severe but understudied psychiatric disorder,” Mahjani told PsyPost. “Our previous study showed that sisters of women with postpartum psychosis have a markedly elevated risk, but its heritability had not been quantified and no specific risk genes had been identified. We therefore examined the contribution of both common and rare genetic variation to the disorder.”
The researchers first used data from Swedish national registers to estimate the overall genetic risk of the disorder. They examined health records from over 1.6 million mothers who gave birth to their first child between 1980 and 2017. Among this massive group, 2,514 mothers, or 0.15 percent, developed postpartum psychosis.
By tracking the health records of the mothers’ sisters and cousins, the researchers estimated the heritability of postpartum psychosis to be 55 percent. This indicates that more than half of the variation in who develops the condition can be attributed to genetic factors, a rate similar to that of bipolar disorder.
“The genetic contribution is substantial,” Mahjani explained. “Heritability in this range means that inherited variation accounts for a large share of the differences in vulnerability between individuals, comparable to what is seen for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.”
“This supports the view that postpartum psychosis reflects an underlying biological vulnerability rather than being simply a psychological reaction to the stress of childbirth,” he added.
To see how much of this heritability comes from common genetic variations, the team turned to the All of Us Research Program, a large national database of genetic and health information. They focused on whole-genome sequencing data from 198 mothers of European ancestry who had experienced postpartum psychosis, comparing them to 2,013 matched controls.
The team found that common genetic variants explained about 45.6 percent of the risk for postpartum psychosis. Because this is slightly lower than the 55 percent heritability estimated from family histories, it suggests that rarer genetic variations also play a role in the disorder.
The researchers then looked closely at rare genetic changes, specifically focusing on protein-truncating variants. These are severe mutations that essentially break a gene, preventing it from producing a functional protein. They analyzed a larger sample of 461 cases of postpartum psychosis and 4,610 unaffected controls.
Women with postpartum psychosis had an unusually high number of these disruptive mutations in genes that are generally highly constrained, meaning the genes do not usually tolerate mutations well without causing major biological problems. Based on these mutation patterns, the researchers estimated that there are around 81 specific genes that contribute to the risk of postpartum psychosis.
When analyzing which individual genes were most affected, the gene HMGCR stood out strongly. This gene contains the instructions for making a key enzyme that controls how the body produces cholesterol. A second gene, DNMT1, which helps maintain how DNA is regulated and read by the body, also showed a possible, though less certain, link to the disorder.
“The rare variants in HMGCR have large effects in the people who carry them, which is what allowed us to detect the gene despite a relatively modest sample,” Mahjani noted.
However, he cautioned against oversimplifying this connection. “HMGCR should not be read as ‘the postpartum psychosis gene,'” he said. “It is one of the many genes contributing to risk, and like other severe psychiatric disorders the condition is highly polygenic.”
To explore the broader impact of these genes, the researchers checked for mutations in HMGCR and DNMT1 across hundreds of thousands of individuals in two large medical biobanks. They found that rare mutations in HMGCR were also linked to conditions like vascular dementia and unspecified mental disorders, indicating the gene influences brain health outside of the postpartum period.
Finally, the researchers compared their list of genetic risk factors for postpartum psychosis against genes known to cause other illnesses. They found that a substantial percentage of the top risk genes for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia were also linked to postpartum psychosis. Additionally, they noted a genetic overlap with autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, and Crohn’s disease, with HMGCR appearing as a top risk gene for both schizophrenia and rheumatoid arthritis.
“The results were largely consistent with what genetic studies of related psychiatric disorders would predict,” Mahjani said.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. First, definitions of postpartum psychosis can vary across different medical records. The registry data used in the study often lacked the precise end dates of episodes, which makes it harder to classify the exact duration of the illness.
The researchers also did not separate women whose postpartum psychosis was their very first psychiatric episode from those who had a pre-existing condition, such as bipolar disorder. As a result, some of the genetic patterns they found might reflect severe mental illness in general rather than factors entirely unique to the postpartum period.
Additionally, the genetic sequencing data relied heavily on individuals of European ancestry, meaning the results might not fully capture the genetic risk factors present in other populations. Future studies with more diverse groups will help provide a more complete picture of the condition’s genetic roots.
“Our immediate priority is to replicate these findings in larger samples,” Mahjani said of the team’s next steps. “Beyond that, we want to understand how the genes we identified actually function in the disorder, and how genetic vulnerability interacts with the hormonal and immune changes that occur during and after pregnancy.”
“Mainly that postpartum psychosis has been remarkably understudied relative to its severity,” he concluded. “Progress will depend on continued access to the kind of large-scale genomic resources that made this work possible, such as the All of Us Research Program, and on studies large enough to identify additional risk genes with confidence.”
The study, “Genetic architecture of postpartum psychosis: from common to rare genetic variation,” was authored by Seulgi Jung, Madison Caballero, Adrianna Kępińska, Shelby Smout, Trine Munk-Olsen, Thalia K. Robakis, Veerle Bergink, and Behrang Mahjani.

Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:35 UTC
19:00:35 KST

In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile.
But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary.
Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy.
The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more.
Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East.
While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents.
“The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.”
Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.”
After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple.
The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party.
Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation.
The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year.
The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long.
The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post.
‘The past six months has failed’
“I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after?
“We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability.
“We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.”
Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade.
“It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength.
As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions.
The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May, has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination.
In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets.
The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”.
Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts.
A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank.
In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN.
Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis.
The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain.
Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.”
Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said.
‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld
Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war.
Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the World Bank.
During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein.
But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth.
“Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now.
“But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat.
“If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.”
Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced.
He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa.
“We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.”
Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.”
This article was amended on 5 September 2026. An earlier version erred in saying that Robert McNamara became head of the International Monetary Fund; he was head (as its president from 1968 to 1981) of the World Bank, the IMF’s sister organization.

‘It cost me many friendships’: former Brazil military chief reveals inside struggle to stop Bolsonaro’s coup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:34 UTC
19:00:34 KST

The far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro was in his final days as Brazil’s president when, six weeks after losing the election and still refusing to recognise the result, he summoned the heads of the armed forces to a meeting.
The defence minister, Gen Paulo Sérgio Nogueira de Oliveira, took out a document from a plastic folder and handed copies to the commanders of the navy, army and air force.
It was a draft decree proposing to invalidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s election in October 2022 and keep Bolsonaro in power.
“The draft coup decree – which some people still insist to this day never existed – was there, awaiting approval or rejection; consensus or a majority,” writes the then head of the air force, Lt Brig Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior, in a new book coming out this month.
After learning that the document would prevent Lula from taking office, Baptista Júnior told the defence minister he refused even to receive it: “The air force will not take part in this.” He then stood up and left the room.
The extensive investigation and trial that convicted Bolsonaro of attempting a coup concluded that the plot failed to move forward mainly because the heads of two of the three armed forces – Baptista Júnior and the army commander, Gen Marco Antônio Freire Gomes – refused to take part.
The navy commander, Adm Almir Garnier Santos, was convicted, as was Nogueira. Both are serving their sentences at military facilities, while Bolsonaro is under house arrest.
Freire Gomes has kept a low profile, but Baptista Júnior, speaking to the Guardian by video call, said he had decided to write a book to help prevent history from repeating itself.
In the book, the 65-year-old former fighter pilot gives a detailed, first-hand account of the various ways in which Bolsonaro tried to cling to power.
Baptista Júnior said he was motivated by the fact that, despite the abundance of evidence presented during the former president’s trial, opinion polls still showed that about a third of the population did not believe there had been an attempted coup.
“Keeping in power someone who lost an election is a coup d’état,” he said, speaking from his home in Brasília, where he was dressed in civilian clothes – having recently retired – and about to pick up his grandson from school.
The book, the Portuguese title of which translates as I Said No! – An Anti-Coup Bulwark, is due to be published on 15 September, about two weeks before the first round of the presidential election, in which Lula will face one of Bolsonaro’s sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro.
Some Bolsonaro supporters have accused Baptista Júnior of trying to influence the vote, although he makes clear that he will vote for neither Lula nor Flávio, and criticises both in the book. He said the timing of the book was simply the result of the writing and editing process.
Despite writing that he voted for the far-right populist in the 2018 and 2022 elections, and even recounting a lighthearted moment at a barbecue when he saw the first lady reprimand the president for drinking beer, Baptista Júnior is critical of Bolsonaro, a former army captain who spent 30 largely undistinguished years as a city councillor and then congressman before reaching the presidency.
He describes his former boss as someone with “significant limitations in political, institutional and administrative experience” and an “almost total imperviousness to outside opinions or information that did not conform to the ‘truths’ he had already established as his own” – citing his refusal to accept facts such as the scientific evidence supporting Covid-19 vaccination.
During the election, Bolsonaro became “entirely consumed by his own efforts to remain in office”, writes Baptista Júnior. After repeatedly casting doubt on the vote, the president ordered the armed forces to investigate the electronic voting system, but refused to accept their reports when they found no irregularities.
“He may still not believe the election result even today. Whether that is a matter of character, personality or something pathological, I don’t know,” said Baptista Júnior.
The book touches on, but does not go into detail about, one of the most shocking revelations from the coup investigation: a plan drawn up by army special forces to kidnap or assassinate Lula, the newly elected vice-president and a supreme court justice. Baptista Júnior writes that he was not summoned to those meetings and only learned about them through the press.
He does, however, recount more than a dozen meetings in which Bolsonaro summoned the heads of the armed forces to discuss ways to remain in power. At one of them, he witnessed the army chief tell the president, after hearing a proposal for an institutional rupture: “If you do that, I’ll have to arrest you.”
Baptista Júnior had already given that account in testimony, and during the trial both Freire Gomes and Bolsonaro denied it. But he stands by his account in the book, writing that it was not something anyone present would forget.
Saying no to the coup cost the pilot “many friendships”, he said. Even some military personnel still call him a “traitor” or a “watermelon”, a slur for soldiers seen as green on the outside because of their uniforms, but communist red within.
The attacks started soon after the air force chief refused to join the plot, when the army general Walter Souza Braga Netto, whom Baptista Júnior considered a friend, ordered other military officers to attack him on social media and “make his life and his family’s hell”. Braga Netto, Bolsonaro’s running mate, was also convicted over the attempted coup.
Most of Baptista Júnior’s revelations in the book initially emerged in 2024, when he was summoned to testify to federal police and only then, more than a year after leaving office, revealed that he had witnessed an attempted coup.
Juliano da Silva Cortinhas, who worked on the civilian side of the defence ministry between 2013 and 2016, before the Bolsonaro administration, said: “It’s positive that he [Baptista Júnior] and the army chief said no to the coup, but as a matter of duty they should have reported it to the police as soon as it happened.”
Cortinhas, who heads a security research group at the University of Brasília, said the armed forces could not present themselves as the “saviours” of democracy because that would be like “tripping society up and then holding out a hand to help it back to its feet”.
“It was the commanders who allowed active-duty officers to take part in politics,” he said, noting that the Bolsonaro administration had by far the largest number of military personnel serving in civilian posts since the end of the brutal 1964–85 military dictatorship.
Cortinhas sees as positive the fact that high-ranking officers were convicted of an attempted coup for the first time, but noted that others involved in the plot escaped justice, and many were not even identified.
“The risk of a new coup is even greater today,” he said.
The new factor, he said, was the US president, Donald Trump, who has sought to influence elections across Latin America in support of far-right candidates such as Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2022, when Joe Biden was in the White House, Bolsonaro’s vice-president acknowledged that attempting a coup would leave Brazil in a “difficult position before the international community”.
Cortinhas said he feared that if Lula was re-elected and Trump refused to recognise the result, some members of Brazil’s military could feel emboldened. “Coup-supporting groups remain within the armed forces,” he said.
Baptista Júnior confirmed that, although it was difficult to know how many, there remained active-duty military personnel who believed a coup d’état would be justified under certain circumstances.
“That’s why eternal vigilance is the best path,” he said.

‘I don’t have any friends’: why do young people today have fewer mates?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:34 UTC
19:00:34 KST

On Tess Lavanda’s YouTube channel there is one video with substantially more views than the rest: it is titled “I don’t have any friends” and has been watched more than half a million times since she posted it a month ago.
Over on Instagram she has posted dozens of reels with titles like “I turned 22 alone”, “Living alone in London” and “Feeling alone this summer is OK”, each garnering thousands of views and hundreds of comments, many from people feeling the same way.
A quick search for terms like “solomaxxing”, “loneliness influencer” and “no friends aesthetic” brings up hundreds of videos and posts from people – many of them teenagers and young adults – talking about what life is like without friends.
“I think people feel relieved it’s finally being spoken about,” says Lavanda, 22. “No one felt brave enough to speak about it because there is this culture where people think being alone is embarrassing and wrong.”
New research from the Institute for Public Policy Research published this week found the number of young people in England with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, now standing at one in 20, and a growing number saying they are not happy with the friends they do have.
Lavanda says: “I think there’s a lack of drive for people to go out and meet people, and when you do go out, people are on their phones so it’s harder to approach them.”
She has always struggled with making friends but it was only during the pandemic when “that lack of a genuine friendship really hit” and she started to feel isolated. “I had no one to talk to and I went into quite a dark place,” she says.
Then one night when she was about to head out alone feeling “so scared and awful”, she put on her camera and started talking.
Lavanda says: “I had no intention of posting it. This was just purely a video for myself, about how I was feeling to try and hype myself up, really. But then I thought maybe this will help someone, so I posted it.
“I was fully expecting to be judged and bullied but the response was overwhelmingly positive. People were sharing their own stories, and I realised that so many people feel the exact same way.”
She says there is a growing trend for solo life to be “aesthetic or romanticised” but her videos are more about showing people without friends they’re not alone. “I think people take comfort in the fact there’s now a voice about this topic,” she says. “It’s more important to just be honest and speak up.”
There has been growing discussion around why young people today report having fewer friends than previous generations – a combination of social media, mental health problems, the Covid pandemic and financial instability are all often thrown into the mix.
Pamela Qualter, the UK’s leading scientific expert on child and adolescent loneliness, says there are no straightforward answers. But it is clear that, as a society, we’ve stripped back places where young people can practise basic social skills like saying “hello”.
“We’re really lacking those very simple conversations you have each day with somebody you just bump into,” she says. “More people are working from home, and people have less disposable income at a time when there are very few free or cheap places for people to come together.”
Qualter says it is these “weak ties” – small interactions with acquaintances – that form the building blocks and social skills that can build into solid friendships.
But she emphasises there is not much evidence to suggest young people are actually getting lonelier: those aged 14 to 24 report the highest levels of loneliness in the UK but this has always been the case.
“Maybe our expectations of friendships are changing. Maybe those people with fewer close friends are happy with that,” she says.
However, there is also evidence to suggest young people are increasingly dissatisfied with the friendships they do have.
Jodie-Leigh Foster, a training and development officer at UK Youth, teaches youth workers about youth loneliness and isolation, as well as empowering teenagers to launch their own projects tackling the problem.
She says it is the quality of friendships that many young people struggled with. “These are friendships that often play out on social media and group chats, which can quickly turn to bullying and harassment,” she says. “That leads to them becoming isolated and withdrawn.”
Money is also often an issue: some young people reported not being able to afford to get transport to see people outside school. Others struggle with large crowded spaces, especially since the pandemic, which increased levels of anxiety.
Foster says: “People make assumptions about being a young person, that it’s a carefree time in their lives, and the whole world’s at their fingertips. But for some young people, that’s actually really overwhelming and daunting. It’s a tough time to be a young person.”

Gaza refugee says sister-in-law ‘would be alive’ if Home Office had let her come to UK
Unknown

A man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza would still be alive today if the Home Office had agreed to bring her and her family to Britain.
Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, fled Gaza in 2020 and was granted refugee status in the UK in 2021. After the destruction of large areas of Gaza by Israeli forces following the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023, he applied to bring his brother Hassan, Hassan’s wife, Maryam, their two young children and other family members to the UK in October 2025. He said the Home Office rejected their application.
The process required them to travel to a visa application centre (VAC) for biometric checks, but there was not, and still is not, a VAC in Gaza. It is difficult for Palestinians to leave the territory to access a VAC elsewhere.
In April this year the family asked the Home Office to waive this requirement and grant permission for “predetermination” of their application and “biometric excusal”.
The Home Office is understood to have rejected this request, so the family launched a legal challenge. The Home Office agreed to reconsider its decision but issued a new refusal in July.
Prior to the second Home Office refusal, and shortly after Maryam gave birth to Ismail, who is now seven months old, she was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, which had spread to her lungs. Doctors in Gaza said they did not have the facilities to treat her.
The family provided the Home Office with medical evidence concerning Maryam’s condition, including cancer test results and medical referral reports. They also provided evidence of their living conditions in Gaza, which involved sleeping in tents and shortages of food, medicine and clean water.
Anwar said the Home Office again refused the family’s request for predetermination and biometric excusal but that it accepted the evidence of Maryam’s cancer.
In the Home Office’s letter refusing the visa application on 31 July, seen by the Guardian, officials stated: “Given the current situation in Gaza, reliable healthcare may not be accessible.”
They accepted that Maryam was facing a significant risk of harm because she was in a conflict zone and could not travel to a VAC. Although the Home Office officials found the circumstances relating to travel to a VAC “somewhat compelling”, they concluded that owing to the difficulty in travelling to the VAC, it was “in the best interests of the children to stay with their parents and delay travel to the UK” for the time being.
They concluded the family’s situation did not meet the threshold for “compelling circumstances” and said that pre-entry checks needed to be carried out because the family came from “a territory where terrorists operate”.
In the legal challenge, the family’s lawyers stated: “It is difficult to understand what circumstances would ever qualify as compelling if the present circumstances do not.”
Maryam died from cancer on 28 August.
Gordon McKee, the Labour MP for Glasgow South, raised the family’s case with ministers in June. He warned about Maryam’s deteriorating health and the consequences of the collapse of reliable healthcare in Gaza.
In his letter to Mike Tapp, then a Home Office minister, McKee said the case involved “exceptional humanitarian circumstances”. He asked Tapp to consider reviewing the case personally.
Anwar said: “We believe Maryam’s case raises serious questions about how the UK government deals with Palestinian families in Gaza who are trying to reunite with their families in Britain, particularly when a family member becomes seriously ill while trapped in a conflict zone and unable to safely reach a VAC.
“I believe that if the Home Office had agreed to bring Maryam and her family from Gaza to the UK when we first applied last October, Maryam would still be alive today.
“Maryam is now gone, but her family remains in Gaza. We are now urgently asking the UK government to intervene to protect Maryam’s surviving family members and to find a way to bring them to safety and reunite them with their family in the UK.”
Speaking from Gaza, Maryam’s husband, Hassan, said: “I am struggling to come to terms with losing my wife while I remain trapped in Gaza with our children, including our seven-month-old baby.
“Throughout Maryam’s illness, we were trying to find a way for our family to overcome the biometric requirement and move forward with our applications. The Home Office accepted that Maryam had cancer and acknowledged the evidence, but decided that our circumstances were still not compelling enough to justify biometric deferral or predetermination.
“Now I have lost my wife, and I am left trying to protect our children and find a way to get them out of Gaza and to safety.”
Home Office sources said they did not routinely comment on individual cases.

Hong Kong mega bridge’s popularity takes toll on helicopter, ferry services: lawmaker

Transport Department figures obtained by the SCMP showed that vehicle flow via the popular Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge reached a record high of 5.21 million last year, up more than 19 per cent from 4.36 million in 2024.
The 2025 figures were the highest in the past five years, following border closures due to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021. The bridge was opened to traffic in 2018.

The bridge’s peak in popularity coincided with helicopter service operator Sky Shuttle’s announcement that it would axe its scheduled flights between Hong Kong and Macau, which had operated since 1990.
Sky Shuttle said the service suspension took into account the coming relocation of Macau Heliport to the new heliport at Macau International Airport Terminal 2. It added that its Macau-Shenzhen route was excluded from this suspension and would operate as a scheduled flight service.
Starting this month, the company said its helicopter services would switch to a charter-only model, operating five days a week.

War on Earth could spill over to the moon, Chinese space scientists warn
Study models how geopolitical tension could extend into orbit with rival spacecraft dogfighting, evading each other or blocking strategic routes
Spacecraft could hide in the complex gravitational environment around the moon, where their trajectories are difficult to predict, before emerging and moving towards targets closer to Earth when needed, according to a team from the Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xian.
The craft could also be stationed near “choke points” – regions where important or fuel-efficient routes converge – ready to intercept rivals and potentially force them to break through or take less efficient routes, the researchers wrote in the Chinese-language Journal of Command and Control in July.
Such capabilities could have an impact without an actual confrontation, they argued.
“Without directly using force, [a country could] compel an adversary to change its route, delay a mission, give up a launch window or incur higher costs,” said Dang Zhaohui, the report’s lead author and an associate professor at Northwestern Polytechnical University’s school of astronautics.
“What is at stake in cislunar orbital competition is not any single spacecraft, orbit or route, but the ability to access, control and use space – and to deter adversaries – that they provide.”

The Price of Privacy When It Comes to Dementia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Ronald Reagan, Charlton Heston, Tony Bennett, and Danny Glover have something in common. So do Margaret Thatcher, Norman Rockwell, and Sean Connery.
All had been afflicted with Alzheimer’s or dementia—the progressive neurologic disease characterized by memory and functional loss—but with an important difference. The first group chose to make a public announcement of their diagnosis during their life, and the second chose to keep their dementia diagnosis private, their condition revealed by their survivors only after their death.
Maintaining the confidentiality of one’s health information is a fundamental right, but when a public figure receives a life-limiting diagnosis, does disclosure matter? Some choose to do so as a form of farewell to their supporters and fans, others to raise public awareness of the illness that has afflicted them.
When the actor Michael J. Fox announced almost three decades ago that he had been diagnosed with early-stage Parkinson’s disease, a bright spotlight was shone on the then relatively unknown neurologic disease. His namesake foundation has since raised over $3 billion for Parkinson’s disease research, his testimony to the U.S. Congress helped boost federal funding for neurologic and stem cell research, and his patient advocacy empowered persons with Parkinson’s to come forward, share their experiences, and receive support from others as they go through their Parkinson’s journey.
In my decades-long career as a memory disorders specialist, I have found that one characteristic shared by patients with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia is a preference, at least in the early stages, for secrecy about the diagnosis. After I informed a famous patient of her Alzheimer’s diagnosis, I handed her an informational brochure on memory loss. Her husband promptly took it from her, folded it neatly, and hid it underneath his coat, saying “In case we bump into one of her fans in the elevator.”
Perhaps more than other diseases, the desire for privacy is particularly strong for dementia, which is still viewed by many as a mental health disorder rather than a neurologic disease like Parkinson’s disease or ALS.
My patients and families typically limit the disclosure of the diagnosis on a need-to-know basis, and many choose to hide it till the end. Doctors, clinics, and hospitals are complicit with this secrecy, with only around 50% of people with dementia having their diagnosis documented in their medical records.
Since dementia tends to begin later in one’s life, many simply fade into retirement and anonymity, which inevitably leads to social isolation and misleading others of their whereabouts. Interestingly, the shame associated with dementia is not typically shared by people afflicted with other neurological disorders such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or ALS.
When singer Celine Dion was diagnosed with the rare, progressive neurologic condition called stiff-person syndrome, she came forward with a message to her fans, putting an end to speculation about the mystery illness that caused her to cancel a series of performances. In her documentary, she bravely allowed a glimpse of the painful muscle spasm she experiences daily. Through her foundation, Dion personally donated millions of dollars towards research into the rare disease that afflicts fewer than 5,000 people in the United States.
There are over 57 million people with dementia globally, with nearly 10 million new cases diagnosed every year. In 2050, an estimated 152 million people will have Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia. In the United States alone, there are currently 7.4 million people age 65 or older living with dementia. While many important advances have been made in research on prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment of Alzheimer’s, many more of its mysteries need to be unraveled and a cure remains elusive.
While I understand and respect people’s desires for privacy, the potential upside of destigmatizing dementia are significant. If every person, famous or not, whose life has been touched by dementia—in a spouse, parent, friend, or in themselves—were willing to share their stories and advocate for more research funding, better public policies, and greater community and caregiving support, perhaps the stigma and shame associated with this neurologic disease would be eased, and we would be closer to finding a cure.
The desire for secrecy of a dementia diagnosis can sometimes have serious consequences. The actor Gene Hackman was living with dementia in private for years. The public became aware of his plight only when he was found deceased inside his home after his wife, who was his primary caregiver, unexpectedly died before him. Interviews with their neighbors painted a picture of a private and secretive couple who were rarely seen outside their home. It was believed that Mr. Hackman died alone after his wife and primary caregiver passed. Left to fend for himself, he was unable to provide for his basic needs: food, water, medications.
It took a brain autopsy for Robin Williams to get diagnosed with Lewy body disease, a form of dementia that produces visual hallucinations, sleep disturbance, and tremors. For years, his condition was misdiagnosed as depression and Parkinson’s disease, as his doctors were unable to connect the constellation of classic symptoms to recognize that dementia has set in. After Williams died by suicide, his widow Susan Schneider Williams became a public advocate for Lewy body awareness, putting a public face to a disease that many have not even heard of.
Most people who are diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia are not public figures, but like these famous people, they need to decide the price they are willing to pay for privacy. Even in the early stages of the disease, many decide to withdraw from their social circles, cease the activities they enjoy, and retreat to a life that is much too small. A big part of this unfortunate decision stems from the shame that comes with the diagnosis of dementia, which is often viewed not just as a loss of memory, but of intellect, social status, and identity.
So pervasive is the secrecy surrounding a dementia diagnosis that I now ask every family caregiver of my patient a telling question: If you became unavailable, who would take care of your loved one? Invariably, they declare that they are not going anywhere, that they will never leave their husband, wife, parent, or friend, so I ask a more direct question: If you were hit by a Mack truck on your way home today, who will feed, administer medication, and keep your loved one safe tonight?
If they provide anything other than a reassuring response, I counsel them on the importance of having a back-up plan: a relative, friend, or neighbor who can check in on the person with memory impairment to make sure they are safe. I remind them of the benefits of socialization and maintaining relationships with others in people with dementia. I tell them that even with cognitive changes, there is still a lot of life left to be lived—new places to see, new people to meet, new experiences to enjoy.
I reassure them that whether they decide on privacy or disclosure, we will be there to support them, minimize dementia’s impact on their daily lives, and provide comfort when we can.

We Need a Cure for AI Health Hype
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

“I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!).”
This is what Dario Amodei, the co-founder of Anthropic recently posted on X.
Truth be told, this is not an uncommon take among AI leaders. On 60 Minutes last year, Demis Hassabis, co-founder of Google DeepMind, declared that “we can cure all disease with the help of Al… maybe within the next decade or so, I don’t see why not.”
Actually, there’s a big reason why not: human nature. An estimated 80% of chronic diseases and premature deaths are not driven by our genes, but by the way we live: what we eat, how much we move, how we sleep, how we manage stress and stay socially connected. It’s true AI can accelerate drug discovery and personalize nudges for our daily behaviors, but it can’t “cure all disease” while ignoring human nature, free will, and how we live.
The view among those currently working to lower the disease burden is considerably less utopian than in AI. “Diabetes, Alzheimer’s, heart disease—we don’t have cures for any of those common diseases,” says cardiologist Dr. Eric Topol. “To think that in the next five or 10 years new drugs are going to change everything, there’s no precedent for that. It’s unrealistic, and it sets the expectations for AI too high. It’s hype.”
“Cancer is not one disease. It is more than 200 distinct diseases, all with different causes, biology and mechanisms,” explains Dr. Catherine Young, a Senior Fellow at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. “Scientists who study cancer rarely talk about ‘curing cancer’ because it’s nothing more than an empty slogan.”
As Amy Dockser Marcus writes for The Information, we’ve been here before. In 2000, on the heels of the first sequencing of human DNA, Francis Collins, then-director of the Human Genome Project, predicted that “in another 20, 25 years we should be able to prevent or cure most cases of cancer, of diabetes, of heart disease, of multiple sclerosis, of asthma.” And yet, here we are, 26 years later, facing a growing epidemic of chronic diseases.
Daphne Koller, CEO of the AI-driven drug development company insitro, calls it the “magic wand” assumption. “Hundreds of years into modern medicine,” she writes, “our understanding of most human disease, and much of healthy physiology, is best captured by the parable of the blind men and the elephant; in this case, a really huge elephant.”
The current debate about whether AI can cure all diseases is more than a tempest in a GPTeapot. It points to a larger problem: we are too often focused solely on improving the machines, and too rarely focused on investing energy and resources in improving humans.
In 2024, Amodei wrote about the limiting factors that stand in the way of AI transforming the world for the better: “speed of the outside world,” “need for data,” “intrinsic complexity,” “physical laws” and “constraints from humans.”
Of those, I would argue that the constraints imposed by humans will be the ultimate limiting factor. And I'm not alone.
“If for every dollar and every minute that we invest in developing artificial intelligence, we also invest in exploring and developing our own minds, it will be okay,” suggests Yuval Harari in his book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. “But if we put all our bets on technology, on AI, and neglect to develop ourselves, this is very bad news for humanity.”
As we work to realize all the possibilities of AI, the bottleneck that will hold us back from maximizing its benefits will be what it has always been throughout human history: human nature. That is why I believe the greatest risk we face is that AI will get better but humans won’t.
We need the same relentless focus on helping humans tap into their better selves and achieve better health outcomes through healthier daily behaviors as we have on helping the machines achieve better frontier models.
What we don't need is hype.
