Police probe death of Tesla driver after collision on Hong Kong road
Crash along Island Eastern Corridor temporarily closes some Central-bound lanes near North Point Ferry Pier
Police are investigating the death of a 54-year-old driver of a Tesla whose vehicle collided with two other cars along Hong Kong’s Island Eastern Corridor.
The police force said it received a report at 10.37am on Saturday that the man was driving west along the corridor when he was suspected to have lost control of the Tesla and collided with two other vehicles near the North Point Ferry Concourse Promenade.
Police added that the Tesla driver sustained “no superficial injury”, but was rushed unconscious to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai. He was certified dead at 12.08pm.
The driver of one of the other vehicles was a 44-year-old man. The force did not specify whether he sustained any injuries in the accident.
Dashcam video of the incident circulating online shows a black Tesla drifting across lanes before colliding with a white seven-seater and another white vehicle, which appears to drive away without stopping.
Images of the incident showed the airbags had deployed in the Tesla while the right side of the white seven-seater was dented.

French presidential candidates clash over aid to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05

French presidential candidates clash over aid to Ukraine
French presidential candidates – far-right leader Marine Le Pen and former prime minister Édouard Philippe – have clashed over a pledge by Le Pen's National Rally to halt aid to Ukraine.
Source: Statements by the politicians on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: The dispute began with a comment by Louis Aliot, vice-president of the National Rally. Responding to a question from BFMTV about the possibility of "turning off the tap" on aid to Ukraine, the mayor of Perpignan confirmed that the far right planned to halt support if it came to power.
"The healthcare system, the education system, the entire economy – everyone is on the verge of exhaustion, yet they still find money to continue financing weapons (...) but who pays for all this?" the politician said.
Former prime minister and presidential candidate for the centre-right Horizons party Édouard Philippe, currently one of the strongest contenders to face the National Rally leader in the second round, criticised the far right for this position.
"'Turning off the tap' on Ukraine means serving Russia... Weakening Ukraine, as Marine Le Pen seeks to do, is a threat to the security of Europe and France. I will do everything I can to prevent this," Philippe stressed.
Le Pen sharply responded to her opponent, saying that his "international track record is just as pitiful as his results in the economic and budgetary spheres".
"Since the beginning of Russia's aggression against Ukraine, I have been calling on France to urgently convene a major peace conference to promote not the continuation of bloodshed, but a diplomatic settlement to this terrible war, which, I remind you, has already claimed the lives of two million people – something you failed either to stand up for or achieve," the far-right leader added.
She also recalled that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was received at the Palace of Versailles and later at the Fort de Brégançon when Édouard Philippe was prime minister during Emmanuel Macron's first five-year term.
In response, Philippe highlighted the National Rally leader's ties to Russia, calling her "the voice of weakness and criminal appeasement of the Kremlin".
"Since Russia invaded Ukraine, everything has become clear: there is a dictator-aggressor and a democracy that has been attacked. Putting them on the same level is not diplomacy; it is criminal weakness. You opposed arms supplies to Ukraine and sanctions against Moscow. Had you been elected, Ukraine would have been abandoned long ago. You can rewrite your speeches about Russia, but no one will be able to forget your ties to Russia," the politician stressed.
The French presidential election will be held in two rounds in late April and early May 2027. Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, remains the frontrunner in opinion polls.
Background:
- In August, Gabriel Attal, former French prime minister and presidential candidate, filed a complaint regarding a suspected Russian disinformation campaign ahead of next year's presidential elections.
- French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot warned that Paris "will not tolerate any attempts at foreign interference".

Over 40% of Ukrainians live below poverty line, complicating medical access – infectious diseases specialists
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:00:49 EEST
17:00:49 KST

Honored Doctor of Ukraine and President of the Ukrainian Society of Infectious Diseases Doctors Olha Holubovska has declared a threat to national security due to the spread of infectious diseases against the backdrop of a sharp wartime increase in the proportion of the population living below the poverty line.
"41.6% of Ukrainians are not just poor, but are living below the poverty line... Infectious diseases are social diseases, and they always increase during times of cataclysm. These are diseases that concern not only a specific individual, but form the foundation of the country's national biosecurity," Holubovska said on Friday during a round table held at the Interfax-Ukraine agency on "Responding to the challenge of poverty: New initiatives for State Social Protection Policy," initiated by the Association of Frontline Cities and Communities of Ukraine.
"I cannot get used to a situation where a person with limited financial resources to support their health or treat an illness simply says: 'I will not ruin my family financially.' This is simply unacceptable, especially when it comes to treatable conditions. People living below the poverty line, and all Ukrainians, require attention from the state and social protection," the Honored Doctor added.
She also drew attention to health expenses, including various transportation costs when people are forced to travel for medical care following the closure of a significant number of hospitals, as well as mass layoffs of doctors and medical staff, which complicates access to care.
Holubovska emphasized that the absence of modern medications in state treatment programs threatens the effectiveness of therapy. "These packages do not correspond to the actual cost of treating a particular infectious disease, and no medical facility can guarantee quality medical care. It does not matter to a person how many items fall into the 'accessible medicines' category—over a thousand items—a specific individual receives one specific drug, and if this drug is missing or if the available drugs belong to outdated treatment regimens, it makes no difference to them. The same applies to inpatient treatment: if the state prohibits demanding that patients purchase guaranteed supplies, it must at least guarantee the actual availability of these medications in hospitals rather than prohibiting patients from saving themselves," Holubovska stressed.
She called for a review of the criteria for effective resource utilization in the healthcare system. "Many issues do not require money at all, but simply proper organization. When I repeatedly hear that prevention is expensive, I ask: have you calculated how many people, if treated in a timely manner, do not subsequently become disabled, how much you save on sick leave payments, and how productively that person continues to work for the country? No one calculates this," Holubovska said.
For his part, People's Deputy of Ukraine and co-founder of the public organization VPO Ukraine Serhiy Kozyr noted that Ukraine lacks a comprehensive state policy regarding internally displaced persons (IDPs) and human capital, creating risks for citizens' social protection.
"There is a lack of preventive measures to avoid certain consequences—whether a person ending up below the poverty line or contracting infectious diseases. According to recently published research, the number of homeless people in our country has increased by 46%. In terms of demographics, 40% of them are internally displaced persons. These are people who lived in their own homes, were more or less successful, and certainly not poor, who are now becoming homeless and deprived of social protection. When we see that there is no state policy even for IDPs who are currently struggling and renting apartments, what can we say about people living under such conditions?" he said during the round table.
The parliamentarian emphasized that the number of displaced persons remains consistently high at around 4.6 million, and the state is not prepared for new waves of displacement from frontline areas. "The cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk have already been included in the active combat zone. Over 90,000 residents living in these two cities could potentially relocate. Is the state ready to receive them? Believe me, no. All of this will once again fall on the shoulders of municipal authorities... According to current data, there are 71,000 spaces in temporary accommodation centers. But believe me, they exist only on paper. Today we see that people are simply left to their own devices, without an authority to systemize and guide the process," Kozyr said.
He stated that there is no single central authority to systemically respond to challenges related to IDPs, highlighting the necessity of developing a state policy to address these challenges.
In turn, Member of Parliament and member of the Parliamentary Budget Committee Lesia Zaburanna stated that the poverty rate among Ukrainians has doubled since the start of the full-scale invasion, with both internally displaced persons and residents of the capital in need of critical support.
"The poverty rate currently recorded, which has doubled since the start of the full-scale invasion, is something I clearly observe in my constituency on the Left Bank of Kyiv, where the vast majority of people—both local residents and internally displaced persons, who currently number nearly 450,000 in Kyiv, or even more—face a situation where they can only afford a fraction of the food items they need," she said during the round table.
According to her, this extends to providing for children and obtaining proper medical care.
Zaburanna stressed the need to review social policy and account for risks prior to the onset of critical situations. She also initiated proposals for the state budget aimed at raising social standards, including a review of VAT policy on food products and medicines.

Rich Dad, Poor Dad author’s vast debts spark awe – and some bitterness – in China
Robert Kiyosaki’s claim to be US$1.2 billion in debt has sparked heated debate in China, where property investors have suffered steep losses
The revelation that Rich Dad, Poor Dad author Robert Kiyosaki has amassed a staggering debt pile has sparked heated discussion in China, where property investors have suffered painful losses in recent years amid a deep market downturn.
The 79-year-old Japanese-American author, who inspired generations of investors to take on leverage to scale up their investments, claimed in a series of podcast interviews over the summer that he owed US$1.2 billion.
His ex-wife and long-term business partner Kim Kiyosaki clarified in an interview with Vanity Fair in late August that the figure covered borrowings related to investments in roughly 1,500 flats, which were shared with his partners rather than personal liabilities.
Others recalled reading the book when they were younger and credited it for encouraging them to invest in stocks and funds, in posts on the Chinese social media platform RedNote.

Units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces have been ordered to observe a ceasefire along the line of contact from 00:00 on September 5 until 23:59 on September 8.
This was reported by the publication Ukrainska Pravda and confirmed by Militarnyi’s own sources.
According to the sources, Ukrainian troops may open fire only in response to Russian actions. It is currently unknown whether Russia will implement a reciprocal ceasefire.

Japan's 2027 budget requests hit record high for 4th consecutive year: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:59:32 UTC
16:59:32 KST

Saadet Gokce
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Japan's ministries requested a record 143 trillion yen ($918 billion) for the fiscal 2027 budget, marking a record high for the fourth consecutive year, according to the Finance Ministry.
The total includes 12 trillion yen ($76 billion) under a new uncapped special investment category, Kyodo news agency reported Friday, citing the ministry.
The category was created to support Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's “responsible and proactive” fiscal policy as financial markets remain concerned about the government's rising spending commitments.
The government is seeking to shift spending long funded through supplementary budgets into the initial budget.
Japan already has the worst fiscal position among major advanced economies, while rising interest rates are increasing the cost of servicing its debt after years of low rates.
The initial budget for fiscal 2026 totaled 122.3 trillion yen.
“We will craft a budget that achieves both strong economic growth and fiscal sustainability,” Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told reporters.
“The budget-making process will closely assess each initiative's contribution to growth and its potential to spur private investment,” she said.
“The goal is to fundamentally reshape Japan's budget to strengthen its growth potential.”
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said at a separate news conference that the increase from the combined total of the fiscal 2025 extra budget and fiscal 2026 initial budget is “not that big.”
Kihara added that Takaichi's government has not ruled out compiling a supplementary budget.
Debt-servicing costs reached a record 36.64 trillion yen ($234 billion), with the assumed interest rate used to calculate payments raised to 3.8% from 3% in the fiscal 2026 budget.
The Health, Labor and Welfare Ministry submitted the largest request at 36.58 trillion yen ($234 billion), reflecting the country's aging population.
The Defense Ministry requested 8.84 trillion yen ($57 billion), including funds to develop attack drones.
Many ministries also submitted “itemized requests” without amounts, raising the possibility of further increases.
The Cabinet is expected to finalize the draft by year-end, with the government aiming to pass the budget by the end of March after submitting it to parliament next year.

Saudi Arabia set to buy over 10,000 guided bomb kits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:55:42 UTC
16:55:42 KST

- The State Department approved a possible $5 billion sale of over 10,000 JDAM-ER guidance kits and bombs to Saudi Arabia, with Boeing as the contractor.
- The extended-range wing kit more than triples a standard JDAM's glide range to over 45 miles, and past Saudi JDAM purchases have drawn congressional scrutiny tied to the Yemen war.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible $5 billion sale of Joint Direct Attack Munition kits to Saudi Arabia, notifying Congress on September 4 of a deal covering more than 10,000 guidance kits and bombs.
It is one of the largest single munitions packages Washington has cleared for a foreign buyer in years, and it centers on a weapon whose sales to Saudi Arabia have drawn political controversy in the past.
The request covers 5,004 KMU-572 and 5,000 KMU-556 guidance kits, the hardware that turns an ordinary “dumb” bomb into a GPS-guided precision weapon, along with 5,004 BLU-111 500-pound bombs and 5,000 BLU-117 2,000-pound bombs to attach them to. The package also includes fuzes, target detectors, spare parts and years of contractor support. Boeing, based in Arlington, Virginia, would be the sole contractor.
What Saudi Arabia is actually buying is the extended-range version of JDAM, known as JDAM-ER. The standard JDAM kit, in service since the late 1990s, straps a GPS-guided tail fin and steering system onto an unguided bomb, letting it hit within about 40 feet of a target instead of missing by hundreds. The ER variant adds a pop-out wing that unfolds after release, more than tripling the weapon’s glide range from roughly 15 miles to over 45 miles. Developed jointly by Boeing and the Australian government, the wing kit doesn’t add meaningful weight or bulk, so it can be bolted onto any aircraft already cleared to carry a standard JDAM, from F-15s to B-52s. The extra range matters operationally because it lets a pilot release the weapon farther from a target’s air defenses rather than flying directly overhead.
Saudi Arabia has bought JDAM kits from the United States for more than a decade, and those purchases have not always been routine. During the Saudi-led military campaign against Houthi forces in Yemen, which began in 2015, reports of Saudi airstrikes killing civilians using U.S.-supplied JDAM kits drew sustained criticism from human rights groups and members of Congress. The Obama administration froze a sale of precision-guidance systems to Saudi Arabia in December 2016 over those concerns, and the following year a bipartisan Senate resolution attempting to block a $500 million bomb sale to Riyadh failed by a narrow 53-47 vote after senators debated the war’s civilian toll on the floor. Yemen’s civil war has been under a broadly held ceasefire since 2022, and this new notification does not mention Yemen or reference any conditions tied to that history.
As with all Foreign Military Sales notifications, the State Department framed the deal in standard terms: it would support U.S. policy goals by strengthening a Major non-NATO Ally, improve Saudi Arabia’s ability to defend its own territory and operate alongside American and other Gulf forces, and would not shift the region’s military balance. The department said it isn’t aware of any offset agreement, an arrangement where a contractor invests in the buyer’s domestic industry in exchange for the deal, and that any such arrangement would be negotiated separately between Boeing and Saudi Arabia. Officials also said the sale would not require any additional U.S. personnel in Saudi Arabia and would not hurt American military readiness.
Congressional notification triggers a review period during which lawmakers can object, but it does not guarantee the sale goes through as proposed, or on this timeline. Past Saudi arms packages have been delayed, scaled back or, in at least one case, formally paused after congressional pushback. Nothing in the current notification indicates a specific timeline for delivery if the sale is finalized.

Where's the snow? Could 2026 be Australia's worst season?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:49:12 UTC
16:49:12 KST

IN BRIEF
- Snow depth has reached a record low with five ski resorts closing operations almost a month early.
- The unusually warm winter is believed to be the cause of the short season.
Australian ski resorts are being forced to close a month early due to record-low snow depth.
Snowy Mountain's Spencers Creek hit a historic Australian low, recording a snow depth of 31.2 centimetres on 3 September.
The peak depth was 94.5cm on 13 August — the third lowest depth recorded in the region since 1954.
On average, peak depth is recorded in the first weeks of September. From the 1950s to the 1970s, the average depth in the first week of September was just over 180 centimetres — compared to the 120cm average from 2020 to 2025.
Deep Creek and Three Mile Dam also recorded record-low snow depths in 2026.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Deep Creek registered record-high snow depths of over 200cm in 1964 and 1981, while Three Mile Dam had record-highs just over 100cm in 1956 and 1995.
The 2026 ski season was the shortest on record, with five of Australia's ski resorts already shutting the slopes.
Victoria's Mount Baw Baw and Selwyn Snow Resort in NSW closed operations before the end of August — with Mt Hotham, Falls Creek and Charlotte Pass closing over the weekend.
Only three of the eight mainland ski resorts in Australia remain open — Perisher, Thredbo and Mount Buller.
Ski season's premature end can be chalked up to the winter warmth and a lack of snow-bearing cold fronts.
The unusual winter warmth can be attributed to a multitude of weather behaviours, including El Niño, above-average sea surface temperatures, limited cold air in frontal systems and the ongoing impacts of climate change.
Australian Climate Council councillor and meteorologist Dr Andrew Watkins told SBS News in May it would be a warm winter.
"It's a winter of grabbing the skis when you can," he predicted.
He said Spring would come early with "clearer skies and more frosts".

Boss of STIHL: Time for reforms – this is how we will safe prosperity and welfare state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:48:40 UTC
16:48:40 KST

The German economy has been in crisis for years. Writes Nikolas Stihl in an OpEd für Euronews. Better business conditions are the key to breaking out of this stagnation. What’s at stake is nothing less than securing prosperity and welfare state. STIHL is the world’s best-selling chainsaw brand.
The state of the German economy is serious, very serious. Over the past eight years, we’ve lost approximately 15 percent of our industrial production. Month after month, Germany loses around 15,000 industrial jobs. And the industrial base that underpins our prosperity is starting to erode. Private net investment has fallen to almost zero. On balance, companies are doing nothing more than replacing what wears out. High costs are paralyzing companies’ willingness to invest. Even the special depreciation package (the “Investitionsbooster”) that the German government introduced in mid-2025 has done nothing to change that.
Of course, US tariffs, China’s aggressive industrial policy, and geopolitical tensions weigh on investment too. But the real problems are of our own making: an overregulated economy, high energy costs, high labor costs, high taxes, and falling levels of education and skills.
Planned reforms are not enough to reverse the economic trend
At the beginning of the year, many entrepreneurs had almost lost faith in Germany’s ability to reform. In July, the German government surprised everyone with a reform of statutory health insurance, along with reform plans for pensions, taxes, and the labor market. This package isn’t enough to pull Germany out of its structural crisis. But the current coalition showed it can compromise to help move the country forward. If those compromises were now unpicked and watered down, the damage to business confidence in politics would be devastating. The planned reforms are still not the breakthrough we were hoping for, the one that would actually turn the economy around.
Right now, we need to put everything into the next round of reforms, the ones that deliver real momentum for investment and growth. And that means the governing coalition, employers, and unions all stepping outside their comfort zones to live up to their responsibility for Germany. The special funds for defense and infrastructure will hardly lead to a self-sustaining upswing in the economy unless conditions for doing business here improve noticeably. The next reform steps have to keep cutting bureaucracy, raise the total hours worked, bring labor costs down, and give companies real reasons to invest in research and development.
Public authorities should enable, not obstruct
What we should expect from public authorities is nothing less than high-quality administration: rules people can understand, procedures that are lean and fast, reporting requirements that are reasonable. Digital, and supported by artificial intelligence. Clear rules and fast, straightforward decisions should make investment possible, not hold it back.
The draft law presented by the new Baden-Württemberg state government on reducing reporting and documentation requirements could send an important signal. The principle is simple: statutory reporting obligations should be dropped across the board and only retained where their necessity is explicitly justified. If public authorities acted far more as service providers for people and businesses, it would strengthen confidence in Germany as a place to do business – and in politics too.
Increase hours worked
People working in industry are hugely dedicated, responsible, and highly professional. Without that commitment, German companies would not be succeeding the way they do around the world. STIHL is just one example among countless others.
But demographics are slowing the whole economy down and putting massive pressure on the welfare state. To protect our prosperity and to ensure high levels of social benefits, the total number of hours worked has to rise. More hours worked means more economic output. So the debate about working more is really a debate about holding on to what we have – and it is in no way a debate about employees being lazy.
Germany has to use every lever it has to get those hours up. Incentives to work more hours. A longer working life, with fair exceptions for physically demanding jobs. Better use of the labor we already have, meaning people out of work and people in part-time roles. Skilled immigration. No sick pay for the first day of illness. An end to doctor’s notes issued over the phone. Productivity gains from digitalization and AI won’t offset what demographics are doing to us.
Reduce labor costs
The collective bargaining round in the metal and electrical industry, which will begin in fall 2026, will be a key factor in determining whether Germany remains an industrial nation or falls further behind. The reason is simple: we no longer have the productivity edge over our main competitors that justifies those high labor costs. That’s why I’m calling for a 40-hour workweek – with no increase in pay. I know I’m asking a great deal of unions and employees. But I’m not trying to take anything away from anyone. Quite the opposite. I want industrial companies to be able to compete, production to stay in Germany, and jobs to be safe.
And the current debate pays far too little attention to non-wage labor costs. Contributions to pension, health, long-term care, and unemployment insurance should not go above 40 percent of gross wages. That is the economic limit. Getting there means overhauling the social security system from the ground up. The German government’s latest reform measures do at least address the stabilization of contribution rates for pension and statutory health insurance. However, the 40 percent limit has already been far exceeded.
Priority for research
The close links between world-class research institutions, universities, innovation clusters, and innovative companies rank among Germany’s greatest strengths as a business location. Give innovative companies better conditions and you speed up the whole chain: knowledge moves faster, and so does the production and marketing of what comes out of it, new business models included. Regulatory leeway would do that. So would higher tax incentives and more venture capital. Overall, innovations and the approvals they need must be given far greater priority than before, and they must not be held back by bureaucracy.
Future-oriented fields deserve far more targeted support: the industrial use of AI, robotics, biotechnology, medical technology, space technology, and quantum technologies. The Germany Fund, launched at the end of 2025, is only a start, measured against other countries with strong research bases.
Act decisively
We have no more time to lose. Because only a strong, competitive place to do business can secure prosperity and a strong welfare state.
Germany has shown many times that it can reinvent itself. But if people are going to understand what’s coming, we have to start with an unflinching look at where we actually stand. And then set out a plan they can follow, one that spells out what will change for them. With a plan like that, the government can give direction, bring people with it, and win back trust. It’s time to act.
Dr Nikolas Stihl is the grandson of the company’s founder, Andreas Stihl, and represents the third generation at the helm of the world’s leading chainsaw brand and a global technology company. Under his leadership, STIHL has further expanded its international presence and, in 2025, achieved a turnover of 5.48 billion euros with 20,246 employees worldwide. STIHL has been the world’s best-selling chainsaw brand since 1971.

====================================================================================================

when the power goes out, how can the architecture keep a house cool?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:45:23 UTC
16:45:23 KST

COOLING MOVES BACK INTO THE HOUSE
At Jalmanjar Farmhouse outside Ahmedabad, cooling begins with a perforated facade of compressed earth blocks. This outer skin filters the sun while windcatchers draw air through the enclosure. Behind it, verandas and balconies occupy the shaded space between the outer jali and the inner rooms, and an open courtyard cuts through the center of the plan. The house does have active systems, but much of its thermal work has already started in the wall and in the void before a machine enters the equation.
Before cooling became an appliance, it was an integrated part of the building. Openings faced prevailing winds because air needed a route through the house, and courtyards created cooler pockets close to occupied rooms. Thick masonry slowed the passage of heat, and deep overhangs shaded from solar gain in the first place.
Mechanical air conditioning loosened architects’ reliance on these passive methods. Once a compressor could correct the temperature indoors, architecture gained far more freedom to ignore what the sun and nighttime air were doing outside. Of course, summers are getting hotter and demand for electricity is growing. Designers are revisiting how much of that work the house can take back, and how architecture can regain responsibility for temperature.
Jalmanjar Farmhouse, PYHT — BioArchitects, Ahmedabad, India, 2025 | image © Amalgamate
WHEN THE THERMOSTAT GOES DARK
During power outages, the idea feels much more urgent. It’s during these events that the envelope and the plan determine how quickly heat enters, where it accumulates, and whether cooler air can move through after sunset. Researchers describe this capacity as passive survivability: the ability of a building to maintain tolerable indoor conditions when the systems it normally depends on stop operating.
A 2022 Applied Energy study modeled apartments during the Pacific Northwest heat wave of June 2021 and found that integrated shading and natural ventilation could have lowered peak indoor temperatures in Portland by about 14°C (25 °F) during the three-day event. The same strategies reduced active cooling loads by as much as 80 percent.
With this in mind, a deep overhang or operable window becomes more valuable. It can reduce energy use on an ordinary afternoon, or even become part of the house’s emergency behavior when electricity disappears. The 2022 study focused on a dry-summer climate where cooler nighttime air can be harnessed effectively, which already suggests one of the limits of passive cooling.
A 2026 review mapping 197 residential studies makes the same point at a much larger scale: envelope design, ventilation, shading, and thermal storage work in climate-specific combinations. Their effectiveness changes with building type, local conditions, and how residents operate the house. Of course, there’s no single passive strategy which can be just copied from one climate to another.
Jalmanjar Farmhouse, PYHT — BioArchitects, Ahmedabad, India, 2025 | image © Amalgamate
SHADE CREATES A new ROOM
At Nedarag Guesthouse in southeastern Iran, NextOffice places three residential units beneath a broad palm canopy that floats over a shared courtyard. The roof takes the force of the sun while the dry-stacked stone rooms sit beneath it, separated from the hottest surface by a layer of moving air.
The courtyard becomes part of the cooling system, yet its environmental role is inseparable from how people use it. Guests pass through it and children play there, while local gatherings occupy the same shaded space. Cooling extends beyond the sealed room and starts producing territory where habitation can move outside.
Jalmanjar works through a similar thickness at the edge of the house. PYHT — BioArchitects uses the compressed-earth jali as a porous outer boundary that shades the enclosure and allows air to enter through integrated windcatchers.
The zone behind the screen holds verandas and planted pockets alongside circulation, giving residents a sequence of thermal conditions instead of a hard line between interior and exterior. The payoff is both spatial and environmental, as shade becomes a place to sit and airflow creates a reason for a passage to stay open. A climatic buffer becomes part of the home.
Nedarag Guesthouse, NextOffice, Baluchestan, Iran, 2026 | image © Ehsan Hajirasouliha
THE WALL BUYS TIME
In Jaipur, Malik Architecture turns black sandstone into its House of Solid Stone. Hollow interlocking walls create a thermal break while reducing the amount of stone used, and narrow courtyards slice into the heavy mass to pull light and air deep into the plan. Glazed areas sit behind deep overhangs and hand-cut operable screens. The house makes heat feel physical. Simply put, there is an enormous amount of material between the afternoon sun and the spaces where people sleep and gather.
Thermal mass changes the timing of heat instead of making it disappear. A thick wall absorbs energy and slows its journey toward the room, creating a delay between the hottest part of the day and the moment that heat reaches the interior face.
Meanwhile, at Karm Architecture Lab’s Breathing House in Marsa Alam, where summer temperatures can approach 50°C, fossilized coral-limestone walls reach 45 to 60 centimeters thick. A secondary skin shades the southern elevation, while the plan opens toward prevailing winds from the Red Sea. The wall buys time, meaning that when nighttime temperatures fall enough, accumulated heat can move back out before the next day begins.
Breathing House, Karm Architecture Lab, Marsa Alam, Egypt, 2023 | image © Farah Faheem
HANOI NEEDS A DIFFERENT HOUSE
Bat Trang House in Hanoi breaks the visual pattern of heavy desert masonry with a porous ceramic envelope. VTN Architects wraps the family home in locally made bricks whose openings filter direct sun and let air pass through. Green spaces occupy the layer behind the facade, followed by the inner enclosure, creating a three-part ventilation system through a dense urban house.
The architects say the arrangement removes the need for artificial air conditioning. Its logic belongs to a hot-humid climate, where the dramatic day-to-night temperature swing available to many desert buildings is far smaller and permeability takes on greater importance.
Vo Trong Nghia learned that relationship with climate long before founding VTN Architects. Speaking with designboom in 2021, he recalled growing up in a Vietnamese village without electricity, air conditioning, or even an electric fan: ‘trees, water, ventilation, and sunlight became the most important issues in our lives.‘
His description of cooling was equally direct, with shade from a large tree and wind moving across a pond before entering the home. The sequence is simple, but it points toward a broader principle. Climate-responsive architecture starts with the conditions already present on the site and decides what the house can do with them.
Bat Trang House, Vo Trong Nghia, Hanoi, Vietnam, 2021 | image © Hiroyuki Oki
WHEN HEAT STARTS DRAWING THE PLAN
In Ahilyanagar, Kaushal Tatiya Architects organizes its 7,000-square-foot Anthill House as interconnected brick chambers, borrowing the thermal logic of insect mounds without turning the building into a literal imitation. Courtyards bring air into the plan, while perforated brick walls and ventilation shafts create stack-driven airflow.
A water cascade cools the central living area through evaporation. The need to move heat upward starts shaping the section, while the route of air through the building begins influencing where voids and openings appear.
Kaushal Tatiya Architects, Anthill House, Ahilyanagar, India, 2026 | image © Avesh Gaur
monolithic walls enclose a tall atrium
Casa 1736 brings that same idea into the compressed fabric of Barcelona. HARQUITECTES faced a deep urban lot where the center could easily have become dark and poorly ventilated, so the architects emptied it out. A tall atrium now rises through the house, drawing light downward and encouraging warm air to escape through a roof opening. Thick low-cement monolithic walls add thermal inertia around it.
The environmental device is also the social center of the home, with family spaces gathering around the void. Here, the demand for ventilation helps decide where the household meets.
Casa 1736, HARQUITECTES, Barcelona, Spain, 2024 | image © Adrià Goula
A HOUSE THAT USES THE WHOLE DAY
Zyme Studios considers the sharp temperature changes of California‘s Yucca Valley desert over a full 24-hour cycle with its proposed Oscillation House. Heavy walls store thermal energy, broad overhangs hold direct sun away from the glazing, and an east-side pool cools air through evaporation before operable openings draw it across the interior. Each move contributes a little. Together they reduce the amount of heat the mechanical system eventually has to remove.
A house organized around these exchanges asks for a different relationship with comfort. The afternoon and the night are allowed to behave differently. A shaded exterior room may become useful when the sun shifts. Openings gain value after temperatures fall, while thermal mass releases energy accumulated hours earlier.
The building is working across time, and the resident begins reading it that way. The thermostat’s promise of one stable indoor temperature is replaced by a home whose cooler and warmer zones move through the day.
Oscillation House, Zyme Studios, California, USA, 2023 | image courtesy Zyme Studios
PASSIVE SURVIVABILITY ENTERS THE FLOOR PLAN
Recent research is beginning to put numbers around how much the geometry of a home can change its performance in extreme heat. A 2026 Energy and Buildings study analyzed 6,931 real apartment plans and grouped them into 36 representative types before simulating them across 20 historic heat waves in a hot-humid climate.
Every archetype crossed the study’s thermal-safety threshold within 36 hours during the modeled outage conditions, with survivability pressure rising sharply around 20 to 22 hours. Smaller units experienced greater peak heat stress, while differences in spatial configuration affected how overheating developed within the apartments.
Austin’s City Park Residence brings that concern into a contemporary American house. Alterstudio uses breezeways and deep eaves to reduce heat gain and encourage passive cooling, while the wider design responds explicitly to Texas power-grid instability and extreme weather.
The project shifts the conversation from efficiency toward resilience. An efficient house may consume relatively little energy while all of its systems are available. Passive survivability asks another question: how long can the architecture keep supporting its occupants after those systems disappear?
City Park Residence, Alterstudio, Austin, Texas, 2025 | image © Casey Dunn
THE a/c CAN STAY
Passive cooling has limits, and many designers view those limits as useful instead of inconvenient. A strategy that performs well in a hot-arid climate can behave very differently in a humid city. Thermal mass needs a way to release stored heat. Natural ventilation depends on useful outdoor conditions and acceptable air quality. Extreme heat can still demand active cooling for safety. The strongest contemporary houses treat passive design as a way to reduce the distance the air-conditioner has to cover.
Homes can bring responsibility back into walls, courtyards, openings and shaded thresholds. They can delay heat and divert it to create places where air can breeze through the rooms. Mechanical cooling can handle the remaining gap. As heat intensifies and electricity grids strain, that shared responsibility could become increasingly useful. Homes can employ the A/C later, use it less, and remain inhabitable for longer after it stops.
Bat Trang House, Vo Trong Nghia, Hanoi, Vietnam, 2021 | image © Hiroyuki Oki

U.S. approves $750M tank engine sale to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:44:45 UTC
16:44:45 KST

- The State Department approved a possible $750 million sale of 60 AGT-1500 tank engines to Saudi Arabia, built by Honeywell at Anniston Army Depot, Alabama.
- The AGT-1500 is a gas turbine engine that powers every M1 Abrams tank worldwide, and Saudi Arabia has operated the tank since a 1989 purchase of 315 units.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible $750 million sale of 60 AGT-1500 tank engines to Saudi Arabia, notifying Congress of the deal on September 4. The engines, along with spare parts and years of contractor support, would go toward sustaining Saudi Arabia’s existing fleet of M1 Abrams tanks rather than funding new tank purchases.
The AGT-1500 is the only engine that has ever powered an M1 Abrams. It’s a gas turbine, the same basic technology used in helicopters and small jets, adapted in the 1970s to drive an armored vehicle instead of a rotor. When the Army tested it head-to-head against a conventional diesel engine at Aberdeen Proving Ground in 1976, the turbine won because it could start instantly in extreme cold, run on almost any liquid fuel without adjustment, and produce enough torque to take a 72-ton tank from a standstill to 20 mph in about six seconds. It also runs quieter than a diesel, part of why crews nicknamed the Abrams the “Whispering Death” during the Gulf War, since armored units could close on a position with far less warning than tank crews had grown used to.
That combination of power and stealth came at a cost the Army has managed for nearly five decades: gas turbines are notoriously fuel-hungry, and keeping the fleet running has meant a continuous cycle of engine swaps and depot rebuilds rather than routine field maintenance. Honeywell, which absorbed the engine’s original manufacturer, Avco Lycoming, has kept it current through a program called TIGER, for Total Integrated Engine Revitalization. Production itself moved in 1995 from a shuttered plant in Stratford, Connecticut, to the Anniston Army Depot in Alabama, where it remains today and where this new batch of engines would be built.
Saudi Arabia has operated the Abrams since 1989, when it bought 315 M1A2 tanks in a deal worth roughly $3.1 billion. Rather than buying new tanks since then, Riyadh has spent the years since steadily converting and rebuilding that original fleet into a Saudi-specific configuration called the M1A2S, including a 2016 deal worth $1.15 billion that added dozens more conversions and battle-loss replacements. Every one of those tanks, regardless of how many times its turret or electronics get updated, still needs an AGT-1500 underneath it, and turbine engines wear out and get pulled for depot overhaul on a schedule diesel engines simply don’t require. This new order functions less like a tank purchase and more like the maintenance bill for keeping that fleet operational for another decade.
Honeywell would be the sole contractor on the deal if it goes through, and the State Department said it isn’t aware of any offset arrangement, the kind of side deal where a contractor agrees to invest in the buyer’s domestic industry, attached to this sale yet. Any such arrangement would be worked out separately between Honeywell and the Saudi government.
Congressional notification doesn’t mean the sale is final. Lawmakers have a review period during which they can object before the U.S. government, Honeywell and Saudi Arabia sign an actual contract, and past Foreign Military Sales notifications have occasionally been scaled back or delayed at this stage. The State Department said the deal would not require sending any additional U.S. personnel to Saudi Arabia, since the Kingdom already operates and maintains its own Abrams fleet with existing contractor support in place.

Longer exclusion orders cut domestic violence repeats, police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:40:00 UTC
16:40:00 KST

Longer exclusion orders cut domestic violence repeats, police say
New rules on barring perpetrators of domestic abuse from re‑entry to their homes for up to 72 hours have led to a fall in repeat offenses, police say.
The exclusion orders provide more time for the victims of domestic violence and abuse to gather their thoughts as well as to re‑enter the home safely and to attend to practical matters.
While the 72‑hour maximum barring from the home is shorter than the periods in some other EU countries and concerns have been raised about those who violate an exclusion order, the changes have led to improvements, stakeholders say.
At the same time, shelters have noticed an increase in psychological abuse, which is harder to prosecute.
Kristi Mäe, deputy director general of the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), said the regulations which took effect in mid‑April have allowed police to impose exclusion orders for longer periods than before.
"Looking at the overall statistics, exclusion orders have been imposed in 142 cases during this period," Mäe said, noting that in around 20 percent of cases, the maximum period of 72 hours was imposed, while in 25 percent of cases a 48‑hour exclusion order was issued. Previously, the maximum duration of barring entry to the home had been 12 hours.
Mäe said the rules permitting longer exclusion orders have fully justified themselves, as violence is less likely to recur when longer orders are imposed.
"When we looked at specific cases, we found that where a longer exclusion order had been imposed, particularly for 72 hours, there was less of a recurrence of violence," Mäe said.
The duration of an exclusion order is assessed based on factors including whether children are involved and whether the period provides enough time to access services and seek help, she noted.
"We have drawn up a risk assessment matrix for exclusion orders lasting 48 to 72 hours, meaning orders at or near the maximum duration. It is based on the specific situation at the scene, but indicators to consider include previous incidents, recurrence and an assessment of whether the danger could escalate. The timing of the incident is certainly important — for example, whether it is Friday or Saturday, or whether a long holiday period is just beginning. In such cases, with a 12‑hour exclusion order, the victim may not have an opportunity to contact victim support or access services," Mäe said.
Mäe noted officers also consider a victim's condition: Whether they need more or less time to calm down, receive initial counseling or gain an understanding of their legal options.
"Fourth comes the availability of services — whether victim support, social services, child protection or the courts will be available over the following days. If services are immediately available, the period does not have to be 72 hours, but if they are not, a longer exclusion order gives the victim time to plan protective measures. That is what we base our decisions on," Mäe outlined.
Police nevertheless continue to impose 12‑hour exclusion orders most frequently.
"This means it has been assessed that the risk of escalation is lower and that it is not a recurring incident. If it happens on a weekday, for example, the victim can immediately turn somewhere for help and is in a position to make decisions — that is why a 12‑hour exclusion order is imposed. Whether the perpetrator is taken to sober up or has to find somewhere to stay for those 12 hours depends on the specific circumstances," Mäe said.
Mäe gave two examples in which a 72‑hour exclusion order had been pressed into use. One incident took place in southern Estonia in August, when a man became verbally and physically aggressive after a woman went to rouse him from the sofa. Since three small children were also present during the incident, the man was given a 72‑hour exclusion order. At a meeting with a local PPA officer five days later, both the woman and the man who had acted abusively were put in touch with the necessary services following a joint discussion.
The second example dates from May, and happened in Tallinn. In this incident, a man had ejected a woman from her home reportedly as he was angry she had gone to a party with colleagues. The incident also culminated in physical violence; the PPA imposed a 72‑hour exclusion order, which allowed the woman to return home safely.
Margo Orupõld, head of the Pärnu Women's Support Center, said the impact of the legislative amendment has not yet been directly felt at the facility, adding she does not have precise information about the effects of the new rules. Orupõld explained that clients who contact the support center may not even be aware if police have imposed an exclusion order on the perpetrator or not, or if they have, how long its duration might be. This is mainly since during a stressful time of crisis, such details are not the victim's primary concern.
Nevertheless, Orupõld said she sees the legislative amendment as representing a supportive measure for women as it gives them time to make decisions calmly, knowing that the violent party is not currently present in the home.
Orupõld says she considers a rise in psychological abuse to be the greater problem. She said psychological terror in the home is characterized by constant controlling behavior. Police are often not called in such cases as these don't always involve physical violence and there is no direct evidence, something which Orupõld considers a very serious issue. Another obstacle is that even when violence can be proven, women often later decline to give statements, meaning cases cannot be resolved even if proceedings were initiated at the scene.
"If the woman herself refuses to give a statement, the police can bend over backwards — without the woman's cooperation, the case will not get very far," Orupõld noted of the discrepancy.
Pille Tsopp-Pagan, head of the NGO Women's Support and Information Center, likewise said that support centers in Tartu and Põlva counties have not noticed any change resulting from longer exclusion orders as yet, though added this could also indicate the extended exclusion periods' rationale has been met. "It is possible that these victims have not ended up with us because they have time to pack their things and think," Tsopp-Pagan said. However, the most direct impact on support centers would be a decline in the number of people urgently needing temporary accommodation, and this has not happened, she added.
"At the same time, that number is small for us anyway: Of around 300 women who came to us, 26 needed a shorter or longer stay," Tsopp-Pagan said, citing last year's figures. "This year, that number has not changed."
Mäe acknowledged that there is still room for improvement in both the practice and regulation of exclusion orders. For instance the PPA does not have information on how many cases there have been in which exclusion orders were violated, she noted. "I am not currently aware of any cases in which an exclusion order has been violated. But we have not yet looked into it in that level of detail; we will certainly do so in the future," Mäe said.
At present, there are no provisions under criminal law or criminal procedure allowing the PPA to penalize violations of exclusion orders.
"In principle, we ask the person violating the exclusion order to comply with that. Where needed, we have the right to utilize direct coercion, and if a violation goes on, we can impose a coercive payment of up to €9,600," Mäe explained.
Mäe noted that some other countries have stricter systems in place when it comes to violations, and exclusion orders themselves can last for weeks rather than days. In Mäe's view, this is certainly an area where Estonia could further improve the range of measures available in the future.
At the same time, the changes had been a definite step in the right direction.
"I would say that we have made a fairly good start on implementing the new exclusion‑order regulations. We can certainly improve further, because there are still many IT solutions that could help speed up the process. We will definitely continue working on that, and training our staff on domestic violence is an ongoing process. I certainly would not dare to say that everything is perfect and there is no room for improvement," Mäe concluded.
A rise in domestic violence cases in Estonia was reported this year.

U.S. Air Force opens bids for its Megatron contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:38:13 UTC
16:38:13 KST

- The Air Force opened industry feedback on a new command-and-control purchasing contract nicknamed "Megatron," part of its DAF Battle Network program.
- A contract award is targeted for summer 2027, following a draft plan released September 4 and an industry day scheduled for October 7.
The U.S. Air Force has given one of its newest contracting vehicles a name that sounds like it belongs in a Hollywood blockbuster: Megatron.
The Department of the Air Force posted a notice on September 4 on the government’s public contracting portal, opening a new multi-year purchasing arrangement called the “DAF Battle Network ‘Megatron’ Multiple Award Contract.” The deal will let the Air Force and Space Force buy a wide range of command-and-control technology from several companies over time, rather than negotiating a separate contract for each purchase. Despite the name recalling the shape-shifting villain from the Transformers franchise, Megatron here refers only to the contract’s internal nickname, not a weapon system, robot or any single piece of hardware.
The contract falls under an Air Force office that oversees the service’s effort to link sensors, data systems and decision-making tools across the Air Force and Space Force, known by the acronym PAE C3BM. That broader effort, called the DAF Battle Network, grew out of the Advanced Battle Management System, the Air Force’s contribution to the Pentagon’s push to connect sensors and weapons across every branch of the military so commanders can act on information faster.
Under Megatron, companies would compete to supply technology across several categories: digital infrastructure, sensor integration, secure data processing, network connectivity, software applications and computer-simulated training environments. The Air Force plans to split the winning companies into two groups, one reserved for small businesses and one open to companies of any size.
The September 4 notice released a draft version of the contract’s requirements for companies to review and comment on before the Air Force finalizes its plan. That draft document is restricted, meaning interested companies must formally request access and pass a review of their business registration before they can see it. Companies have until September 30 to send written feedback to the Air Force contracting officer overseeing the program, Julianne Payne.
The Air Force will also hold a virtual industry day on October 7, running from 8 a.m. to noon Eastern time, where the program’s manager, Jeffery “Ryan” Compton, and Payne will brief companies on the formal bidding process expected to follow. Air Force officials said they won’t hold one-on-one meetings with individual companies during the event because of how many are expected to attend, though all questions submitted live will be compiled and made public afterward.
According to the timeline the Air Force released, officials approved the plan for Megatron in early August. A draft request for bids is expected by the end of this year, with a final version following in early 2027 and a contract award targeted for the summer of 2027.

By dpa correspondents.
Wolfsburg, Germany (dpa) – The surprise agreement of a comprehensive savings package featuring 50,000 job cuts at Europe’s largest carmaker Volkswagen caused consternation across Germany on Friday, with the future of four major plants still uncertain.
Hanover Mayor Belit Onay said he was “extremely frustrated” by the deal on the company’s “Future Plan 2030,” which was unanimously approved at a meeting of the supervisory board on Thursday evening.
The northern German city is home to one of the four sites, alongside Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm, where Volkswagen said it cannot guarantee production beyond 2031, with alternative uses for the plants being assessed.
“Uncertainty remains for staff, and the coming weeks will be difficult,” said Emden Mayor Tim Kruithoff.
Investors were more impressed by the carmaker’s plans: on Germany’s DAX stock exchange, Volkswagen preference shares were up almost 10% on Friday.
The Volkswagen Group – which owns brands such as Audi, Porsche and Škoda – is one of several German carmakers seeking to become more efficient and cost-effective in the face of intense competition from China. The company announced 50,000 job cuts in 2024, meaning the total of lost positions by the end of the decade is now set to reach six figures.
Not all are to be in Germany, however. Olaf Lies, premier of the northern state of Lower Saxony, where Volkswagen is headquartered, said on Friday that only half of the 50,000 cuts would affect Germany. The company employed around 284,000 across the country at the end of 2025.
Chief executive Oliver Blume called the agreement, which received the backing of union representatives and the company’s works council after weeks of speculation about cuts, a “strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group.”
German government spokesman Sebastian Hille also praised the deal on Friday.
But questions remain, particularly regarding the future of the four affected sites. Options under discussion include using the plants temporarily for defence production, or manufacturing VW models that until now have only been made in Chinese factories.

USS Pinckney destroyer set for new depot work through 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:29:46 UTC
16:29:46 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded General Dynamics NASSCO $149.6 million for a depot modernization period on the destroyer USS Pinckney (DDG 91), running through September 2028.
- The San Diego-based Arleigh Burke-class destroyer previously completed a similar depot availability in 2023 and a SEWIP Block 3 electronic warfare upgrade the same year.
The U.S. Navy has awarded General Dynamics NASSCO $149.6 million to carry out a scheduled maintenance and modernization overhaul of the destroyer USS Pinckney (DDG 91), the ship that served as the lead hull for the Navy’s broader effort to upgrade its Flight IIA Arleigh Burke-class destroyers.
The fixed-price incentive fee contract covers what the Navy calls a Chief of Naval Operations Availability, a scheduled depot-level maintenance period. The scope includes all labor, equipment, testing, facilities and quality assurance work needed to complete the modernization and repair effort. The contract includes options that could raise its total value to $149.9 million. Work will take place at NASSCO’s San Diego shipyard and is expected to run through September 2028, more than two and a half years from award.
The Navy is funding most of the contract, 91%, through fiscal 2026 other procurement funds, totaling $135.8 million. The rest comes from operations and maintenance funds and a small amount of weapons procurement money. About $12.9 million of that funding will expire at the end of the current fiscal year if not obligated. The Navy awarded the contract without competition, citing federal law that permits sole-source awards when only one contractor can meet the government’s requirements. Naval Sea Systems Command is managing the deal.
The USS Pinckney is an Arleigh Burke-class Flight IIA destroyer built by Ingalls Shipbuilding and commissioned in 2004. It is homeported in San Diego as part of Destroyer Squadron 23 and is named for William Pinckney, a Navy Cross recipient who rescued a fellow sailor aboard the carrier USS Enterprise during the Battle of Santa Cruz in World War II.
This new depot period follows the ship’s role as the pathfinder for the Navy’s DDG Modernization 2.0 program, a mid-life upgrade effort covering roughly 20 Flight IIA destroyers at an estimated cost of $17 billion across the fleet. Pinckney was the first ship selected to receive the program’s initial phase: installation of Northrop Grumman’s AN/SLQ-32(V)7 SEWIP Block 3 electronic warfare suite, which improves a ship’s ability to detect and jam anti-ship missiles. NASSCO completed that work on Pinckney in a roughly two-year modernization period that wrapped up in November 2023.
The DDG Modernization 2.0 program continues in two steps. After a ship receives the SEWIP Block 3 upgrade, it later returns for a second-phase overhaul that adds Raytheon’s SPY-6(V)4 radar and updated combat systems software. The Navy has already accepted two other Flight IIA destroyers, USS Chung-Hoon (DDG 93) and USS James E. Williams (DDG 95), after they completed their own modernization periods ahead of schedule earlier this year, while USS Halsey (DDG 97) remains in progress. Navy officials have said the program is structured deliberately to avoid the cost overruns and schedule delays that plagued the service’s earlier Ticonderoga-class cruiser modernization effort, which spent nearly $4 billion modernizing seven ships without extending their service lives as originally planned.
The Navy has not said whether this new $149.6 million depot period for Pinckney will include the second-phase SPY-6 radar installation or focus on other maintenance and repair work separate from the broader DDG Modernization 2.0 upgrade sequence.

Can Fatah’s Democratic Reform faction handle peace with both Israel and Hamas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
07:29:23 UTC
16:29:23 KST

Peace with Israel and unity between rival Palestinian factions may seem like very different challenges, but both require some of the same difficult abilities: putting aside a history of conflict, accepting vastly different ideologies, and confronting reality as it is, rather than holding out for an idealized society.
The Fatah Democratic Reform faction appears to be trying to manage just that.
Dimitri Diliani, a former member of Fatah’s Revolutionary Council, spokesperson for the FDR faction, and president of the National Christian Coalition in the Holy Land, made his views clear to The Jerusalem Post earlier this week.
He described Israel as a “morally bankrupt” society, while arguing that the policies of “incapable” Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas have helped produce the disaster facing the Palestinian economy.
Though critical of Israel, Abbas, and those who use violence, which he said would only lead to a “failed society,” Diliani is among a group of politically active Palestinians arguing that Palestinians must learn to coexist with people they may profoundly disagree with, and do so peacefully, if they are to build a functioning society.
“Our faction looks at the State of Israel as a state that we need to make peace with in accordance with international law.... We don’t characterize its nature. It’s none of our business.
“And we demand, as victims of that state, that the state also mind its own business in terms of our composition, our views... and look at us as a people that you need to make peace with to continue your survival in this Middle East,” he told the Post.
That same pragmatic approach appears to inform the reform faction’s efforts to engage with Hamas.
The faction’s leader, Mohammad Dahlan, the first head of the PA’s Preventive Security Service, spent years battling Hamas and, according to an exclusive report by Vanity Fair, was involved in a Bush administration-backed plot to oust the group from Gaza in 2008. Dahlan was removed from his position in Khan Yunis, where he was born, following Hamas’s violent takeover of the Gaza Strip. After years of political confrontation, Dahlan also eventually left the West Bank amid allegations from officials within his own Fatah party.
Following a leaked recording in which Dahlan criticized Abbas and his sons, the PA brought a series of allegations against him, including that he had attempted to mount a coup against Abbas, been involved in the circumstances surrounding Yasser Arafat’s death, and embezzled approximately $16 million in public funds.
Dahlan has consistently denied the allegations.
Some analysts have argued that Abbas’s campaign against Dahlan was also linked to concerns that Dahlan was being positioned by the Bush administration as a potential deputy and successor.
The bad blood between Dahlan, Hamas, and the Fatah leadership was notably absent from a letter penned by the Dahlan obtained by the Post, and did not prevent him from meeting with Hamas leadership in Cairo earlier this month.
“The catastrophe that has struck Gaza, the dangers facing the West Bank and Jerusalem, and the collapse, weakness, and fragmentation that have affected our national institutions require us to undertake an honest and courageous reassessment – not to put the past on trial or settle scores, but to understand what happened, draw lessons from it, and prevent its repetition,” he wrote.
“Therefore, the most important question is no longer who was right and who was wrong. Rather: How do we protect our people and our cause, save our people in Gaza, and protect our people and our land in the West Bank and Jerusalem? What kind of political system do we want to establish for future generations?”
For Diliani, the explanation for Dahlan’s rapprochement with Hamas is simple: Hamas exists, will continue to exist, and it isn’t pragmatic to plan for a political future on an impossible premise.
“We believe that Hamas exists. Hamas was not eliminated by the genocide, and Hamas will not be eliminated by force. Hamas is there as a resistance to the occupation. So, as long as there is a military occupation, there will always be Hamas.... As long as there is one Palestinian out there, there will be a faction that will resist the military occupation,” he argued.
Palestinian politicians accept the reality that Hamas will continue to function, regardless of the fact that the US-backed agreement signed by both Hamas and Jerusalem demanded that the Iran-backed group “agree to not have any role in the governance of Gaza, directly, indirectly, or in any form.”
Diliani claimed that Hamas has “so far honored the Trump plan... [and] the law” – though the IDF has frequently accused Hamas of violating the agreement – and so would likely “adhere” to restrictions surrounding the Palestinian Legislative Council elections in November.
Husam Badran, a senior member of Hamas’s political bureau, confirmed on Al-Aqsa TV last month that the group plans to participate in the PLC elections. Prof. Kobi Michael, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies, told the Post at the time that it may do this by forming a new party, not under the name of Hamas, or by allying with Dahlan.
To participate in the elections, a party needs to recognize the Palestine Liberation Organization as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people and be a Palestinian citizen with permanent residency in the Palestinian territories. Hamas does not recognize the PLO’s authority, partially because it rejects recognition of the Israeli state, and Dahlan is a resident of the United Arab Emirates, not the Palestinian territories, making the issue of their running all the more complicated.
Still, an alliance could give Hamas supporters a way to cast their votes, empowering the FDR fragment of Fatah, while allowing Hamas a say, protection, or control over the future of the Palestinian territories.
“Whether Hamas will have a role or not... the ideology is there,” Diliani said. “...To [claim] that the idea, the ideology, has disappeared would be ignorant, to say the least.”
PA presidential election could take place in 2027
BEYOND THE PLC election, which is only months away, a presidential election could finally take place in 2027.
The election has been postponed for the past 15 years, allowing Abbas to remain in office well beyond the end of his four-year term.
Palestinian polls have repeatedly shown his limited support, with the latest survey by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research finding that just 14% of Palestinians would vote for him if a presidential election were held today.
Convicted in absentia by a Palestinian court, Dahlan would currently be barred from running for president under Article 37 of Decree-Law No. 1 of 2007 on General Elections, and under Article 75 of the Palestinian constitution, which prohibits candidates who have been convicted by a competent court of a felony or a misdemeanor involving dishonor or breach of trust.
His eligibility could be restored if the conviction were overturned or otherwise removed by an appeals court, or if amnesty were granted as part of a national unity agreement.
With Abbas pushing hard to see his son take his place, Diliani said there was also motivation among the Palestinian voters to stop the same style of power transfer that allowed the Assad regime to control Syria.
“What took place in Syria between Hafez al-Assad and his son is a mutation, and in the Arab world, it will never happen again. No one has succeeded in doing that except Hafez al-Assad, and we know how that ended up,” he said.
“His [Abbas’s] son [Yasser Abbas] is not going to take his place. His son is unelectable, even within Fatah, let alone beyond it. Even within his father’s faction. Let’s remember that he was appointed to this position in a very choreographed, controlled environment, which would not be possible if any reconciliation within the movement took place.”
'No authority acquires or is armed with weapons legitimately over the will of the people'
ON THE renewed push to unify the Palestinian factions, Dahlan wrote in his letter: “We may disagree with Hamas, Islamic Jihad, or the leadership of the Palestinian Authority...” but “no authority acquires or is armed with weapons legitimately over the will of the people.”
Since Hamas violently ousted the PA from Gaza in 2007, tensions between Palestinian factions have periodically erupted into armed clashes. Most recently, in December 2024, Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad fighters clashed with PA security forces during a crackdown in Jenin. Hamas also called for Palestinians to mobilize against the PA’s security forces.
Hamas has agreed in principle to disarm under Trump’s plan, but the process has yet to begin, amid disagreements over which weapons, if any, it would be allowed to retain, and whether Israel must first withdraw fully from the Strip.
That vision of unity would also require the factions to determine how armed resistance fits into a broader national strategy, particularly given Hamas’s refusal to recognize Israel and its long-standing commitment to a single Palestinian state, while a significant portion of the FDR faction has publicly supported a two-state solution based on the 1967 lines.
The challenge for the reform faction is that pragmatism can only go so far. Recognizing Hamas as a political reality does not resolve the fundamental dispute over weapons, recognition of Israel, or the future political system in Gaza. Nor does support for a two-state solution necessarily make reconciliation with a faction that rejects Israel’s existence any easier.
Diliani said that the idea of armed resistance was growing less popular, though he insisted the Post make clear that he maintained “all forms of resistance are legal under international law in internationally recognized occupied territories. A siege is part of military occupation, and resisting it in any way, shape, or form is totally legitimate.”
Against any and all violence, Diliani said “even if armed resistance does achieve its goals, it would result in a failed society,” and on a practical level it doesn’t make sense to rely on armed resistance when Israel has a more capable military.
“If I’m going to have a competition with Mike Tyson, I’m not going to pick the boxing ring, even though he’s older than I am. Most definitely, he’s more fit, more skilled, and more powerful,” Diliani reasoned. “He would knock me out in a split second. I would take him on and compete with him in chess. We cannot stand up to Israel with violence.”
He suggested many in Hamas had come to that same realization.
Diliani’s argument about nonviolent resistance was accompanied by a far more sweeping condemnation of Israeli society. He claimed that polling showed a stark contrast between Palestinian support for civil resistance and Israeli attitudes in the Israel-Hamas War, describing Israeli society as “pretty much genocidal” and, in his words, a “genocidal death cult.”
Diliani argued that Israel is a perfect example of a society failed by violence, citing the issues of emigration and the Israeli economy as prime examples of that and a leading reason to focus the collective energy on improving education and healthcare.
As Dahlan wrote in his letter, “Our responsibility today is to open a different path: one that makes difference of opinion a right, not a threat; pluralism a source of strength, not a cause of division; elections a means of transferring power; institutions greater than individuals; and the homeland greater than everyone.
