War update: 236 clashes on front line over past day, Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka sectors remain hottest
This was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in an operational update as of 8:00 on September 5, according to Ukrinform.
The enemy launched 87 airstrikes, dropping 317 guided aerial bombs. In addition, Russian forces used 10,816 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,723 shelling attacks, including 22 using multiple-launch rocket systems.
In the Sumy region, the settlements of Sopych, Baranivka, Neskuchne, Korenok, Potapivka, Mohrytsia, Kucherivka, Iskryskivshchyna, Rohizne, Hirky, Bachivsk, and Volfyne came under artillery fire.
Ukrainian Defense Forces aviation, missile forces and artillery struck 11 clusters of Russian personnel, four guns and artillery positions, one UAV command post, one air defense system, and another important enemy target.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, three Russian assault actions took place. Russian forces carried out 168 shelling attacks and launched four strikes using 13 guided aerial bombs.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukrainian units repelled 12 Russian attacks. The invaders attempted to advance toward Loshakove, Okhrimivka, Chuhunivka, Zarubynka, Izbytske, and Lyman, as well as near Starytsia.
In the Kupiansk sector, the enemy launched 11 assaults, attempting to advance toward Radkivka, Kivsharivka, Dovhenke, Kurylivka, and Kupiansk.
In the Lyman sector, Russian forces attacked nine times, advancing toward Shyikivka, Drobysheve, and Lyman, as well as near Dibrova and Novoselivka.
In the Sloviansk sector, Russian troops launched six assaults near Ozerne, Rai-Oleksandrivka, and Kryva Luka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian forces conducted one offensive action toward Nykonorivka.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, 21 enemy attacks were recorded. The invaders conducted assault operations near Kostiantynivka, Illinivka, Rusyn Yar, Sofiivka, and Nove Shakhove, as well as toward Pavlivka, Vilne, and Stepanivka.
The enemy launched 40 attacks in the Pokrovsk sector, attempting to advance toward Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Shevchenko, Matiashеve, Serhiivka, Myrne, and Novopavlivka, as well as near Udachne and Molodetske.
Ukrainian Defense Forces repelled two Russian attacks in the Oleksandrivka sector near Novoheorhiivka and Nove Zaporizhzhia.
In the Huliaipole sector, Russian forces attacked 13 times, attempting to advance toward Dobropillia, Vozdvyzhivka, Kopani, Verkhnia Tersa, Huliaipilske, Tsvitkove, and Charivne.
In the Orikhiv sector, Ukrainian defenders stopped four attempts by Russian forces to advance near Mala Tokmachka, Stepnohirsk, and Shcherbaky.
No Russian offensive actions were recorded in the Dnipro River sector.
No signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected in the Volyn and Polissia sectors.

EXPLAINER - From Ethiopia border to Darfur: Where are Sudan’s war fronts heating up?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:19:05 UTC
15:19:05 KST

Sudan’s most active battlefronts stretch across a vast arc from the Blue Nile state near the Ethiopian border in the east, through three Kordofan states, to Darfur in the west.
Al-Baraka, Bakori, Geissan and Kurmuk in the Blue Nile; Bara, Al-Abbasiya and Kauda in Kordofan; and Um Baru, Kernoi and Abu Suruj in Darfur have emerged as some of the most significant centers of fighting and military movement.
Control of the areas is divided among the army, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and armed groups allied with each side. Drone attacks have increasingly carried the war into towns and villages far from traditional front lines.
Anadolu reviewed the main hotspots, their military significance and the current balance of control.
Al-Baraka, in the Kurmuk locality in the southeastern Blue Nile state, has become one of the newest fronts between the army on one side and the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), on the other.
The area lies on the outskirts of Kurmuk near the Ethiopian border, giving it strategic importance for movements between border zones and the interior of Blue Nile.
On Friday, the army said it repelled an attack by the RSF and SPLM-N on Al-Baraka.
The army’s 4th Infantry Division said forces inflicted personnel and equipment losses on the attackers and forced them to retreat toward the Sudan-Ethiopia border.
Bakori, in the Geissan locality, is another key hotspot in Blue Nile.
The area hosts a military base and the headquarters of the army’s 14th Brigade, making it a contested position for both sides.
Bakori lies 170 kilometers (106 miles) southeast of Damazin, the state capital.
In recent weeks, the RSF and SPLM-N have taken control of Geissan and Kurmuk, the administrative centers of the two localities bearing the same names.
The army, however, continues to hold other parts of both localities, as well as Damazin, Er Roseires and the localities of Bau, Wad al-Mahi and Tadamon.
Beyond Kurmuk and Geissan, the SPLM-N, led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu, has controlled Yabus since 2011.
The area, one of the movement’s main strongholds in Blue Nile, lies near the borders with Ethiopia and South Sudan, around 80 kilometers from Kurmuk.
The SPLM-N has fought the Sudanese government since 2011, demanding greater autonomy in Blue Nile and South Kordofan before joining forces with the RSF during the current war.
In North Kordofan, Bara remains one of the most strategically important towns because of its location on the national highway linking it to Omdurman, west of the national capital, Khartoum.
In late July, the army retook Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh and Um Sayala, allowing it to secure the highway and reshape the military balance in the state bordering Darfur and West Kordofan.
Fighting around Bara has since shifted largely from direct ground clashes to drone attacks on military positions and villages surrounding the town.
Villages west of Bara that contain no military deployments have also come under RSF attacks, according to the Emergency Lawyers and the Sudan Doctors Network.
Other military movements are concentrated in northwestern North Kordofan, where the RSF controls Hamrat al-Sheikh, Al-Mazroub and Sodari.
Their importance stems from their proximity to Darfur and West Kordofan, and their location along movement and supply routes connecting the two regions.
North Kordofan has also faced repeated drone attacks, alongside similar strikes in South and West Kordofan.
In South Kordofan, Kadugli and Dilling remain among the most important army-held positions.
The army broke the siege on both cities months ago, and strengthened its control in large parts of the state, except for areas still held by the SPLM-N under al-Hilu.
Although major ground fighting around the two cities has subsided, both continue to face intermittent drone attacks that have killed and wounded civilians.
The Al-Abbasiya locality has become another hotspot in South Kordofan amid repeated attacks and deteriorating security conditions.
On Thursday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said 6,420 people had been displaced from nine villages in Al-Abbasiya because of worsening insecurity from Sept. 1 to 2.
Kauda, in the far south of South Kordofan, remains under SPLM-N control and is one of the movement’s most important strongholds.
Alongside its role in the broader conflict between the SPLM-N and the government, Kauda has also witnessed local fighting between SPLM-N forces and members of the Otoro tribe because of a land dispute.
The clashes began in late June after a dispute about border demarcation between the Shawaya and Otoro tribes escalated into armed conflict, killing dozens and displacing thousands.
North Darfur remains one of the most active fronts in the Darfur region, with the army and the Joint Force of Armed Movements conducting operations against the RSF.
The Joint Force includes armed groups such as the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Minni Arko Minnawi, and the Justice and Equality Movement, led by Jibril Ibrahim.
Um Baru and Karnoi have emerged as key hotspots after the army and Joint Force gained control of large parts of both localities.
Their proximity to the Chadian border makes them important bases for advancing into other parts of North Darfur and securing supply routes in the state.
In West Darfur, army and Joint Force movements have been concentrated north of El Geneina, the state capital.
In June, the forces captured Kulbus, about 160 kilometers north of El Geneina, before withdrawing more than two weeks later and repositioning around the town.
The army and the Joint Force later took Bir Saliba and Jebel Moon north of El Geneina as part of efforts to expand their foothold in the state.
On Aug. 29, West Darfur Gov. Bahr al-Din Adam Karama said the army and the Joint Force had taken control of Abu Suruj in the Sirba locality following clashes with the RSF.
Abu Suruj is among the latest areas where territorial control has shifted in West Darfur as military movements continue north of El Geneina.
The RSF and allied forces still control most of Darfur, while the army and the Joint Force maintain positions in parts of the region’s north and west.
Despite the different strategic value of each front, displacement remains the most consistent consequence of the widening conflict.
In Blue Nile, the IOM said 3,000 people had been displaced from three villages in the Kurmuk locality, while the UN estimated that 22,000 people fled fighting in Geissan in one week.
In South Kordofan, 6,420 people were displaced from villages in Al-Abbasiya, in addition to thousands forced from their homes by the conflict in Kauda.
The growing use of drones has also expanded the threat well beyond frontline areas. The UN said 1,100 civilians were killed in drone attacks between January and June.
The army and RSF have been at war since April 2023 because of disputes surrounding the political transition and plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the regular military.
As front lines continue to shift between Blue Nile, Kordofan and Darfur, Sudan’s map of military hotspots remains fluid, with no clear prospect of an end to the war.

State to order shelter plans for up to 400 buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

State to order shelter plans for up to 400 buildings
Riigi Kinnisvara (RKAS) is ordering shelter plans and proposals for how rooms could be adapted for up to 400 buildings, and the expected cost is €520,000.
In the spring, the government approved a regulation concerning the construction of shelters and the adaptation of sheltering spaces, with the aim of increasing sheltering possibilities.
Now the state real estate firm RKAS has taken up the plan to order shelter plans for buildings it owns.
Priit Valk, director of facility services at RKAS, said that shelter plans will first be ordered only for the objects required by the regulation — that is, those with a net area of at least 1,200 square meters or more.
"There are around 200 buildings over 1,200 square meters in the ownership of RKAS. In the scope of the procurement, we have accounted for up to 400 buildings in total, which means that within the procurement we can also prepare shelter plans for buildings smaller than 1,200 square meters, for which the regulation does not impose a plan requirement," Valk said.
He added that shelter plans for smaller buildings can be taken into work by RKAS once all buildings of the size required by the regulation have received their shelter plans.
In addition to preparing shelter plans, RKAS is also ordering an assessment of sheltering possibilities and proposals for how rooms should be adapted, as well as a checklist for the person responsible for organizing sheltering in the building and for building users. Shelter routes must also be marked according to requirements, and building users must be trained.
Thus, according to Valk, the procurement covers both plans prepared on paper and other accompanying activities.
RKAS is expected to spend €520,000 on ordering the shelter plans. The procurement does not include reconstruction work; according to Valk, these will be carried out separately after the shelter plans are completed.
"We are following the requirements of the regulation throughout the process, according to which we must have the shelter plans completed no later than 1 July 2027, and construction work related to adapting the rooms must be carried out by 1 July 2028," Valk said.
He added that in terms of the deadlines set by the regulation, this is an ambitious task.

Ganga rises above 'highest flood mark' in Patna; several low-lying areas face inundation risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:06:04 UTC
15:06:04 KST

A view of riverside ghats submerged amid the rise in Ganga River's water level, in Patna earlier this week
NEW DELHI: The Ganga breached the ‘highest flood mark’ at Patna’s Gandhi Ghat amid heavy rain in Bihar, with the river’s water level rising 10 cm in four hours on Saturday morning, according to an official bulletin.The river was flowing 1 cm above the highest flood level at 10 am, reaching 50.53 metres at Gandhi Ghat, the Water Resources Department (WRD) said.
“The Ganga water level at Gandhi Ghat in Patna rose by 10 cm in the past four hours, reaching 50.53 cm, which is 1 cm above the highest flood level, at 10 am on Saturday,” the department said in its latest bulletin, as quoted by PTI.The situation could worsen further, with the WRD forecasting a continued rise in the river’s water level. “The forecast is that the Ganga water level at Gandhi Ghat is likely to rise further to 50.62 cm by 8 am on Sunday. People have been advised to exercise caution,” it said.The rising water has raised concerns over possible inundation in low-lying areas of Patna, with people being urged to remain cautious.
Several districts across Bihar are already facing flood-like conditions as heavy rainfall in the state and neighbouring Nepal has pushed multiple rivers above their danger marks.
The Ganga, Gandak, Kosi, Burhi Gandak, Bagmati, Punpun and Ghaghra are among the rivers flowing above danger levels.Chief minister Samrat Choudhary conducted an aerial survey of the affected areas on Friday and reviewed relief and rescue operations.He directed officials to identify affected families and ensure they receive relief on time. He also ordered continuous monitoring of vulnerable areas and the Ganga embankments between Buxar and Bhagalpur to prevent erosion and possible breaches.

A Message to China from Japan’s Takaichi Administration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:05:00 UTC
15:05:00 KST

The Taiwan Strait came up as an example during a debate on the legal applications of Japan’s right of collective self-defense at the Budget Committee of the Lower House on November 7, 2025, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi gave her response when asked under what circumstances a “survival-threatening situation” would be legally applicable. China reacted sharply, to say the least: verbally accusing Japan of “neo-militarism” and then moving to normalize activities by the Chinese Navy — especially its aircraft carriers — in the waters between the First Island Chain and the Second Island Chain, while its coast guard began deploying east of Taiwan’s coast. On the economic front, security provisions were applied to Japanese companies, restrictions were imposed on rare earth exports, and measures were taken to curtail tourism and other exchanges with Japan, with economic, local-governmental, and academic ties all affected to a significant degree. China has demanded that Takaichi retract her November 7 statements, but she has refused.
An APEC summit is scheduled in China in November 2026, hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Takaichi is expected to attend. Significant progress in Japan-China relations has been elusive, however. A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson made remarks in late June 2026 that appeared to give the green light for private exchanges between Japan and China, and a range of business associations and parliamentary groups are now scheduled to visit China this fall. Whether this supposed “green light” actually came from China’s leadership remains unclear.
So what message is the Takaichi administration sending to China?
First, on the Taiwan Strait. Three days after the original remarks, at a Budget Committee session on November 11, 2025, Takaichi said that “Peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are important not only for Japanese security but also for the stability of the international community as a whole. Japan has consistently held the expectation that issues surrounding Taiwan will be resolved peacefully through dialogue.” At a plenary session of the House of Representatives on December 3, she added: “Our government’s basic position regarding Taiwan hasn’t changed and is as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Joint Communiqué.” In short, she made clear that the November 7 statement did not represent a change in Japan’s Taiwan policy.
Then, on Japan-China relations broadly. At the Joint Meeting of the Committees of Both Houses on Fundamental National Policies on November 26, 2025, Takaichi said the two sides had “agreed to building constructive and stable Japan-China relations” and that “if there are concerns or challenges between us, they will be resolved through communication, communication between the leaders,” adding that “Japan is always constructive and open to dialogue with China.” Meanwhile, Diet speakers have repeatedly reached for a now-standard phrase: to “closely monitor the situation and respond appropriately, including to the effects of the various measures from China.” At the House of Councillors plenary session on February 25, 2026, Takaichi went somewhat further, saying “Japan is open to different forms of dialogue with China” and citing cooperation with “our allies, the United States and like-minded countries” — remarks likely made with her March visit to Washington in mind. In her post-visit statement at the House of Representatives plenary on March 26, however, Takaichi mentioned “cooperation with the United States” in the context of China policy but otherwise repeated the same formula.
Takaichi’s public statements since November 7, 2025 have largely been repetitions of standard phrases, repeatedly asserting that Japan’s existing Taiwan and China policies are unchanged. She has also signaled that Japan is “open” to dialogue. Chinese protests have escalated regardless, and while dialogue between Japan and China has not disappeared entirely, it remains limited. Ministerial exchanges this year appear confined to APEC-related matters, given China’s role as host. Yet more recently the Takaichi administration appears to be sending a new signal.
First, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi apparently exchanged a brief greeting with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi at the ASEAN-related Foreign Ministers’ Meetings. China has denied this, but it appears certain that Motegi made the approach on July 23. The day before, on July 22, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Wang in their meeting that he saw a worrying trend of deteriorating Japan-China relations. Whether Motegi’s approach was a direct response to Rubio’s remarks is unclear, but Japan is at minimum signaling a proactive stance toward dialogue with China.
Second, Takaichi’s remarks at a press conference on July 27 are telling. When asked about the November APEC summit, she said simply: “I am looking forward to it.” The likelihood of a formal Japan-China bilateral meeting is low, but as host Xi would be expected to greet all attending leaders, making some form of contact difficult to avoid.
These signals from the Takaichi administration are likely driven by more than just American expectations. Following what may have been a green light from the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson on June 26, Japanese business associations and parliamentary groups have announced China visits in quick succession. Whether any of this can truly “normalize” Japan-China relations remains to be seen, but the mood on the Japanese side is clearly shifting.

US peace envoys Witkoff and Kushner to visit Kyiv and Moscow with plan to 'end war'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:04:47 UTC
15:04:47 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier said Ukraine would hold off on strikes while Witkoff and Kushner made the trip, while calling on Moscow to do the same.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his forces to pause strikes on Kyiv while US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visit Moscow and Kyiv this weekend.
Putin has called for a halt to strikes on the Ukrainian capital for three days, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the Russian news agency Interfax. The pause is in place from midnight tonight, he said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine is ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process during the US peace envoys visit.
'From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, expecting the Ruiussian to do the same regarding Kyiv', he wrote on X.
Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday ahead of meetings with officials in Russia and Ukraine this weekend.
The pair come armed with a "proposal to end the war," US President Donald Trump has announced, as the US makes its latest push to break a diplomatic deadlock over the war in Ukraine.
"I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on Friday.
The duo is then due to head to Kyiv on Sunday, in what will be their first visits to the city since Trump returned to the White house in January last year.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the planned visit to Ukraine in a post on X.
"We need to look for real options for how to move this war toward an end," Zelenskyy wrote. "We will see what proposals Steve and Jared bring and what they are told in Moscow in response".
He added that Ukrainian forces would ensure the "normal functioning of Russian airspace" to ensure the envoys could make the trip to Moscow safely.
Zelenskyy had warned airlines and insurers on Tuesday that Russian airspace would "effectively be closing" due to the scale of Ukrainian drone operations making flying unsafe.
Russian strikes kill four overnight
The announcement came as Russian strikes on the city of Kamianske in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region killed four overnight, per local authorities.
Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, said five people were also injured in the strikes, which hit an industrial facility.
On Friday, Zelenskyy announced that a Russian drone had also hit the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) in central Kyiv, adding that it had been "aimed directly" at the head of the agency's office.
In response to the attack, he said he had ordered the SBU to carry out an "appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike."
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had also struck airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight, calling them "deliberate" and a "reaction" to the planned envoy meetings.
"We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace," he wrote on X.

Autumn literary season: a uniquely French phenomenon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:01:41 UTC
15:01:41 KST

Again this year, several hundred novels come out at the end of summer for the "rentrée littéraire". But what does this event look like in other European countries?
Sonia Devillers, Philippe Jaenada, Amélie Nothomb, Philippe Besson, Ananda Devi. They all have one thing in common: they will be part of the 2026 literary season. Between now and October, some 461 novels, including 344 French titles, will reach bookshops. That is a slight drop compared with the previous year, when 484 books were published.
For publishers and booksellers, this period is unmissable, all the more so at a time when reading is playing a smaller and smaller role in our daily lives. "The share of French people who spontaneously describe themselves as readers is falling across all categories, particularly among regular readers (down 5 points vs 2023)", notes the 6th barometer from the Centre national du Livre (CNL), published in 2025. "Over the last 12 months, 63% of French people say they have read at least five books (down 6 points vs 2023) and the share of daily readers is declining (down 4 points vs 2023), reaching its lowest level in 10 years", the study also points out.
"It is our shared duty to reassert the central place of reading in our lives. Reading is a vital time, time for oneself, that absolutely must be protected", argues Régine Hatchondo, president of the CNL.
And the trend is even more pronounced among young people: they spend an average of 3 hours and 1 minute a day in front of screens, but only 18 minutes reading books, according to the study "Les jeunes Français et la lecture" ("Young French people and reading"), published in 2026. "Regular reading is declining and young people very often do something else at the same time as they read", adds the head of the CNL.
In Belgium and Switzerland, all eyes on France
Although it is a particularly big deal in France, the literary season also exists in several other European countries.
In Switzerland, the phenomenon does not have the same impact. "There is far less media hype and fewer prizes [literary] at that time of year too", observes Nicolas Julliard, a literary journalist at RTS, speaking to Euronews. "It is not the same phenomenon."
However, he acknowledges that Switzerland is aligning more closely with the French market. "More and more publishing houses are matching their schedules to this calendar in order to release their biggest titles", the journalist continues. One reason is that this allows Swiss publishers to gain greater visibility in France. "Quite a few books are exported and are even starting to appear in certain prize lists." In short, the Swiss literary season "is increasingly becoming a key date for publishers, particularly for the newer publishing houses", concludes Nicolas Julliard.
In Belgium, it is "quite a paradoxical period", says Nausicaa Dewez, editor-in-chief of the journal "Le Carnet et les Instants", speaking to Euronews. "Driven by the pull of the French literary season, there is intense media and public attention on books and literature, and at the same time the space is saturated by titles published in France. [...] Belgian publishing houses are present during this period, but they also know that commercially they cannot compete with much larger and more powerful structures. So they do not throw all their strength into the autumn season."
Nausicaa Dewez adds another nuance: "For most literary publishers in French-speaking Belgium, the first major moment of the year is the Brussels Book Fair, held in March", which explains why the start of the year is also an important time for Belgian literature.
An important phenomenon across Europe as well
In Spain, this period is known as the "temporada editorial de otoño" ("autumn publishing season"). While the country "does not reach France's level of activity, publishers prepare major titles every year for the beginning of September", explains journalist Pepa Blanes in the pages of the Cadena SER (source in French). "Events also start to fill much of the month."
In Germany too, the end of summer means a wave of new books, though again with less impact than in France. Across the Rhine, this period is called Bücherherbst ("book autumn") or Literaturherbst ("literary autumn"). The press then showcases the big new releases and regards this season as an important one for bookshops. It is an event that is "planned long in advance", reports the Tagesspiegel (source in French).
Above all, this flurry of new releases comes a few weeks before the Frankfurt Book Fair, held every October and a key date for the industry. It is there that the Deutscher Buchpreis is awarded, a prize created along the lines of France's Prix Goncourt, notes Deutsche Welle (source in French).
In Italy, "autumn is when some of the year's most important books are concentrated, although in recent years this market approach has changed and publishers, to avoid an overload of titles in autumn, have started to spread their output more evenly over the rest of the year", explains Paolo Ambrosinin, president of the Associazione librai italiani, speaking to Euronews.
The British literary season perhaps comes closest to what we see in France, even though it follows a different timetable. "'Super Thursday' is an exciting day for booksellers, because hundreds of new books arrive in bookshops on the same day", says Kate Skipper, chief operating officer at the book chain Waterstones, speaking to The Guardian (source in French).
It usually falls on the first or second Thursday in October. "It is always an extremely busy day, but there is a real buzz when you unpack so many big titles for Christmas all at once", Kate Skipper continues. In 2024, more than 1,900 books were published for this "Super Thursday", reported The Guardian (source in French).
That exceptional volume dropped sharply the following year: the number of releases was almost halved, as publishers adopted a strategy summed up by the slogan "publish less, but publish better", reported The Bookseller (source in French) at the time.

Across the Rhine, this period is called Bücherherbst ("book autumn") or Literaturherbst ("literary autumn"). The press then showcases the big new releases and regards this season as an important one for bookshops. It is an event that is "planned long in advance", reports the Tagesspiegel (source in French).
Above all, this flurry of new releases comes a few weeks before the Frankfurt Book Fair, held every October and a key date for the industry. It is there that the Deutscher Buchpreis is awarded, a prize created along the lines of France's Prix Goncourt, notes Deutsche Welle (source in French).
In Italy, "autumn is when some of the year's most important books are concentrated, although in recent years this market approach has changed and publishers, to avoid an overload of titles in autumn, have started to spread their output more evenly over the rest of the year", explains Paolo Ambrosinin, president of the Associazione librai italiani, speaking to Euronews.
The British literary season perhaps comes closest to what we see in France, even though it follows a different timetable. "'Super Thursday' is an exciting day for booksellers, because hundreds of new books arrive in bookshops on the same day", says Kate Skipper, chief operating officer at the book chain Waterstones, speaking to The Guardian (source in French).
It usually falls on the first or second Thursday in October. "It is always an extremely busy day, but there is a real buzz when you unpack so many big titles for Christmas all at once", Kate Skipper continues. In 2024, more than 1,900 books were published for this "Super Thursday", reported The Guardian (source in French).
That exceptional volume dropped sharply the following year: the number of releases was almost halved, as publishers adopted a strategy summed up by the slogan "publish less, but publish better", reported The Bookseller (source in French) at the time.

Could an EU custodian break the long deadlock on the Russian assets?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

The debate on Russian money held in Belgium has returned. Could an EU custodian convince Belgium and break the political deadlock?
The Russian assets are back on the table. And with them, the same old problems.
Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, backed by the Baltics, are leading a new push to channel the Russian Central Bank's immobilised assets into additional financial support to Ukraine as the war-weary country faces ballooning costs.
It did not take long for the campaign to collide with a familiar opponent: Belgium.
The country holds the bulk of the €210 billion in Euroclear, a depository based in central Brussels, and fears any move to channel the funds to Ukraine would leave it exposed to unpredictable dangers and ruinous litigation. Euroclear is currently battling a lawsuit in Russia.
Belgium led the charge last year to dismantle an audacious plan that would have turned the €210 billion into a zero-interest credit line for Ukraine. It now vows to do the same.
"The reasons behind our opposition have not magically disappeared," Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said this week. "Using these assets through a process amounting to confiscation would entail very significant risks."
But what if Belgium were no longer in the eye of the hurricane?
An idea gaining traction across capitals envisions moving the sovereign assets held at Euroclear into a new custodian owned and controlled by the EU itself. This, the thinking goes, would remove the liability and exposure of Euroclear and consequently Belgium.
Sergii Marchenko, Ukraine's finance minister, is keen on the concept.
"The proposal which we would like to discuss is a possibility to transfer the custodian of frozen assets from Belgium to the European Union," Marchenko told Euronews.
"It will help settle everything and mitigate the risk."
Marchenko argued the custodian would avoid the complex structure of national guarantees and offset mechanisms that the European Commission had designed to protect Belgium against Moscow's scorched-earth tactics.
"It will be the joint responsibility of the European Union. All 27 countries will be signing one accord in this discussion," he said. "It's a totally different scenario."
The Commission knows the custodian is being informally floated as a solution, but remains reluctant to reopen the debate on financing for Ukraine without a guarantee of success. The executive insists it has never given up on the sovereign assets.
A custodian for all
The idea, as such, is not necessarily brand new.
For the past few months, three personalities – Hugo Dixon, a commentator-at-large at Reuters; Lee Buchheit, an honorary professor at the University of Edinburgh Law School; and Daleep Singh, vice chairman at PGIM who served the Biden administration – have led a project called The Russian Transfer that advocates the switch.
They recommend using the emergency powers under Article 122 of the EU treaties to move the Russian assets held by Euroclear and private banks into an EU-owned custodian, citing reasons of public security and financial stability. (Article 122, which requires a qualified majority, was previously used to immobilise the assets indefinitely.)
The custodian, they say, would not represent a corporate entity and therefore would not need to be domiciled in an individual member state that Moscow could target. Belgium would receive an indemnity for the "slim risk" of incurring damages from moving the assets, which the EU regulation would mandate.
The Russian Central Bank would stay the nominal owner of the funds and be entitled to recover them after paying war reparations to Ukraine.
Dixon, Buchheit and Singh argue history already offers a precedent: in March 2003, right after the US invaded Iraq, the White House ordered the move of $1.7 billion in Iraqi sovereign assets to a special account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
"If the EU deploys the €210 billion in assets to help Kyiv, Putin will know he cannot win just because Ukraine runs out of cash. He may then conclude that it is best to make peace," they say.
Karel Lannoo, chief executive at the Centre for European Policy Studies, has pitched an alternative scenario: a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) that would hold the entire bulk of the Russian assets but use exclusively their extraordinary revenues (about €4 billion per year) to back the issuance of bonds. This would help the EU mobilise larger upfront amounts to assist Ukraine.
Notably, the principal (€210 billion) would remain untouched at all times.
Under Lannoo's template, the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), created in 2012 as a permanent firewall for the eurozone, would provide the necessary guarantees for the bonds. The ESM has a maximum lending capacity of €500 billion.
"It takes too long for member states to sign off on national guarantees," Lannoo said, referring to the Commission's failed proposal. "It's better to use what you have to make sure there's as little friction as possible."
"We need to have a structure in place and the solidarity around it."
Interestingly, the SPV was mentioned by the Commission itself in an options paper sent to member states last year. The document, however, warned that the funding costs of an SPV would be "higher" than traditional common borrowing.
Reputational crisis
Proponents of the idea are convinced that changing custodianship would mitigate Belgium's entrenched concerns, break the political deadlock and bestow on the EU massive financial firepower to support Ukraine.
Belgian officials have taken note of the informal pitch and admit it could remove some of their long-standing objections, as Euroclear, a systematically important institution, would no longer be at the centre of the dispute.
But the custodian could face challenges beyond its control.
One of the reasons last year's bold plan fell apart at the eleventh hour was the fear that foreign states and investors would perceive the move as confiscation of sovereign assets, which is strictly forbidden under international law, and relocate their own assets to other jurisdictions, triggering a reputational crisis for the entire eurozone.
This cascading effect weighed heavily in the mind of the European Central Bank (ECB) during last year's fraught negotiations.
Its president, Christine Lagarde, privately advised EU leaders to tap the Russian assets in conjunction with other Western allies to avoid singling out the eurozone.
The bank later declined to provide emergency liquidity for the guarantees.
The ECB, Euroclear and some member states are still wary of any high-risk proposal that could set off an investor exodus, unleash financial instability and undermine the euro as the world's second-most important currency at a time when global turbulence already hits hard.
It remains to be seen to what extent a change of custodianship could convince them otherwise.

UK subsidence claims surge after hottest summer on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

UK insurers are experiencing a surge in the number of homeowners making claims for subsidence after the hottest summer on record, with Hastings Direct reporting a near 140% jump to an all-time high for August.
Insurance firms have been overrun by calls and online queries, as well as a rise in claims during the five heatwaves that followed the warmest spring ever recorded in England and Wales.
Subsidence claims typically peak during late summer and autumn, but this year they jumped in number during the summer.
Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, the British Geological Survey has said.
As hotter, drier summers become more frequent, the ground under houses can shrink and drag down a property’s foundations. Older properties are more at risk. The most vulnerable areas for subsidence include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford up to the Wash on England’s east coast, according to scientists.
Hastings Direct, which has 4.8 million home and motor insurance customers, said it had had a significant increase in subsidence claims over the summer and received a record number in August, almost 140% more than in the same month last year.
After two unusually dry summers, subsidence activity has increased significantly, the company said.
Hastings predicted the large volume of claims would continue into the autumn even though temperatures had returned to more normal levels and there had been some rainfall in recent weeks.
“We expect claim volumes to remain higher than normal through to around October unless sustained rainfall helps restore soil moisture levels,” the insurer added.
Signs of subsidence range from diagonal cracks around doors and windows that often widen over time; windows or doors that stick or will not close properly and uneven or sloping floors. Wallpaper creasing or rippling can also be a sign of subsidence, as well as damp.
The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a record £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, up from £60m in the same period last year.
About £297m in total was paid out on claims in 2025, up 6% from the year before, and 89% higher than in 2022, the ABI said.
Charlie Inwood, the general insurance policy adviser at the ABI, said: “Following this summer’s hot weather, it’s likely we’ll see more subsidence claims over the coming months.”
Aviva, which completed a £3.7bn acquisition of its rival Direct Line in July, and dominates the UK home insurance market, has also reported subsidence claim numbers had increased in recent months. “This is likely to continue unless there is significant rainfall,” it said.
Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said last month that the company was reviewing the reserves it had set aside for subsidence claims, and would also look at its pricing models and exposure management. The insurer is also investigating what homeowners can do to prevent property damage from subsidence and flooding.
Small shrinkage and movement cracks were normal after hot dry weather, Aviva said, while diagonal cracks that were more than 2.5cm wide, roughly the diameter of a £1 coin, could be a sign of subsidence.
Axa, another home insurer, said it expected a “surge year” but could not say whether it would be a record year for subsidence claims.
Adam Holland, the head of retail underwriting, fraud and pricing governance at the French company’s UK arm, said: “The Met Office’s announcement about summer 2026 being the hottest on record in the UK puts the impact of climate change into sharp focus … and we expect to see an increase in weather-related property damage this year.”

====================================================================================================

A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:00:29 UTC
15:00:29 KST

Sometimes travel delivers a real shock. I’m moving along the boulevards in the Polish city of Łódź, enjoying the excellent cafes and warm sunshine, when I spot the vans. They are parked up on the verge, with racks of clothing and heavily laden tables behind. I can’t resist a Sunday morning market and walk towards a group of men huddled around a car that is covered in blankets. And then it happens. They turn – and I see they are weighing pistols in their hands. I recognise the lean profile of a German Luger, and then the bulkier Colt 45.
There is a second of doubt. I hesitate. They replace the weapons on the display and walk away laughing. I approach. On the car roof is a row of dusty soldiers’ helmets. “We were repairing a pavement in the centre of town,” says the seller cheerfully, handing me a badge to inspect. “Imagine! For 80 years, all this stuff was just under our feet.”
It’s a Wehrmacht shoulder badge from Kuban 1943, a last-ditch post-Stalingrad action on the Crimean peninsula. Who wore this, I wonder? A veteran of the Russian front who almost made it home? Nothing is clear, except that in Łódź, the past is never far away.
I arrive the previous night, a little disoriented, whizzing past unlit buildings, huge brick structures like Victorian factories. “Are we in the city yet?” I ask.
The taxi driver gives me a quizzical look. “Yes, this is Łódź.” I note the pronunciation, like “wudge”. I glimpse five-storey blocks, tree-lined streets, a tramline. “I could never live anywhere else,” he adds. A huge blue graffito is caught in the headlights, like a monstrous alien creature.
“Why?” I ask, but we are already pulling up outside an immense red-brick building, my hotel, and he never answers my question. The reception area is huge, with a strange scalloped ceiling in red brick that hints at a previous incarnation as a factory.
This is my first visit to Łódź, a city about 75 miles (120km) south-west of Warsaw. My interest has been piqued by a list of notable people associated with the place. It features an astonishing number of Oscar-winning or nominated film directors connected to the city: Andrzej Wajda (The Promised Land), Roman Polanski (The Pianist), Paweł Pawlikowski (Ida), Agnieszka Holland (Europa Europa), Krzysztof Kieślowski (Three Colours trilogy) and Zbigniew Rybczyński (Tango).
But under the bonnet there is a vast array of talent in acting, production and technical excellence. The city’s film school is responsible, of course, but Łódź itself features as a setting, too, notably in David Lynch’s Inland Empire and Wajda’s masterpiece The Promised Land.
Łódź, I had decided, must be fascinating. Any visit starts with Piotrkowska Street, the longest shopping street in Europe at about 2½ miles. My guide, Anna, takes me through Plac Wolności (Freedom Square), where a dance festival is in progress, with hooded hip‑hoppers rubbing shoulders with troupes of line dancers and girls in colourfully embroidered traditional dress. This is a city where music and dance are never far away. We dodge down a side alley and emerge in a striking art installation – an entire street, Pasaż Róży (Rosa’s Passage), covered in mirrors by the artist Joanna Rajkowska. Back on the main pedestrianised route, the mix of ancient and modern continues: 19th‑century porticoed palaces adorned with colourful graffiti.
I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. “It was not too badly damaged,” she says. “Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.”
There is no medieval heart, no ornate houses like in Wrocław or Kraków. What Łódź possesses is an impressive array of 19th-century factories, mostly textiles, built to show off their owners’ power, wealth and architectural aspirations. Now, this heritage has become a stunning example of urban regeneration.
We turn into OFF Piotrkowska, a complex of beautiful old textile mills reborn as a hive of small businesses. There are lots of vibrant restaurants and bars, but Anna wants to show me a shop that she likes: Pan Tu Nie Stał. “It was a saying in communist times: ‘You’re not in the queue.’ We said it to people trying to push in,” Anna says.
This is the spot to pick up a T-shirt featuring Soviet combine harvesters or some Czas Pokaże (Time Will Tell) socks. The shop says a lot about the Polish attitude to communist times: none of the maudlin ostalgie of East Germany; this nostalgia comes with healthy dashes of colour and humour.
It did all start, however, with a disaster. The old mills had survived two world wars, but died in the economic collapse after communism ended in 1989. “Everything closed down,” says Anna. “We call that time the transformacja. It was very hard.”
We stroll into the Manufaktura area, once the site of a vast textile business started by a local scrap metal dealer, Izrael Poznański, in 1872, and now another beautifully restored collection of red-brick buildings housing restaurants, bars, shops and the fascinating Museum of the Factory. Next door is the palace that Poznański built, a neo-baroque monstrosity of bulging wealth, now the city museum.
After the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Łódź became part of the Russian empire, a melting pot of German, Jewish, Polish and Russian influences. In the 1870s, Poznański was one of a group of men who saw the potential of steam power. They imported looms from England and were soon amassing unimaginable wealth, constructing a city of handsome red-brick factories, the core of which still remains.
The Museum of the Factory houses a collection of working looms that date back to the 1880s. Only four machines are ever turned on due to noise pollution laws – in the old days, one factory might have had hundreds. This was the city of the deaf, but the deafest of all were the bosses, oblivious to the terrible hardships of their workforce, from the founders through to their communist successors. When Wajda came to these mills in the early 1970s, planning The Promised Land, he needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming. The tired faces, the crashing looms, the heat and the dust – it was all very much like 1880.
Is that your favourite film, I ask Anna? She shakes her head. “Cold War by Pawlikowski,” she says. “I love that film.”
This 2018 masterpiece is the story of a tragic love affair conducted across the Iron Curtain in the years following the second world war. Based on the lives of Pawlikowski’s parents, it is dark and sensuous, full of great music and dance. Pawlikowski has used Łodż as a location.
We move on to the Museum of Cinematography, a tour de force that warrants some preparation (watch films by Polish directors). They have everything from early working equipment to props from the most recent Oscar triumphs. By the time I get to the end, I have only a few minutes to rush to the Central Museum of Textiles.
There I find a technician, Przemysław, about to start up a 1893 Greenwood loom. He’s a former policeman with a few tales to tell, but right now one question is bothering me. “Why did film-making succeed so brilliantly in this city of textiles?” I ask him.
He taps the cast iron loom and chuckles. “I’ll show you.”
With the flick of a switch, the loom begins to clank and turn. The noise is incredible. Przemysław is moving around, adjusting and calibrating, his face concentrated. I see the spools of thread begin to unwind, the shuttle dashing back and forth, the warp and weft rhythmically rising and falling. The different colours, each no more than a thin line, but magically coming together. And from the lip of the machine spills a beautiful multicoloured cloth.
Przemysław looks at me and raises a questioning eyebrow. “Like weaving a story, right?”
The trip was provided by the Polish Tourism Organisation, with Holiday Extras lending travel support in car parking, insurance, airport transfers and hotels

Food delivery riders call on platforms to open up AI ‘black box’ they say has cut pay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:00:29 UTC
15:00:29 KST

Gig economy workers are urging delivery platforms to open up the “black box” of computer-driven algorithms that determine the jobs they are offered and how much they are paid, blaming increased use of AI for lowering wages.
A group of food delivery riders in Edinburgh say their rates of pay have fallen and their working conditions have deteriorated at the same time as Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat, the three dominant gig economy platforms in the UK and Ireland, have increased their use of automation.
“I am making half the money I was making four years ago, for the same amount of hours. It makes no sense,” said David, a food delivery rider in Edinburgh for the past seven years who did not want to share his surname.
On a weekday afternoon in the Scottish capital, David and other food delivery riders are sharing their experiences of worsening pay and conditions before they go their separate ways to carry food and groceries to customers’ doorsteps during the dinnertime rush.
Standing next to their bikes and insulated food delivery bags in central Edinburgh’s Bristo Square, many have cycled the city streets for several years and tracked a gradual decline in the amount they are paid, even though they continue to deliver similar numbers of orders.
The group has come together through the Workers’ Observatory, a charity founded by gig economy workers alongside academics at St Andrews and Edinburgh universities. Its aim is to help riders research the parts of their working experience that are mostly concealed by the companies that operate delivery platforms, to help them to challenge their working conditions.
David’s experience is echoed by Xabier Villares, who has been riding for eight years and is now the observatory’s lead organiser. “There has been a dramatic change in the last three years,” he said. “I used to work four or five days a week, especially evenings and some lunchtimes, and was able to pay my rent and bills and make a decent living with that. But that’s not an option any more.”
The observatory, which has just gained research funding for the next decade, has previously carried out experiments to monitor the variable levels of pay offered to different workers by algorithms, a system known as “dynamic pricing” that purports to match real-time supply and demand.
Trades unions are campaigning to ban the practice, saying it leaves workers uncertain about their earnings.
The introduction of a dynamic pricing algorithm in 2023 resulted in Uber drivers earning “substantially less” an hour, according to research from the University of Oxford and New York’s Columbia business school.
This week drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries launched a landmark class action against the ride-hailing app claiming they live in “constant fear” of the “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs.
The legal case lodged in Amsterdam, which could run into billions of dollars, alleges the AI-powered system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings based on what each driver is willing to take. Uber denies adjusting trip prices based on an individual driver’s behaviour and has put discrepancies down to other features of its system such as GPS.
Cailean Gallagher, director of the observatory and a lecturer at St Andrews university business school, said “there is so much infrastructure of knowledge and data that’s concealed” by the platforms, leaving gig economy riders “working in the dark”.
He added: “What we are trying to do with the observatory is to get on the ground floor in terms of understanding how the whole apparatus works.”
In one Workers’ Observatory test, a group of riders in Dunfermline, Fife, logged on to a delivery platform at the same time, with some rejecting job offers below a certain rate. This boosted the rate for some workers in the short term, while others were penalised – with one deactivated from the platform shortly afterwards, although it was unclear why – in a way that Gallagher says “seemed very arbitrary”. The major delivery platforms insist riders are not deactivated for rejecting job offers.
Dylan* has notched up more than five years riding for Deliveroo in Scotland. Since mid-2023, he has kept meticulous records tracking his monthly income, number of orders delivered and what the average pay per order is.
The number of orders Dylan delivers each hour has remained constant between 3.6 and 3.8 for the past three years. However, his records highlight how the average fee paid for each order has steadily declined over that period, from £3.67 in 2023, to £3.63 in 2024, £3.51 in 2025 and to £3.42 in the first half of 2026.
“I like to keep a close eye on everything, normally just to make paying my taxes easier,” he said. “I started noticing a couple of years ago there was actually a big drop-off in my earnings. If you are doing the same amount of work, that equates to getting paid quite a lot less for the same work.”
Dylan blames the algorithm for constantly undercutting rates, along with the introduction of what Deliveroo calls “stacked orders”, where riders can accept two or three orders from restaurants located close to each other, but not receive the level of fees they would get for delivering these separately. “Some of the offers they give you view you as a clown,” he said.
Rider Graeme Frances believes the delivery platforms “rely on [the work] being opaque”. He said: “You don’t know what is in the black box of how they work out what to pay to whom.”
Deliveroo has named its algorithm Frank and has previously described it as “super smart” and able to decide “which rider to offer which order”. The company, which was taken over by its US rival DoorDash in 2025, said Frank was “made up of machine-learning technology, which predicts the timings of every order”, allowing food to be delivered “in the most efficient and reliable way”.
Frances also blames increased use of AI by the platforms for more log-on difficulties. After ending up with a black eye following an accident outside work in August 2025, the facial recognition technology did not allow him to log-on to the Deliveroo app, preventing him from working. He was unable to get help from human support staff.
Deliveroo acknowledged Frances failed the facial recognition checks multiple times, stopping him from working, which it said was due to a blurry picture.
Frances says he requested a manual review of his facial recognition check and was not aware he had passed this until the next time he logged in, leading him to believe he could not work until his injury had healed. Deliveroo says Frances would have been able to work after the manual review.
Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat all say their riders earn more than the national living wage while they are on an order, but this does not include time waiting for job offers.
A Deliveroo spokesperson said: “Riders are guaranteed to earn a minimum hourly fee while on an order, which … rose by 3.8% this year – an above inflation increase.
“The vast majority of riders are satisfied working with us, and we continue to partner with the GMB Union to raise the bar on security and wellbeing standards. Information on our algorithm and fees are set out on our rider website.
“We have a dedicated team in place to support riders, and any significant decision over a rider account is not automated, but reviewed by our team.”
An Uber spokesperson said: “Our matching tools follow a process that balances a number of different factors, such as time and distance, to provide the best possible experience for everyone using the app.”
A Just Eat spokesperson said: “As a delivery platform we use technology, overseen by a human team, to match deliveries with available couriers.”
* Name has been changed

Fancy up to £500 of “free” cash – or how about a complimentary eco-friendly electric toothbrush? Many of Britain’s banks are offering sizeable “welcome bonuses” and other freebies in an attempt to convince people to switch to their current accounts.
This week the battle was turned up a notch. Santander is offering £240, while NatWest is hoping to tempt high-earners to defect by dangling the carrot of £500.
Several other banks are also offering cash bonuses, though digital bank Starling has taken a different tack. Eligible customers who open one of its personal current accounts before 11 October will be emailed a voucher code and instructions for how to claim a Suri Pro 2.0 electric toothbrush and UV clean-and-charge case “worth £105”. This “sustainable” toothbrush was awarded four out of five stars by the Guardian.
Alternatively, the “free money” offered by many banks could provide a welcome boost during the cost of living crisis. But some of these deals come with quite a lot of strings attached.
Take Santander’s new offer. You can now get £240 when you switch to its Everyday current account, which has no monthly fee. However, to be eligible, customers need to pay at least £1,500 into the account and set up at least two household direct debits, plus open and pay at least £200 into a Santander Regular Saver (which now pays a headline 8% interest), among other requirements.
Meanwhile, HSBC is offering £220 when you switch. You must open the new account using its mobile banking app, set up at least two direct debits, pay in at least £2,000 and spend at least £500 on your HSBC debit card.
HSBC’s First Direct brand is running its own offer, where you get £175 for switching to it. You have to set up at least two direct debits or standing orders, deposit £1,000-plus, make five or more debit card payments, and log on to digital banking.
Nationwide is also offering £175, with not dissimilar requirements relating to funding and using the new account.
The Co-operative Bank has a £200 offer, but it ends on Monday 7 September, so you will need to move fast. New customers switching to its standard current account, or Everyday Extra account (the latter carries a £12 monthly fee) can get £125 upfront, plus £25 a month for three months when they actively use the account.
Again, there are requirements relating to how much you must pay in and how you use the account.
As of this week, NatWest is rewarding people who switch to its Premier Select or Premier Reward account (the latter has a £2 monthly fee) with a £500 “welcome bonus”. To be eligible, you must meet one of three criteria: at least £100,000 income (or £120,000 joint income) needs to be paid into your new account, or you have to hold at least £100,000 savings or investments with the bank, or have a mortgage of at least £500,000 with it. (There are other requirements, too.)
The NatWest offer is very similar to one that HSBC has been running that also offers high earners a £500 welcome bonus if they switch to its Premier account.
With these offers, to get the free cash or freebie, you usually have to fully switch an existing current account from another provider using the industry’s current account switch service (Cass).
Rachel Springall, at the website Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, says Cass is quick and easy: “The service moves over any balance, and redirects standing orders and direct debits to the new account.”
She says current account switching offers come and go throughout the year and can be pulled with not much notice, but adds that customers must not feel rushed. “There is no real ‘one-size-fits-all’ current account, as many are tailored for different needs.”
If you sign up for a packaged current account – typically they offer various perks and add-ons in return for a monthly fee – you need to keep a close eye on it to make sure it is still good value; otherwise you can end up wasting your cash on the fee, says Springall.

Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and 167 drones - how many were shot down and where there were hits
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Russia attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and 167 drones - how many were shot down and where there were hits
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones; 128 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed. The Russian strikes resulted in fatalities.
On the night of September 5, Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones at Ukraine, up to half of them jet-powered. 128 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed. Missiles and drones hit their targets, but some did not reach them. UNN reports this citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Updated as of 9:35
What was used to attack and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, on the night of September 5 (starting at 6:00 p.m. on September 4), the enemy attacked with Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Rostov and Voronezh regions, as well as 167 Shahed-type attack UAVs (about half of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo, Kursk, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
How many were shot down
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:30 a.m., air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 128 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types. Hits by enemy missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 23 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 1 location. In addition, some enemy weapons did not reach their targets; information about them is being clarified
The attack is ongoing; enemy UAVs are in the airspace.
Where there were hits
Kyiv region. According to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service on September 5, the Russians once again launched a massive attack on Kyiv region, injuring 2 people. The consequences were recorded in three districts:
-  in Bucha district, a warehouse caught fire. During firefighting operations, the enemy launched a follow-up strike on a nearby warehouse building; 
-  in Boryspil, a hit caused a fire and partially destroyed a nine-story residential building. The roof caught fire, and structures on the ninth floor were destroyed. 2 people were injured, and rescuers evacuated 15 residents. Psychologists from the State Emergency Service provided people with the necessary assistance; 
-  in Obukhiv district, rescuers extinguished fires in ecosystems caused by falling debris from Russian unmanned aerial vehicles. 
The response to the consequences of the attack is ongoing.
Dnipropetrovsk region. 4 people were killed and another 6 injured as a result of Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk region, the State Emergency Service reported on September 5. The consequences were recorded in four districts:
-  in Kamianske district, the Russians attacked an industrial enterprise. 4 people were killed and another 5 injured; 
-  in Nikopol district, a 62-year-old man was injured. Private homes and an apartment building were damaged; 
-  Synelnykove and Pavlohrad districts were also struck - an enterprise was damaged.  
Rescuers extinguished all fires caused by the shelling.
Mykolaiv. As the State Emergency Service noted on September 5, 2 people were injured in Mykolaiv as a result of Russian attacks. On September 4 and during the night of September 5, Russian forces repeatedly attacked one of the city’s shopping centers with drones. According to reports on social media, this was preliminarily the "Epicentr" shopping center.
According to the State Emergency Service, the hits damaged the shopping areas and caused fires. Those injured included a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl.
Rescuers worked under the constant threat of repeated strikes. Because of the danger, personnel were withdrawn to a safe distance several times. As soon as the situation allowed, rescuers returned to dealing with the aftermath of the attack. This was once again a civilian infrastructure facility - a place where ordinary people had come just yesterday, the State Emergency Service emphasized.
Zaporizhzhia. Explosions were heard in Zaporizhzhia region from the morning of September 5. Ivan Fedorov, the former head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, reported that the enemy was attacking Zaporizhzhia, with fires breaking out in various districts of the city. A private house was destroyed. Russian unmanned aerial vehicles struck a parking lot and non-residential buildings. No information about casualties had been received so far.
Sumy. According to Serhii Kryvosheienko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration, on September 5, the enemy continues to strike infrastructure facilities in the city. Almost at midnight, an FPV drone strike via fiber-optic connection was recorded at one of the shopping centers. The strike caused a fire, which was promptly extinguished. There were no casualties. Information about the consequences is being clarified.
Odesa region. Oleg Kiper, head of the Odesa Regional Military Administration, said on September 5 that during the night the enemy again struck warehouses containing goods that had been attacked earlier. The strikes caused a fire at a warehouse used to store food products. Fortunately, there were no fatalities or casualties. The fire has now been extinguished.
The State Emergency Service showed the aftermath of the Russian attack in Odesa region.
An air-raid alert was also heard in other regions during the night of September 5, reaching as far as the western regions of Ukraine. In particular, in Rivne region.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan criticised police officers over the alleged assault on protesting students during the NEET agitation at Jantar Mantar and said that the detachment expected of officials appears to be disappearing.While speaking at the launch of former secretary (security) Yashovardhan Azad's book "Policing the Republic", Justice Bhuyan said that police must maintain their credibility because people seek their help when they feel wronged.
"All of us are dismayed when we see young officers of the Indian Police Service personally going and assaulting protesters and demonstrators. This is something very, very distressing to observe. The detachment expected of police officers somehow seems to be disappearing, and this is indeed a matter of grave concern," Justice Bhuyan said."For most common people, a policeman on the street wearing a whistle and a lathi represents the power and authority of the state. When they feel wronged, they seek the help of the police. It is, therefore, of utmost importance that the police force maintains its credibility.
It can do so only by strictly adhering to the Constitution, by functioning as a truly professional force, acting impartially, displaying courage and acting with conviction, maintaining integrity and adhering to secular principles, thereby upholding the rule of law," he said.The Supreme Court judge further said that if government functionaries become lawbreakers, it is bound to breed contempt for the law and encourage lawlessness."If the functionaries of the government become lawbreakers, it is bound to breed contempt for the law and will encourage lawlessness. No civilised nation can permit that to happen. Does a citizen shed his fundamental right the moment a policeman arrests him?" Justice Bhuyan said.
The alleged use of force by Delhi Police during the July 20 student protests at Jantar Mantar and the march towards Parliament has come under the Supreme Court's scrutiny, with the court constituting a high-level panel to examine complaints of excessive force.The panel, headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice R Subhash Reddy, will investigate allegations against Delhi Police and examine evidence including CCTV footage and videos of the protests.Among the allegations to be examined are the use of lathis, tear gas, pellet guns and electronic batons, as well as claims of targeted harassment and molestation of women protesters.

The City of Brussels plans to build a new Dutch-medium school campus on the Thurn & Taxis site. The campus will accommodate 800 pupils and will combine primary and secondary education with sports facilities. The final design of the campus will be decided through a design competition. The office of Anaïs Maes (Flemish socialist Vooruit), the alderwoman responsible for Dutch-language Education in the capital, announced the news earlier in the week.
City of Brussels eager to build a new Dutch-medium school at Thurn & Taxis
Tour & Taxis is a massive, former industrial and customs site alongside the Brussels Canal. Today it has been transformed into a trendy urban quarter with exhibition spaces, restaurants, offices, and a public park.
The campus is to consist of a primary school and a secondary school. The aim is to provide places for 800 pupils on campus. There are also plans for a large sports hall, which will be available outside school hours for sports clubs and other local users.
The City of Brussels hopes that the campus will help meet the high demand for Dutch-medium education in the capital. “There is high demand for places in Dutch-medium education, and we want to play an active role in meeting this demand, both for our current and future residents. We also want to invest in high-quality school buildings,” Mayor Philippe Close (Francophone socialist PS) said.
Design competition to crown winning project
The City of Brussels says the school campus forms part of the ongoing urban development of the Thurn & Taxis site. “As new neighbourhoods emerge, we must ensure that there are also sufficient public facilities. A school and sports infrastructure are essential components of this,” added Anaïs Maes, the local alderwoman for Urban Planning and Dutch-medium Education in the Belgian and Flemish capital.

‘Life returned to me’: Lebanese father welcomes son home after release from Israeli detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:46:32 UTC
14:46:32 KST

Naim Berjawi and Rania Abushamala
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
After months of waiting and fearing that his son might never return, Abdullah Ayyash felt life restored to him when Hussein arrived Friday at the family home in the southern Lebanese town of Harouf following his release by Israel.
“I feel like any father who gets his son back after losing him. Life has returned to me,” Ayyash told Anadolu.
He said he lost hope of seeing his son again after receiving no news about him following his detention by Israel.
Israeli forces detained Hussein Ayyash, a resident of Harouf in the Nabatieh district, on June 27, months after a ceasefire agreement had taken effect.
His father said Hussein told him after his release that he had been subjected to torture, humiliation and degrading treatment during interrogations.
Amid the joy of his return and the effects left by months in detention, Abdullah Ayyash said his son needed rest and psychological recovery.
“My son now needs psychological rest. All I tell him is: Continue with your life. This is life,” he said.
Israel released Ayyash, alongside LebaneseAli Shour and Syrian nationals Asaad Hseiki and Wissam Samawi, handing them over Friday to the International Committee of the Red Cross at the Ras Naqoura border crossing.
After completing procedures and undergoing medical examinations, Ayyash returned to his family home in Harouf. Shour went to his home in the southern city of Tyre.
Israel released Lebanese detainee Malek Kamal Razi on Thursday, and handed him to the Lebanese army through the Red Cross at the Naqoura crossing after holding him for nearly 11 months. The other four were released the following day.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said an investigation had found that the five “do not belong to any terrorist organization, did not engage in terrorism, and there is no justification for their continued detention.”
It amounted to an Israeli acknowledgment that the five had been held without grounds for months -- and in some cases for nearly a year -- before Tel Aviv said no links to any organization or involvement in armed activity had been established.
The five cases are part of a broader pattern documented by Lebanese rights groups.
Lebanon’s National Human Rights Commission documented cases of Lebanese citizens being detained or missing while carrying out civilian activities, in a legal document issued in December 2025.
Before the release of the three Lebanese nationals on Thursday and Friday, Lebanese authorities said Israel was holding 36 abductees, while Tel Aviv acknowledged detaining 33, according to Nabih Awada, an academic specializing in Israeli affairs.
Awada previously told Anadolu that 21 of the abductees were detained after the ceasefire took effect Nov. 27, 2024, as they attempted to return to their villages.
Lebanon considers civilians detained by Israel inside Lebanese territory to have been abducted rather than taken as prisoners of war as part of an exchange, particularly because Lebanon holds no Israelis in return.
Israel’s offensive on Lebanon has continued since March 2, killing 4,354 people and injuring 12,325, while displacing more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
