Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
00:00:21 UTC
09:00:21 KST

On the evening of 1 April 2024, a team of aid workers from World Central Kitchen (WCK) stood on Gaza’s Mediterranean shore overseeing the unloading of a barge full of desperately needed food on a makeshift jetty made of sand and rubble.
The Gaza war had been raging for six months and Israel’s closure of land crossings had left the whole territory facing the threat of famine. WCK and local Palestinian contractors had constructed the jetty out of everything they could lay their hands on, including debris from the bombed house of one of the contractors, so that the pallets of humanitarian assistance could be delivered by boat from Cyprus.
A consignment of 200 tonnes of rice, flour and other proteins had arrived two weeks earlier, the first sea shipment to dock in Gaza since 2007. This was the second shipment and it was even bigger, with enough food to prepare more than 1m meals, as well as a Ramadan gift of dates from the United Arab Emirates.
The choreography of the delivery had been coordinated over several days with the Israeli army, and an officer was on the jetty to observe the proceedings. In the midst of a devastating bombing campaign after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023, this humanitarian effort was supposed to be carried out under internationally agreed military protection.
The shipment had been unloaded by 8.30pm but despite the lengthy planning, there was a delay in receiving final Israeli security clearance for the eight hired trucks and two WCK escort vehicles to leave the jetty. By the time the green light came from local Israeli commanders and the convoy began to move south, night had fallen.
There was no initial overhead surveillance but two drones joined somewhere along the route to the first stop, a WCK welcome centre 6 miles to the south. Those drones were assigned to the Israel Defense Forces’ (IDF) Nahal brigade, which had not been fully briefed on the aid convoy’s itinerary.
A special adviser assigned by the Australian government to assess the case (in the interests of justice for the Australian victim Lalzawmi Frankcom), found that “specific details about the pre-coordinated WCK aid mission had not been passed down from higher levels of Southern Command to the brigade and UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operator”.
Local guards
At the WCK welcome centre, a few local men hired as guards were waiting, at least one of them armed. At a time of widespread hunger, many food convoys had been mobbed by desperate crowds as well as organised gangs, some of whom may have had been linked to Hamas, though Hamas never had the grip on food deliveries alleged by the Israeli authorities.
Using local security for aid deliveries was not unknown in Gaza, but it was directly against WCK policy to use armed escorts. The WCK says it is unclear why the local team on that night agreed to accept armed guards. The official Israeli version of events suggests it was “due to the convoy’s delayed departure, during night-time hours,” and noted it “was not coordinated with IDF authorities”.
The official Israeli version does not say how many armed men were waiting for the convoy (unofficial versions vary between two and four), but drone footage reportedly showed one of them climb on top of the cabin of one of the trucks and fire a shot in the air shortly afterwards, for reasons that remain unknown.
The Nahal brigade officers and the drone operators assigned to them concluded it was a Hamas hijack, based in part on the false assumption that such hijackings were commonplace.
“The troops also identified vehicles surrounding the trucks in a manner that, in their assessment and based on accumulated operational experience, corresponded to a scenario in which the Hamas terrorist organisation had taken control of the convoy,” the official account says.
The Israeli military prosecutor’s version of events, published last month to justify his decision not to pursue criminal proceedings, does not mention the breakdown in communication between the army’s coordination and liaison administration, which handles humanitarian needs in the territory, and the Nahal brigade controlling that sector of the Gaza Strip.
Furthermore, the prosecutor’s version says efforts by IDF personnel to contact WCK were unsuccessful. But according to WCK sources and the Australian report on events, contact was established that night with WCK headquarters in the US, which in turn got in touch with an employee in Gaza.
According to the Australian report, the WCK worker on the ground told headquarters staff the guards only had “fake guns”. It remains unclear what the basis for that claim was, but the WCK assured the IDF that it had not lost contact with the convoy and it had not been hijacked.
Arrival at destination
It is unclear whether this exchange with WCK was relayed to the Nahal brigade before the strikes. But even if it was not, the fact that the convoy of eight food trucks continued on its journey and arrived at its intended destination, the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, should have been ample proof that the aid had not been seized by Hamas.
The military prosecutor’s summary acknowledges that the “convoy arrived at the designated warehouse and unloaded the aid” but does not address the seemingly straightforward conclusion that it had therefore not been diverted. The IDF has yet to release audio recordings of military communications that night.
After the trucks entered the warehouse, the WCK workers and the local guards stayed outside by their own vehicles for about 10 minutes. That short period, observed by operators of Israeli drones, appears to have helped seal the aid workers’ fate. As far as the Nahal brigade’s chief of staff, reserve Col Nochi Mendel, was concerned, they were “mingling” with Hamas.
Under the very loose procedures of “incrimination” that delegate much to the discretion of field commanders like Mendel, the WCK workers became unwitting targets as they celebrated the completion of a successful delivery of aid, because they were in the proximity to armed men.
“There was incrimination. The incrimination was according to the rules,” Mendel said. “There were armed men there with certainty. With certainty, they [the aid workers] had mingled with armed Hamas men.”
Other IDF officers have confirmed to the Guardian that such a process of guilt by association is used widely to determine targets, though different field commanders use different standards in making decisions. The Israel military prosecutor, in making his assessment on criminal responsibility, did not address the practice of incrimination in targeting.
Parting of ways
After the brief pause outside the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, the guards and the WCK workers went in separate directions. “The WCK vehicles departed together west towards the coast. Concurrently, the vehicle containing the locally contracted security personnel, including the previously identified gunmen, drove north,” the Australian report says. It also makes clear that the IDF was aware of this parting of the two groups.
“One UAV tracked the locally contracted security vehicle heading north for approximately three minutes until it arrived at another warehouse where up to four gunmen were identified exiting the vehicle and entering the building,” the report says. “A decision was made to discontinue targeting them due to the time available before they entered the northern warehouse.”
The military prosecutor’s version makes no mention of this drone or the fact that the suspected gunmen were seen driving off in a different direction and entering a separate building. It claims instead that “several individuals mistakenly … identified as armed persons” were observed getting into WCK vehicles.
That is at odds with the Australian report and the accounts of Israeli officers familiar with the investigation. They said a bag was spotted by a drone operator being put in a WCK car, and that the operator mistook it for a gun, though sources briefed on the drone video said that later analysis showed no sign of a suspicious bag.
Whether or not it was a gun was irrelevant as far as Mendel was concerned. He saw his task as carrying out the government policy of crushing Hamas governance in Gaza, which included stopping its seizure of aid deliveries.
“If a Hamas operative takes over a truck and after that he sells it and that’s how he recruits more people, then what does it matter if he’s armed or not?” Mendel said.
In its economical, dry prose, the Australian report describes what happened next as the WCK workers left the warehouse at about 11pm. “The WCK vehicles proceeded west to the coast. Due to the time delays encountered, rather than return to the WCK welcome centre as planned, a decision was made to return directly to the accommodation in Rafah,” the report says.
“After turning south on to the coast road, the three WCK vehicles were struck in relatively quick succession, each strike being approximately two minutes apart. There were two survivors from the strike on the first (up-armoured) vehicle who quickly moved to the second vehicle, then two survivors from the second (up-armoured) vehicle who moved to the third vehicle. There were no survivors from the third (soft-skinned) vehicle. Over the four-minute period 23:09 – 23:13, the seven WCK workers were killed – likely one in the first vehicle, two in the second and four in the last.”
The seven victims of the IDF drone strikes were from the UK, Australia, Poland, Palestine and the US. The Britons John Chapman, James Kirby and James Henderson were working as security consultants. Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, a Palestinian driver and translator, was the youngest killed, at 25. Frankcom, Damian Soból, a Pole, and Jacob Flickinger, a US-Canadian dual citizen, were humanitarian workers for WCK.
The military prosecutor claimed that in turning south towards Rafah, the WCK workers were “deviating from the route that the organisation had coordinated in advance with the IDF”, giving weight to the Nahal brigade’s mistaken impression that “Hamas operatives had taken control of the convoy”.
Mendel also mentioned this “deviation” as a mitigating factor. However, the Australian report found that the fact that the WCK workers had changed their route only became known after they were killed, and “as such it did not play a factor” in the decision to open fire.
The official Israeli version of events says Mendel and his brigade fire support commander ignored an order on the night of the airstrike from a superior officer to cease any attacks on humanitarian convoys, but Mendel has said the order is a fabrication.
“It never happened, never existed,” Mendel said. “No operational directive reached the brigade to cease the strikes … We checked it a thousand times.”
In explaining his own decision-making, Mendel stressed he was carrying out Israeli government policy by stopping Hamas taking control of food deliveries. He had been lauded by his superiors for ordering strikes on several earlier alleged Hamas attempts to hijack aid. In his mind, the events on the night of 1 April 2024 fitted the same pattern.
“I didn’t plan to kill the aid workers,” Mendel said, but added: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”
Justifying this conclusion, he said: “They were mixed together with Hamas operatives …near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on.”
In a written statement, WCK said: “It is extraordinary to learn now that some in the IDF considered our humanitarian work to be enemy activity based on the flimsiest evidence, or no evidence at all.
“This undefined, unjustified and unlawful view is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. The IDF’s shifting excuses and explanations for these unlawful airstrikes are precisely why we continue to demand an independent investigation with the full release of the IDF’s evidence.”

====================================================================================================

‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
00:00:20 UTC
09:00:20 KST

Seven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows.
A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery to Gaza. Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed.
The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.
However, interviews with senior Israeli officers involved in the incident or familiar with the official Israel investigation suggest it glossed over the role played in the killings by a common IDF practice used to designate targets, which endangers aid workers and civilians in general, especially when combined with the army’s open-ended mission to end Hamas’s civil control in Gaza.
More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military in the three years of the Gaza war. The army’s own internal data suggests more than three-quarters of the dead have been civilians.
The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, said the WCK workers became potential targets after they had a brief encounter, lasting just minutes, with armed guards assumed to be from Hamas (an assumption later shown to be groundless).
He deemed them to have “mixed together” with alleged Hamas militants, where mixing together was defined as being “near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on”. Asked whether the presence of armed men made the entire convoy a target, Mendel replied: “Certainly.”
He concluded: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”
Mendel was referring to a general policy of haflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association. The manner in which haflala is to be applied in a given sector is often conveyed in a commander’s mission brief delivered verbally to other officers.
He said his unit had been commended by the army hierarchy for its involvement in several strikes on what were deemed to be Hamas's attempted commandeering of aid. “They applauded us and were pleased with our action,” he said. The difference in the WCK incident was that foreign nationals were killed, he said. “That’s the whole difference. Not a substantive difference.”
When the WCK convoy was destroyed, it was nowhere near Israeli troops. Several Israeli officers familiar with the incident said the strikes were not ordered on the basis of an imminent threat to Israeli lives, but to fulfil the mission to thwart Hamas attempts to control aid deliveries.
An IDF statement said the airstrikes were a result of an “erroneous assessment that Hamas military operatives were present in the vehicles, rather than from an intention to target the organisation’s personnel”.
The statement added that “this assessment was compounded by serious failures to comply with applicable orders and procedures”. However, it said: “Following an in-depth examination of the findings and in light of the standards applicable under criminal law, it was determined that, despite the aforementioned failures, the circumstances of the incident did not give rise to a reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence warranting the opening of a criminal investigation.”
The WCK said the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings was “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. “At the time of the lethal attacks, our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” the WCK said. “The IDF had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”
Britain, Australia and Canada denounced the prosecutor’s decision as “shameful”, saying they would “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the slain aid workers. The UK opened an inquest in 2024 into the deaths of the three British team members: James Kirby, James Henderson and John Chapman.
Saifeddin Abutaha, a Palestinian, Australian Zomi Frankcom, Damian Sobol, a Pole, and a dual Canadian-US citizen, Jacob Flickinger, were the other victims. The UK inquest was adjourned pending the outcome of the Israeli investigation.
Mendel, who is the only officer of such high rank to have been dismissed for his actions in the Gaza war, has been portrayed in army command briefings as a rogue operator. Questions have been raised about a political motive. Mendel is a settler who is reported to have been one of the 130 signatories of a 20 January 2024 letter to the IDF calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.
However, the way the Israeli army operates in Gaza – rules of engagement are made contingent on local circumstances and passed on, often verbally, down the chain of command – gives officers at Mendel’s level wide discretion in subjective judgments as to who is a “terrorist” and therefore a target.
The IDF statement said its activity in the Gaza Strip was “regulated by a broad range of binding written orders and standing directives governing the use of force, the approval processes for strikes, strikes against sensitive sites, and other matters” and that these incorporated “the rules of the laws of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions in attack”.
The statement said that “a person does not become a lawful target merely because they are in the vicinity of an armed individual, come into contact with them, or travel alongside them”.
The IDF said: “Carrying a weapon may be a relevant factor in such an assessment, but is not sufficient on its own without meeting the definitions described above. In particular, and in the context of the incident in question, security personnel hired to protect a humanitarian convoy from looting do not become lawful targets merely because they are armed.”
An IDF officer familiar with the WCK killings said that given the circumstances and the standing IDF procedures, the overwhelming majority of officers would have acted in the same way. “There were armed men next to them,” the officer said. “If you took qualified people and put them on the call, in 90% of cases this is what would have happened,” the officer said. “In my guess, 99% of the time the first bomb would have been dropped; 90% of the time the second; 80% of the time the third.”
Reserve Brigadier General Oren Solomon, the battle manager of Gaza Division, said that a mistake had been made in determining that an armed man had entered one of the vehicles, but added that once that error had been committed, the incrimination procedure led inevitably to the three missile strikes.
“If I incriminated this vehicle beforehand as Hamas – anyone who escapes from it and enters another vehicle: death comes,” Brig Gen Solomon said. “Together with him they will die. That meets the incrimination rules, no problem.”
A senior officer involved in the initial Israeli military investigation into the WCK case, argued Mendel overstepped in interpreting the rules of incrimination.
“You can’t incriminate 20 people if there’s one armed,” he said. The officer argued that the first strike could have been justified by the initial misidentification, even at the cost of civilian casualties, but not the subsequent missiles.
“You struck someone you suspected, a vehicle you suspected had an armed man in it. The moment two people came out, nobody with a weapon, the second and third strikes are contrary to orders because you don’t know whom you’re striking,” he said.
The other systemic factor that contributed to the deaths of the seven aid workers, and potentially countless more civilians, was one of the missions given to the army in Gaza by Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government: to destroy Hamas’s influence and control. That meant anyone deemed to be involved in – or assisting – the Hamas administration, including by distributing aid, could find themselves in the sights of an Israeli drone operator.
“I remind you that part of our mission was to crush Hamas’s ability to govern,” Mendel said. “Part of the mission was to hit that [Hamas-controlled aid deliveries], and we hit it.”
Interviews with IDF officers suggest there was a widespread belief in the ranks that Hamas had wrested control of the bulk of aid deliveries into Gaza. That assumption was unfounded, later analysis showed. It was a period of widespread hunger caused by an Israeli blockade, when food convoys were being mobbed by desperate civilians, criminal gangs and Hamas militia.
The belief that Hamas hijacks were widespread meant that the appearance of armed men in proximity to the WCK vehicle in April 2024 fitted a “pattern of activity” that helped incriminate the whole convoy in the eyes of Mendel and his unit.
The IDF officer familiar with the incident said it was common practice to designate any armed man in Gaza as Hamas or a “terrorist”, as Mendel did. The officer added: “How you define that it’s Hamas – he’s in proximity to weapons, and because he touches the trucks, and because he does all sorts of things that look as if he’s going to take over the trucks.”
The role of the incrimination principle in the WCK killings shows how it has become a factor in the historically high proportion of civilians killed in the Gaza war. This sits alongside the routine acceptance of high “collateral damage” in the targeting of Hamas militants, the designation of large and shifting areas as free-fire zones, and the deliberate levelling of neighbourhoods to prevent the return of Palestinian communities.
The common factor is that constraints on targeting were minimised in the interests of an open-ended mission. Since the start of the war in 2023, no Israeli soldier has been convicted of wrongful death or war crimes in Gaza operations.
“I came to defeat Hamas,” Mendel said. “If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing.”
He also dismissed the significance of the killings. “I think it’s an idiotic side event,” Mendel said. “It really isn’t a serious event.”

Trump again seeks to remove protections for wolves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:58:00 UTC
08:58:00 KST

Trump again seeks to remove protections for wolves
- President Trump’s administration seeks to remove endangered species protections for gray and Mexican wolves to aid cattle ranchers in controlling livestock losses.
- The order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to assess if wolves meet recovery criteria and start delisting processes if so, encouraging states to ease killing restrictions.
- Conservationists warn this move threatens wolf recovery, calling it political appeasement for ranchers despite existing compensation programmes and recent weakening of the Endangered Species Act.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s administration on Sept 4 pushed to drop endangered species protections for wolves, outraging conservationists who said the move would jeopardise the iconic predators’ recovery from the brink of extinction.
In an executive order aimed at helping cattle ranchers combat livestock losses, the President gave his Interior Secretary Doug Burgum 90 days to “make a determination as to whether the gray wolf and the Mexican wolf have met the recovery criteria for delisting or downlisting under the Endangered Species Act (ESA)”.
If the recovery criteria are found to have been met, the Interior Secretary is asked to begin the process of delisting.
Upon such a determination, the Interior Secretary and other officials are to meet with state authorities and encourage them to pass similar measures and loosen standards for killing wolves.
Speaking with ranchers at an Oval Office event, Trump appeared confused about what the order did, asking: “But you can shoot them as of today?”
He was corrected by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins who laughed and joked: “Secretary Burgum has to do a little magic.”
It is thought that at least a quarter of a million wolves once roamed from coast to coast before European settlers embarked on campaigns of eradication that endured into the 20th century.
During his first term, Trump delisted grey wolves but not the more endangered Mexican wolves, although Sept 4’s executive order mentioned both.
Former president Joe Biden’s administration fought in court to uphold the Trump delisting, but ultimately lost in 2022, and the policy was reversed.
The Wolf Conservation Centre estimates there are around 7,600 grey wolves in the contiguous United States. The Mexican Wolf Interagency Field Team places the number of Mexican wolves at 317 at the end of 2025.
Ben Greuel, wildlife campaign manager at the Sierra Club, framed the move as a cynical ploy to appease cattle ranchers angered by the administration’s decision to temporarily increase lower-tariff beef imports.
“Trump is putting grey wolves and Mexican wolves in the cross hairs to placate the backlash caused by his own beef import policies,” he said. “Turning wolf protections into political damage control will do nothing to lower grocery bills or help families struggling with the cost of living.”
Conservationists also point out that ranchers are already eligible for compensation for livestock losses to wolves under state and federal programmes – the latter covering up to 100 per cent for confirmed kills under Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Trump’s government in July finalised three rules weakening the landmark Endangered Species Act.
One rescinded the longstanding definition of “harm”, which had covered habitat destruction.
Another scrapped a rule that automatically applied endangered species protections to those listed as “threatened”.
The third requires the government to consider economic and national security trade-offs when deciding whether to designate a particular area as “critical habitat”. AFP

Halis Sünnetci

Hull City head coach Sergej Jakirovic has signed a new two-year contract, the English Premier League club announced on Friday.
The agreement will keep the 49-year-old at MKM Stadium until the summer of 2028, and includes an option to extend his stay through the end of the 2028-29 season.
Jakirovic was appointed in June 2025 after Hull narrowly avoided relegation from the Championship the previous season. He then led the Tigers to Premier League promotion during his first campaign in English football.
He averaged 1.58 points per game as the Tigers secured a Championship playoff spot on the final day of the regular season with a 2-1 victory against Norwich City.
Hull overcame Millwall in the semifinals before defeating Middlesbrough in the playoff final at Wembley, recording three consecutive clean sheets during their promotion run.
Jakirovic became the third Hull City manager to guide the club to the Premier League through the playoffs.
The Tigers have also made a strong start to their first Premier League campaign since the 2016-17 season, beating Manchester United 2-0 at home before recording a 1-0 victory against Coventry City on matchday two.
“I have felt the support from the club and our fans from the minute I arrived, so I am delighted that this journey will continue. Hull feels like my home, and I’m excited for this journey to continue,” said Jakirovic. “Promotion to the Premier League is a dream come true. You have to believe in your work, and we have a special group here who are sticking together as a family.”

‘Small potatoes’: US President Trump downplays war on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:55:50 UTC
08:55:50 KST

‘Small potatoes’: US President Trump downplays war on Iran
The president’s remarks could signal a new strategy towards the conflict, focused on minimising its impact.
As the United States and Israel’s war on Iran enters its seventh month with no clear end in sight, President Donald Trump has become the latest US official to downplay the conflict.
On Friday, Trump said the conflict, which has resulted in the deaths of 18 US service members and a spike in global energy prices, is “small potatoes”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How much oil is going through Hormuz? Why data doesn’t match US claims
- list 2 of 3Iran war: Why US midterms could be a pivotal moment
- list 3 of 3‘Things happen’: How Vance’s comment on Iran wedding strike fits US pattern
“It’s not a big thing,” Trump said, comparing strikes on Iran with other US military campaigns, including the January 3 operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
“We did Venezuela, and we did this. In Venezuela, we lost nobody. In this, we lost 18 people.”
His remarks came at an Oval Office signing event, where reporters asked him to weigh in on remarks from Vice President JD Vance.
A day earlier, at a White House news briefing, Vance appeared to suggest the conflict had cooled, despite a recent exchange of intense fire between US and Iranian forces.
“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting,” Vance said, arguing that major combat operations only lasted six weeks. He then added, “I recognise there have been places where this has flared up.”
Trump on Friday told reporters there was “a lot of truth” to what Vance said. He opted to brand the fighting as a “military conflict”.
“We do intermittent strikes,” Trump said, adding: “We’re not fighting right now. There’s no fighting. We’re taking out a lot of oil. We control the Hormuz Strait. We control it very strongly.”
Since the war began on February 28, Trump has used various phrases to avoid calling the conflict a war.
In the past, he has called the fighting with Iran a “little skirmish”, a “little detour” and a “little excursion, a couple of weeks, few weeks of excursion”.
“It’s an excursion that will keep us out of a war,” Trump said in March.
Experts say such terminology is likely strategic. The Trump administration has faced pushback for not seeking congressional approval before launching its strikes on Iran.
The US Constitution grants Congress the exclusive power to declare war, though successive presidencies have taken unilateral military actions without the legislature’s approval. Legal scholars have repeatedly questioned the legality of those manoeuvres.
In June, both chambers of Congress passed a war powers resolution, calling on Trump to either stop his military campaign against Iran or seek congressional authorisation for it.
The resolution was largely symbolic, though it did signal growing bipartisan opposition to Trump’s war on Iran.
As the conflict enters its seventh month, it remains widely unpopular in the US.
A poll released on Monday by the Reuters news agency and the research firm Ipsos found that nearly six in 10 US adults disapproved of the military strikes on Iran.
As the midterm elections approach in November, and peace talks remain deadlocked, the president’s remarks appear designed to minimise the conflict’s impact across the world.
The war has led to attacks across the Middle East, and fuel prices remain high. In the US, the American Automobile Association (AAA) says the average fuel price is $4.15 per gallon (3.8 litres), up nearly a dollar from last year.
The Trump administration, however, has long argued the war and its effects would be short-term.
It has also signalled that it intends to double down on its economic pressure campaign against Iran, which has long faced US sanctions.
In August, Trump pledged on Truth Social to pursue the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY”.
This week, his administration announced new sanctions aimed at cutting off the country’s access to the international financial system.
On Friday, Trump also did not rule out further attacks, suggesting the US may “very soon” strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a military site near the Natanz uranium enrichment facility. Natanz was bombed in June 2025 and again during the current war.
A recent exchange of strikes this month resulted in Iran firing on US military bases across the Middle East. The US, meanwhile, was accused by the Iranian government of bombing a wedding celebration in the coastal city of Sirik, killing at least four people.
While the future of the conflict is uncertain, Trump said he was pleased with its progress.
“I don’t think it matters what you call it,” Trump said. “What matters is you’ve had tremendous success.”

The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) issued its highest-level landslide warning for the town of Yakushima, Kagoshima prefecture on Saturday following record-breaking rainfall.
"There is a very high possibility that some kind of disaster has already occurred in areas designated as landslide hazard zones," the national authority for weather and geological monitoring said in a statement, noting the rainfall is "unprecedented."

Putin announced battlefield encirclements that the evidence doesn’t show, but Russia’s real offensive is accelerating elsewhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:45:31 UTC
08:45:31 KST

Putin announced battlefield encirclements that the evidence doesn’t show, but Russia’s real offensive is accelerating elsewhere
At a late-night press conference in Bishkek on September 1, Vladimir Putin said what he believed was happening on the battlefield. Once again, his account clashed with the Russian military’s documented gains. Putin is evidently aware that even troops at the front do not accept his reports, so he cited sources in the General Staff and “other agencies.” He said the picture, as it “appears” to him, is “fairly objective.” He immediately said that Ukrainian units had been encircled in two places in the Kharkiv region and that Sviatohirsk, near Sloviansk, had been captured. The claims surprised even the people behind Telegram channels close to the Russian military command, who likely work at the headquarters of the units responsible for the sectors Putin mentioned. Yet, strange as it may seem, Putin’s optimism about these operations is not detached from reality: Russia’s offensive accelerated in late summer and again pushed Ukrainian defenses into crisis along several important axes in early fall.
The Kharkiv region
- Putin said several thousand Ukrainian troops were encircled near Vovchansk and pinned against the border. Russian forces have indeed broken through from two directions southeast of the city, which Russia captured by mid-2026 after two years of heavy fighting. One group advanced from Vovchansk in the north and approached the large settlement of Bilyi Kolodiaz; another is advancing toward it from the Russian border to the east.
- Russia’s Defense Ministry said a month ago that Bilyi Kolodiaz had also been captured. Since then, however, published videos filmed by Russian units have shown strikes on Ukrainian positions inside the settlement. The nearest Russian positions are in tree lines several kilometers to the north.
- Published videos indicate that the force advancing from the east has not moved past Kupyne, 25 kilometers (16 miles) from Bilyi Kolodiaz.
- To be fair, the most recent videos from the area date to mid-August, and the situation may well have changed considerably in the weeks since. Still, it would be unusual for such changes to leave no visual trace at all — the Russian push toward Bilyi Kolodiaz in early August and the Ukrainian counterattacks that followed were both well documented.
- In any case, Russia does not have enough troops in this sector to encircle a 25-by-25-kilometer (16-by-16-mile) area. No encirclement of that size has been completed since May 2022, despite many attempts by both sides.
- An encirclement of Ukrainian units near Pisky-Radkivske, south of Kupiansk, seems even less likely. The Ukrainian army has maintained a large bridgehead on the eastern bank of the Oskil River for four years, centered on Borova, north of Pisky-Radkivske. Ukrainian forces also have numerous crossings over the shallow Krasnooskilske Reservoir. From the bridgehead, they periodically attack near the junction of the Kharkiv and Luhansk regions, trying to keep a small part of the Luhansk region under Ukrainian control so Russia cannot capture the entire region. Overall, this stretch of the front remains a “backwater.” Most troops in the area are fighting either near Kupiansk to the north or near Lyman to the south.
- Russian forces have made gains around Kupiansk and inside the city in recent months, retaking territory Russia lost during Ukraine’s counteroffensive last winter. They have also seized large areas on the eastern bank of the Oskil between Borova and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi. But Putin said last fall that Russia already fully controlled Kupiansk, so this time he did not mention these actual gains. Nor did he mention a new Ukrainian attempt to pressure the northwestern flank of the Russian force advancing on Kupiansk near Dvorichna and Zapadne.
Lyman and Sviatohirsk
- Putin said Russian forces had captured Sviatohirsk, a city on the northern bank of the Siverskyi Donets River, 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Sloviansk. But no Russian positions have been documented in the immediate vicinity of Sviatohirsk in recent months. Moreover, Ukrainian forces have rolled back Russian incursions into the nearby villages of Yarova and Pryshyb, on a small Russian bridgehead on the river’s southern bank.
- Ukrainian forces are also trying to push Russian troops farther from Lyman, a city Russian forces tried and failed to storm in early summer.
- Overall, Ukrainian forces have managed to halt the Russian advance toward Sloviansk on the river’s northern bank, but not on its southern bank.
Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Dobropillia
- After capturing most of Kostiantynivka — where scattered groups of Ukrainian troops still remain — Russian forces found themselves in early August in a situation they had hoped to avoid. Despite their success in the center of the front, which stretches more than 100 kilometers (62 miles) from the Siverskyi Donets River to Pokrovsk, they could not advance directly on the Kramatorsk–Sloviansk urban area. Attacks on the flanks — the Pokrovsk–Dobropillia, Dobropillia–Druzhkivka, and Lyman–Sviatohirsk sectors — were stalling, and a direct push toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from Kostiantynivka or Chasiv Yar was difficult without support from the flanks.
- In recent weeks, Russia’s offensive on the western flank, from Dobropillia to Druzhkivka, has intensified sharply.
- Russian forces captured settlements south of Dobropillia and then reached Annivka on the city’s eastern outskirts. Exactly a year after a failed attempt to break through to the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road, Russian troops struck again at the same point, this time with far larger forces and more extensive preparation. They captured Kucheriv Yar — which Russian forces had also occupied in August–September 2025 — and Rubizhne. Farther east, Russian forces also pushed toward the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road, reaching the area around Novoandriivka.
- Russian forces continue to advance toward Druzhkivka along the Kazennyi Torets River. They have crossed the river and taken up positions in Raiske, 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the city. Along the entire stretch from Dobropillia to the northwestern approaches to Druzhkivka, Ukrainian defenses are in a full-blown crisis requiring urgent measures — such as redeploying major reserves, as Ukraine did in the same area a year ago.
- The situation is also deteriorating southeast of Druzhkivka, where Russian troops are advancing rapidly — by the standards of this war — from the direction of Chasiv Yar. They have already reached Izhivka on the approaches to Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka.
- Farther north, on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets, Russian forces have reached the outskirts of Mykolaivka, which shields Sloviansk.
- The two sides’ starting positions for the battle over the Kramatorsk–Sloviansk urban area will depend on how Ukrainian commanders respond to these advances from several directions. A delayed or inadequate response could mean the battle begins as early as winter. Kyiv has created new command structures but has not yet transferred additional troops, which could be freed up only by weakening other sectors of the front. Ukrainian forces in the northern Donetsk region are clearly feeling the absence of an army corps — an air assault formation. The formation was sent southwest in the spring to the junction of the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk regions to stop the Russian advance deeper into the Zaporizhzhia region, particularly toward Orikhiv.
Orikhiv and Mala Tokmachka
- In August, Ukrainian forces made another attempt to advance near the junction of the three regions. They broke through near the Donetsk–Zaporizhzhia road and advanced 10–12 kilometers (6–7 miles) to the Mokri Yaly River. The breakthrough point seemed well chosen: it was right at the junction of the Russian “Vostok” and “Tsentr” groups, bringing Ukrainian troops onto the western flank of the “Tsentr” group’s 90th Tank Division, whose positions faced north.
- Russian commanders, however, quickly brought in forces from the 90th Tank Division and the neighboring 41st Combined Arms Army to repel the Ukrainian attack from the west. In mid-August, both sides published videos showing their flags raised in about 10 villages. Ukrainian forces did so first, followed by units of the “Tsentr” and “Vostok” groups. The situation has remained unclear since then, but the lack of new information suggests that the Ukrainian advance was stopped, perhaps only temporarily, and that Ukrainian forces lost some of the territory they had previously retaken.
- Ukrainian forces also failed to achieve the offensive’s primary goal. Strikes on the northern flank of the “Vostok” group, which began in the spring, were meant to halt its advance eastward toward Orikhiv, in the central Zaporizhzhia region. The advance was only slowed, and it has now resumed with renewed force.
- Russian forces have reached the Orikhiv–Novomykolaivka road in several places. It is one of the main supply routes for the Orikhiv garrison. Russian troops have often failed to hold positions along the road or in nearby villages, however: Ukrainian forces continue to hold positions behind and on the flanks of the advancing Russian troops and are even counterattacking.
- The clash between small groups of assault troops on the steppe has already had dire consequences for Orikhiv itself. The “Dnipro” group’s 42nd Motorized Rifle Division had failed for two years to break through the Novodanylivka–Mala Tokmachka line south and southeast of Orikhiv; it did so in just two weeks. Russian forces have captured all of Novodanylivka, and assault troops from the 42nd Division have also established positions on the southern outskirts of Orikhiv.
- For the first time in a long while, Russian assault troops have also reached the center of Mala Tokmachka, a large village familiar from its frequent appearances in reports by pro-war commentators. Russian troops have cut the road from the village to Orikhiv. It remains unclear whether the 118th Mechanized Brigade, which had held Mala Tokmachka since early 2024, managed to retain positions even on the village’s outskirts. With Russian forces in their rear and the road to Orikhiv cut, doing so will be extremely difficult.

A private spacecraft approached NASA’s doomed telescope, but could no longer save it
Kyiv • UNN
Link approached NASA’s Swift telescope to within 15 km and collected data. The rescue mission was canceled due to a lack of fuel after its reserves were lost.
The private spacecraft Link operated by Katalyst Space Technologies approached NASA’s Swift telescope to within about 15 km and collected data on its condition, but was unable to complete the rescue mission due to insufficient fuel. Associated Press reports, as UNN writes.
Details
Link was launched in July in an attempt to raise the aging Swift to a higher orbit and extend its operational life. However, shortly after launch, the spacecraft began spinning uncontrollably.
Controllers managed to stabilize Link, but this consumed a significant portion of its fuel reserves. In August, the rescue operation was canceled, although the company decided to use the spacecraft for an additional rendezvous with the telescope and to collect data.
Link managed to approach Swift to within 15 km
This week, Link approached Swift to within about 15 km and took images of the telescope.
We got so close, yet at the same time so far away
NASA paid the company about $30 million for the attempt to rescue the telescope. From the outset, the agency regarded the mission as experimental, in part because of the risk of the spacecraft colliding and creating space debris.
According to Lee, Link likely no longer has enough fuel for another rendezvous with Swift. The spacecraft itself may remain in orbit for several more weeks, after which it will enter the atmosphere and burn up.

US judge blocks Trump order to restrict mail-in voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:40:33 UTC
08:40:33 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
A federal court in the state of Massachusetts issued a nationwide preliminary injunction on Friday to block the US government from implementing restrictive new mail-in ballot rules for the 2026 midterm elections.
Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the United States Postal Service (USPS) overstepped its legal authority by attempting to regulate the "time, place, and manner" of elections. The court emphasized that under the Elections Clause of the US Constitution, the powers are reserved for individual states and the US Congress, leaving the executive branch with no inherent authority to intervene.
Talwani warned that forcing states to redesign envelopes and upload voter data to an unproven digital portal weeks before the Nov. 3 election would cause "inevitable" disenfranchisement.
The ruling noted that the policy stemming from President Donald Trump’s executive order would allow the USPS to "refuse to transmit" ballots that did not meet the new standards. It means millions of Americans could lose their right to vote if the USPS withheld ballots that did not comply with the new, complex standards.
The court found that many small rural jurisdictions lack the technology to print the required specialized barcodes. Additionally, the digital portal the government intended to use is not yet operational. The judge said the record contained "no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting" to justify the sudden policy shift.
The ruling prevents the government from refusing to transmit mail-in or absentee ballots based on the new requirements.
While Trump has frequently advocated for tighter voting restrictions, the court denied the administration's request to pause the injunction.

Little is known about Artem Kirpichenok’s case. Israeli authorities may suspect him of espionage.
Family representatives told Meduza that, based on “unofficial information,” investigators suspect Kirpichenok of espionage and of contacting an agent of a foreign intelligence service.
But “there’s no Arab angle [to the case],” the source said. According to the source, the agent Kirpichenok allegedly contacted is not from Lebanon or Iran.

And Russia is hardly a stranger to Israel: the two countries conduct joint intelligence operations and share information despite friction over Iran and other issues,” the source told Meduza.
The alleged offenses are considered serious, according to the source, but even Kirpichenok’s lawyer does not know exactly what he is accused of. Israeli law has more than a dozen statutes that can apply in espionage cases, with penalties of up to life imprisonment.
“The fact that someone is held in a Shin Bet detention facility indicates that the person is suspected of crimes against state security,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family said.
A separate charge may stem from Kirpichenok’s 2018 trip to Iran, which he wrote about on social media at the time. Israel considers Iran an enemy state, and traveling there without special permission from the Israeli Interior Ministry carries a prison sentence of up to four years.
Nika Dubrovskaya, an artist and friend of Kirpichenok’s, told the outlet Bumaga that he visited Israel several times after his trip to Iran without running into problems at the border. Another friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza the account was accurate and said the historian had also visited Israel the previous winter, before his August trip.
He rented out his apartment in Ashkelon, which was one reason he returned to the country several times a year.
Kirpichenok’s research and columns
Kirpichenok, 51, holds a Doctor of Sciences degree and works as a journalist and researcher specializing in the Middle East and Central Asia. A family representative told Meduza that he is cautious — an “armchair scholar” who dislikes fieldwork.
A friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza that she met him in Israel in the mid-1990s, when she was living there and he was still studying at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She said that after he graduated, Kirpichenok could not find work in his field in Israel and was “very unhappy.”
Kirpichenok, a St. Petersburg native, returned to Russia in the 2000s and inherited an apartment there, she said. During those years, he worked as a tour guide, gave lectures, and wrote articles: “He worked with all kinds of publications and held, I’d say, Trotskyist views. Some minor grassroots activity: tours, and during COVID, he developed routes like ‘Sick Petersburg.’ A kind of intellectual precariat.”
Drawing on his dissertation about Hungarian nationalist movements at the turn of the 20th century, Kirpichenok wrote a book titled Vengriya-1956: drugoy vzglyad (“Hungary-1956: A Different View”). Kirpichenok criticized the 1956 Hungarian uprising, viewing it not as a progressive movement against the Soviet regime but as a far-right conservative revolt.
In recent years, Kirpichenok headed the Slavic studies department at the Center for Arab-Eurasian Studies, which was founded by Amr Abdel-Hamid, an Egyptian journalist, media manager, and former head of Al Jazeera’s Moscow bureau.
He also wrote about the Middle East for the Turkish broadcaster TRT and the Azerbaijani outlet Caliber, sharply criticizing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s actions in Gaza, and its policies toward Palestinians.
In his book Izrail’. Put’ k katastrofe (“Israel: The Road to Catastrophe”), Kirpichenok says Israel is not “the revived state of the Jewish people” but “the last bastion of Western colonialism.”
“Artem never wrote anything that went beyond what he read in the newspaper Haaretz and a couple dozen other sources, like B’Tselem,” his friend said. “I mean, some criticism of the existing regime. Geez, that exists in every country, and it’s a good thing — that’s what the intelligentsia is for.”
She was surprised by the possibility of espionage charges: “He doesn’t have any [classified] information. How would he have access to any?”
Kirpichenok flew to Israel for an academic conference — but officials in the city where it was supposed to take place had never heard of it
Kirpichenok is now being held in a Shin Bet pretrial detention facility in Petah Tikva.
He is alone in a cell where the lights stay on around the clock, with no outdoor exercise and no access to reading or writing materials. “All he can do in his cell is sit or lie down, sleep, or think,” a family representative said.
“Before October 7, 2023, only Arab Muslims were subjected to this kind of repression,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family told Meduza.
A support group of Kirpichenok’s friends believes the international conference may have been a trap set by security services to get the scholar into the country, according to the independent Russian outlet Doxa. Kirpichenok arrived in Israel on August 2 and had planned to leave six days later.
Representatives of Kirpichenok’s family contacted the municipality of the city where the conference was supposedly scheduled to take place, but officials there said no such event had been held. The family said Kirpichenok avoided answering questions about exactly who had invited him to Israel.
Israeli security officers pressured Kirpichenok, according to a family representative
The fourth court hearing in Kirpichenok’s case took place in Ashkelon on Thursday, August 27. The proceedings are closed to the public.
Kirpichenok was brought to court from the pretrial detention facility. Family representatives said he was held in a soundproof glass booth during the hearing. His lawyer, Inna Lebedinskaya-Katz, was unable to speak with her client during the proceedings, a Meduza source said. (Lebedinskaya-Katz declined to comment, citing a court order barring publication of details about Kirpichenok’s case.)
That day, the court extended the gag order on details of Kirpichenok’s case through August 31. A formal declaration of charges — roughly equivalent to an indictment in Russian legal procedure — was due to be filed on September 4. At that point, the defense would be able to access the investigation files, a family representative told Meduza. The family representative expects prosecutors to seek Kirpichenok’s continued detention through the end of the trial.
At the hearing, Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to exclude her client’s confession, arguing that Kirpichenok had been pressured into making it. Israel Shamir, a left-wing Israeli writer and columnist covering the case, said on Telegram that Lebedinskaya-Katz had filed the motion.
Kirpichenok had not been allowed to contact his lawyer, a family representative told Meduza. His only meeting with his defense attorney came on August 23, when he told Lebedinskaya-Katz that he had falsely incriminated himself “under pressure from investigators.”
During that meeting, Kirpichenok, in handcuffs, was held in a glass booth and spoke with his lawyer by phone. He feared the conversation might be monitored and worried that he would “be sent back down to the basement” where the interrogations took place, a family representative told Meduza.
Investigators allegedly threatened to confiscate his apartment in Israel and deport him to Ukraine. “He never supported the ‘special military operation’ that Russia launched, but because he holds left-wing views, he has spoken out against imperialism, including Russian imperialism,” a family representative told Meduza. There is no independent confirmation that investigators pressured Kirpichenok.
At the August 27 hearing, Kirpichenok “looked much worse” than he had when he met with his lawyer. According to Shamir, the defense attorney said: “His face seemed to sag, his eyes were dull, and he could barely smile.”
Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to move Kirpichenok from pretrial detention to house arrest because he has an apartment in Ashkelon, but the judge denied the request, citing the severity of the charges.
Kirpichenok also asked for an interpreter at future hearings — a request that surprised representatives of his family, since he had begun living in Israel as a teenager, served in the Israel Defense Forces, and later graduated from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The lawyer asked the court to allow a psychiatrist to see her client, citing his depressed state and post-traumatic stress disorder.
How Russia reacted to Kirpichenok’s detention
“The irony of Artem’s situation is that he holds two toxic passports. Neither country is particularly eager to stand up for him, you know?” the historian’s friend told Meduza.
Kirpichenok’s support group only recently contacted Russia’s Foreign Ministry, and Russian diplomats “have been emphatic in promising their support,” a family representative told Meduza. But because Kirpichenok also holds Israeli citizenship, Russian Embassy staff have not yet been allowed to see him.
Russia’s ambassador to Israel, Anatoly Viktorov, said the diplomatic mission “had sent a request to the appropriate Israeli authorities.”
Valery Fadeev, head of the Presidential Human Rights Council, sent a letter to Matthew Gillett, chair-rapporteur of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, on August 28. In the letter, Fadeev said: “In Israel, this kind of detention is usually linked to suspected crimes against state security.”
“This suggests that his detention was motivated by [Kirpichenok’s] political views,” the letter says. “Of particular concern is his health: he suffers from hypertension with a risk of retinal detachment, which requires constant medical monitoring.”
The Presidential Human Rights Council called on the United Nations to demand that Israeli authorities clarify the grounds for Kirpichenok’s detention and ensure that he has immediate access to a lawyer and qualified medical care.
Shin Bet had not responded to Meduza’s request for comment as of publication.

SBU exposes Russian spy operating within Ukrainian Armed Forces in Kharkiv
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
One of those detained is a local man who was mobilized into a Ukrainian Territorial Defense brigade. He was working for Russian military intelligence, better known as the GRU, and was passing information to the enemy from "inside" the Ukrainian military.
The investigation established that Russian intelligence recruited the Kharkiv resident through his neighbor, a professor at a Kharkiv university whom the SBU exposed in March this year for adjusting Russian strikes on the city.
After the university lecturer was detained, the suspect, acting on orders from the enemy, joined the Ukrainian military, where he was assigned as a reserve soldier in a reserve company of a combat unit.
There, under the guise of official trips, the agent monitored the locations of Ukrainian air defense and electronic warfare units, as well as defensive fortifications around Kharkiv.
He also marked the locations of local combined heat and power plants and key electrical substations supplying the city and surrounding areas on Google Maps.
The suspect later recruited his unemployed wife to cooperate with the enemy. Initially, she walked around the city to identify locations where Ukrainian troops were based and passed the intelligence to her husband. She later reported directly to her Russian handler.
The man's next assignment was to undergo training as an unmanned systems operator and hand over to Russian intelligence materials obtained during the training.
After completing the courses, the serviceman hoped to receive a promotion to a position in a UAV unit, which would allow him to expand his espionage activities in favor of the aggressor state.
SBU officers exposed the agent couple, documented their criminal activities step by step and detained both suspects: the man during another intelligence-gathering mission and his wife at their place of residence.
During searches, investigators seized 12 smartphones, four laptops and two tablets, which the suspects regularly switched in order to maintain covert communications with the Russian GRU.
SBU investigators notified both detainees that they were suspected of violating Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – high treason committed under martial law.
The suspects are being held in custody without the right to bail. They face life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

Five European nations seek deals to send migrants out of the EU

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

08:34:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Five European nations seek deals to send migrants out of the EU
Five European nations aim to sign deals this year to send migrants without legal residency to countries outside the European Union, they said at a meeting hosted by Denmark on Friday.
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said they had agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with a non-European Union country on return facilities, the latest effort by European nations to reduce immigration.
The countries, known as the Group of Five, did not name the nations they expect to host return centres.
"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year that will enable the establishment of return hubs," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters at a press conference in Copenhagen.
The group, which has held a series of meetings this year, plans to reconvene in Munich, Germany, at the end of September.
The European Parliament in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to set up centres abroad, in what critics say could weaken safeguards for asylum seekers.
HUMAN RIGHTS CONCERNS
The Council of Europe, a non-EU body that promotes human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the continent, in July said return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks", and several other groups have also criticised the plan.
Danish Refugee Council Secretary General Charlotte Slente said it would be better to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which focuses on stricter border screening, faster asylum and return procedures, and expanded digital systems for managing asylum claims.
"Return hubs focus on a small number of returns, they will not stop people from taking even more dangerous routes, and they could violate basic human rights," Slente said.
Denmark expects to be ready to send migrants to the return hub by the end of 2027, Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov said.
"It's a new chance to have a life in a partner country," he said, adding that the five nations would be in dialogue with the UN body, the International Organization for Migration, and the UN Refugee Agency for their next steps.
A UNHCR spokesperson said the agency had not been approached with details of a proposal and could not comment on the arrangements being discussed.

UN approves world map reflecting true size of Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:34:00 UTC
08:34:00 KST

UN approves world map reflecting true size of Africa
September 5, 2026
A yearslong push to change the default view of the Earth came to a vote at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, with 164 countries in favor of a new map, the United States against it and six abstentions.
Known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, the map "offers a more accurate representation of the sizes of continental landmasses and to this end is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," according to the resolution, which was spearheaded by several African countries.
Togo's foreign minister, Robert Dussey, told the UN maps "shape our understanding of the world."
"They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions," he said. "They are, therefore, never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation."
No, Greenland is nowhere near as big as Africa
The resolution pushes for countries to adopt the Equal Earth projection rather than the traditional Mercator projection, which was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
The Mercator projection accurately depicts the shapes and angles of landmasses, necessary for shipping, but distorts their relative sizes.: landmasses near the Earth's poles appear larger while those near the equator look smaller. This makes Greenland appear about as big as Africa, despite the African continent being about 14 times larger.
Togo's Dussey said his country aims to replace the maps used in its schools by the end of the year.
The Mercator projection's use is a result of colonization, Dussey said, adding, "The world is changing. Africa also is changing."
US, China, India, Japan, Mexico and part of EU fit in Africa
France, which co-sponsored the resolution, said on Friday that it would also abandon the Mercator projection.
In that projection, "the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia," while "Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in statement.
"Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," he acknowledged. "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."
In support of the new projection, online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said, "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare."
The UN General Assembly vote is not legally binding and "in no way challenges the use of Mercator projection for maritime and aerial navigation, for which it remains fully suited," the ministry said in a statement.
Equal Earth a 'distraction,' US says
As the only country to vote against the resolution, the United States said the Equal Earth projection pushed an "ideological agenda" and distracted attention from "genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations."
"Instead of focusing on genuine problems... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.
Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Morocco, Serbia and Ukraine abstained from voting on the resolution.

NEW YORK, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks ended lower on Friday as investors raised expectations of an interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve following a surprisingly strong August employment report.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 271.86 points, or 0.51 percent, to 53,414.25. The S&P 500 sank 29.11 points, or 0.38 percent, to 7,718.6. The Nasdaq Composite Index shed 77.07 points, or 0.29 percent, to 26,506.99.
Eight of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the red, with consumer discretionary and health leading the laggards by dropping 1.26 percent and 1.04 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, industrials and technology led the gainers by adding 0.41 percent and 0.23 percent, respectively.
U.S. nonfarm payrolls increased by 162,000 in August, far exceeding the 53,000 expected by economists polled by Dow Jones. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1 percent, as anticipated. Employment figures for June and July were also revised higher.
Following the robust jobs data, traders raised the probability of a rate hike by the Fed at the September meeting to roughly 58 percent, according to CME Group data.
"The August jobs report was stronger than expected, with construction one of the bright spots," said James Knightley, chief international economist at ING. "The stronger number could result in a September rate hike, but we still have next week's inflation numbers."
U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday complained about the selloff in stock markets following the latest jobs report and urged the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates instead.
"Lower the interest rates because the U.S.A. is a much stronger credit than it was just a short time ago! ... We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like 'the old days,'" Trump wrote in a post on social media.
Trump's resumption of a pressure campaign on the Fed and a threat to halt trade with some trading partners also weighed on market sentiment.
Trump asked the Fed Board to "get smart" and be "patriots" for a change and threatened to halt trade with countries with which the United States runs a trade deficit.
In individual stock moves, Lululemon plunged more than 17 percent after the athleisure apparel company cut its revenue and profit guidance and reported a decline in second-quarter revenue. Tesla fell nearly 6 percent after the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a probe to examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying its new Cybercab model and related issues. ■

In Bulgaria, the skeleton of a man was found who may have hidden from an attack in a huge jar 1,600 years ago
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:23:18 EEST

In Bulgaria, the skeleton of a man was found who may have hidden from an attack in a huge jar 1,600 years ago
Kyiv • UNN
In Deultum, a man's skeleton was found in a dolium with weapons. He may have hidden during an attack when the city was engulfed in flames.
Archaeologists discovered the remains of a man inside a large storage vessel—a dolium—at the site of the ancient Roman city of Deultum in southeastern Bulgaria. Scientists presume that he may have climbed inside it to escape an attack. Live Science reports this, UNN writes.
Details
Two iron knives and a belt were found next to the man. One knife remained tucked into the belt, while the second lay between his legs, as if the man had been ready to defend himself.
In the 4th–5th centuries, the Romans in Deultum confronted East Germanic tribes and the Huns. Around the dolium that was found, archaeologists discovered traces of a large-scale fire—ash, charcoal, blackened walls, melted glass, coins, and the burned bones of domestic animals.
Archaeologist Lyudmil Vagalinski of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences presumes that, before the attack, residents may have driven livestock inside the fortifications. Since a layer of ash also lay beneath the man's remains, he likely hid in the vessel after the fire had already begun.
After the attack, the city's residents dismantled and leveled the ruins of the tower, then arranged a new, higher floor level above them. It was beneath this floor that the man's remains were preserved for about 1,600 years.

The head of Memorial, Russia’s Nobel Peace Prize-winning rights group, has told AFP she fears a fresh crackdown after September’s legislative elections, with more people arrested and sent to fight in Ukraine.
Speaking in an exclusive interview in Amsterdam, Elena Zhemkova also vowed to keep up the fight for human rights in Russia, despite her group being declared illegal and herself forced into exile.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, I think that now everything is getting worse, but not so fast,” the 65-year-old said. “But after the elections, there will be a very sharp deterioration.”
Last month, Russia’s Supreme Court banned the only anti-war party, Yabloko, from running in the elections, where opposition to Russian President Vladimir Putin will be minimal.
“More people will be arrested for insignificant things and sent to prison. They are interested in sending people to prison. For them, prison is a way to the front,” she said, referring to the main line of combat in Ukraine.
“The situation at the front is very fragile.”
Memorial was founded in the late 1980s to document victims of Soviet-era political repression during which millions of people perished in the Gulag penal system.
Earlier this year, a court labelled the group “extremist”, making its supporters subject to prosecution and effectively outlawing any cooperation with it.
Will Russia Honor Zelensky’s Proposed Truce for US Envoys?
Memorial group received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022 – months after Russia launched its offensive on Ukraine – alongside jailed Belarusian activist Ales Bialiatski and Ukraine’s Centre for Civil Liberties.
Zhemkova herself has fled the country and keeps the organization running from Berlin where she acts as executive director.
“The more they try to silence or erase the name of Memorial in Russia, the louder it will sound outside Russia,” she promised.
Zhemkova was speaking on the sidelines of an exhibition entitled “Artists Against the Kremlin: Memory Remains”, at the De Balie cultural centre in Amsterdam.
The exhibition features work from artists forced into exile, silenced or persecuted and Zhemkova said it was a good example of Memorial’s work outside Russia.
“If we don’t understand and take lessons from the past, we will repeat mistakes and our present and future will be terrible,” she said.
‘Sophisticated propaganda’
With Russia apparently escalating its offensive in Ukraine and testing Western unity with “hybrid” attacks in Europe, Zhemkova urged a strong response.
When Europe hesitates, Putin “sees this as weakness,” she said.
“And for Putin, what does weakness mean? It means that victory is around the corner and we need to push further,” said Zhemkova.
She highlighted what she described as a “huge repressive mechanism” in Russia and “very powerful and sophisticated propaganda.”
She pointed to a plan to replace Moscow’s Gulag museum with a new exhibition documenting Nazi crimes against the Soviet Union during World War II, the latest move in a crackdown on institutions documenting Soviet-era repression.
“It’s only a part of what they do,” she said, referring to the museum.
“Unfortunately, the process of rewriting history is much bigger, much deeper. It’s also the destruction of monuments,” said Zhemkova.
The human rights leader said she felt safe in Berlin, despite being distanced from friends and home and her family, which she said was now disbursed over eight countries.
“That’s the reason why our meeting point is Zoom every week,” she laughed.
And despite the situation in Russia seeming to get worse by the day, she said she still feels hopeful.
“We are trying to explain that not everybody turned into criminals. That there is another Russia. Even now,” she told AFP.
She said what gives her hope is the bravery of her fellow campaigners and the creative protests of artists such as those exhibiting in Amsterdam.
The objects in the exhibition often tell a sad and tragic story of repression, she said.
“And on the other hand, the other side of the object is always a story about solidarity, love, friendship, family.”

Tunisia arrests journalist Mohamed Yousfi amid crackdown on critics

Tunisian police have arrested prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi, a vocal critic of President Kais Saied’s rule, the head of the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists told Reuters.
According to local journalists, police said that Yousfi, the editor-in-chief of the investigative news website Al-Qatiba, was brought in on Friday for questioning. The focus of the investigation is unknown.

Tunisian authorities have not yet commented on the arrest, which is the latest in a string of prosecutions of media figures and activists in Tunisia this year.

Prominent journalist Zied el-Heni was sentenced in May to one year in prison, while broadcaster Mourad Zeghidi and political commentator Borhen Bsaies were sentenced in January to three and a half years.
Rights groups have warned of a widening crackdown on independent voices in Tunisia under Saied, whose rule has dismantled democratic safeguards, enabling authorities to pursue journalists and critics more aggressively.

“The ruling confirms that the judiciary is not independent,” said Haifa Chebbi, a lawyer whose father, opposition leader Najib Chebbi, was among those sentenced to 12 years.
Tunisia’s Minister of Justice Leila Jaffel said the defendants sought to destabilise the country.

DNA of a dangerous virus that raged thousands of years ago was found in medieval manuscripts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:18:49 EEST
08:18:49 KST

DNA of a dangerous virus that raged thousands of years ago was found in medieval manuscripts
Kyiv • UNN
Scientists discovered sheep pox DNA in ancient parchments and traced its history back 3,700 years. The virus was found in medieval manuscripts.
Scientists have discovered traces of sheep pox virus DNA on the pages of ancient parchment manuscripts and traced its history back at least 3,700 years. University College Dublin reported this, UNN writes.
Details
Researchers analyzed parchment made from animal skins and found that it can preserve genetic traces of ancient pathogens.
The recovery of ancient pathogen DNA has completely changed our understanding of infectious diseases in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve the DNA of animal pathogens
The virus was found in a 1,000-year-old Gospel
Traces of sheep pox were found, in particular, in the 1,000-year-old illuminated manuscript "The York Gospels," as well as in an early English dictionary known as the "Corpus Glossary."
The virus's DNA was also found in parchment made from calfskin and goatskin. Scientists suggest that this may have occurred through interspecies transmission of the virus or contamination during the manufacture of the parchment.
According to the researchers, libraries and archives around the world may contain similar genetic traces of ancient outbreaks of animal diseases. The study's findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

In 2027, Ukraine will receive new 155 mm &quot;Marta&quot; self-propelled howitzers to replace Soviet and Western artillery

In 2027, Ukraine will receive new 155 mm "Marta" self-propelled howitzers to replace Soviet and Western artillery
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine plans to receive 155 mm "Marta" self-propelled howitzers in 2027, funded by Germany. They will replace some of the Soviet and Western artillery.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces are expected to receive new 155-mm self-propelled artillery systems called "Marta" in 2027, the production of which was financed by Germany. Defense Express reports this, citing a representative of the Kramatorsk Heavy Machine Tool Manufacturing Plant, UNN writes.
Details
"Marta" is a version of the "Bohdana" self-propelled artillery system with a 39-caliber barrel and a Mercedes-Benz Zetros chassis. The project is already being implemented, and the system itself began testing in March 2026.
According to the military’s plan, the new self-propelled artillery systems are to gradually replace some Western artillery systems with short barrels, whose maintenance is complicated and expensive. In addition, "Marta" is planned to be used instead of Soviet 122-mm and 152-mm systems.
Defense Express notes that this includes, in particular, American M109s, Soviet 2S3 "Akatsiya" and 2S1 "Gvozdika" systems, as well as Czechoslovak ShKH vz. 77 DANA systems. At the same time, the final list of systems to be replaced will depend on the structure of the artillery units of the Defense Forces.
Germany financed the production of "Marta" in December 2025. According to Defense Express’s assessment, deliveries in 2027 appear realistic, given the need to complete testing of the new version of the self-propelled artillery system.
Systems from the "Bohdana" family, according to the publication, already account for about 70% of Ukraine’s artillery.
